Employees in the North and in isolated posts receive certain tax exemption from employer benefits under two remission orders. subtopic: S O. 22 HEALTH NEED TO CONSIDER RISKS AND COST OF BREAST IMPLANTS
S O. 22 HEALTH NEED TO CONSIDER RISKS AND COST OF BREAST IMPLANTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 wish to raise an important question in the House today which concerns over 17,000 Canadian women, including 7,000 Quebec women, every year. I was made aware of the issue by an eminent researcher at Laval University, Dr. Robert Gui-doin. I am referring to a number of studies that were made on breast implant devices, studies the Department of National Health and Welfare does not seem to take very seriously. According to the analyses, the health of women who resort to this type of operation is at risk. However, no provision has been made by the Department to monitor the silicone implants being used. Research has shown that within two years after the operation, the implants break up or weep, thus causing considerable damage to the tissues of the patient, who then has to undergo a new operation.
In addition to the danger to the health of women who are obliged to resort to this kind of operation, we must realize that although the initial operation is not covered by provincial health insurance plans, the second operation that may be required owing to unsatisfactory implants costs the various provincial governments a lot of money. When the operation is redone, the patient's hospital costs are paid by provincial health insurance plans. Because this serious problem is costing Canadians money and especially because of the health risk to over 17,000 Canadian women every year, I consider this a very important issue and I feel it should be examined and regulated without delay.

subsubtopic: ANNIVERSARY OF HALIFAX EXPLOSION-CALL FOR INCREASED AID FOR ELDERLY SURVIVORS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 68 years ago this month, on December 6, 1917, an explosion occurred in Halifax Harbour which rocked all of Canada and all of the world. Over 2,000 people were killed when two ships collided in Halifax Harbour, and many thousands of others were injured and maimed for life. All Nova Scotians, and I think all Canadians, should remember this terrible event in the light of current events across the world of equal magnitude in terms of disaster.
This was not merely an event in past history. There are many survivors of that explosion in Canada today. I want to take the opportunity once again to remind the Canadian Pension Commission and the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Hees), who now administer the funds available to these people, to take another look at the situation to see whether we can increase the aid provided to the survivors of the Halifax explosion. Most of them are in their very late years, 80 and 90 years of age. The small settlements they received and the minor payments they receive on a monthly basis should be increased now that they are in their senior days. I ask all Members of the House to support that action.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member is absolutely right. Poaching, especially underground organized poaching, is becoming a serious problem in our national parks right across the country. -putting the Bill through, and having had to entertain the delightful questions of the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin) and a host of Conservative Members, one might have thought we had left that interesting piece of legislation behind us. However, I want to say, once again, that this shows the incredible foresight of the legislation. We built into the Act a requirement, an opportunity, for Members of Parliament on the moving of a motion to use a parliamentary day to examine the progress of the Act, and, in particular, to look at some of the outstanding issues which still give rise to debate and which are still of interest to members of the western Canadian farming community, as well as those in other parts of Canada.
I think it should be pointed out that it was our caucus which initiated this debate. It was our caucus which organized the gathering of sufficient signatures to ensure that Parliament would have an opportunity to bring this review, this re-examination, if you will, forward. We did this because we feel that it is one of the most important and significant pieces of legislation which we passed during our time in office. We feel that it has established the groundwork, the framework, for the major development and new direction in constructing modern transportation facilities for the movement of our major commodities.
Since the present Parliament is very much seized day by day with questions of international trade, I wish to remind Hon. Members that in western Canada we do not trade internationally if we do not have an effective transportation system. If we cannot move our grain, our potash, our cattle, our coal or our lumber to market then we do not trade. The question which

faced our Government at the time was: How can we provide the insurance in order that we can have the most up-to-date, modern and effective transportation system so that there will never again be questions about disruptions, stalemates or any form of dislocation of the transportation system when it comes to convincing foreign customers that we can deliver on time?
It is worth noting that the type of commitments which were made during that period of time are now being fulfilled. In looking at the statistics which are at least made available to us publicly, one sees that they point out that the two railroad companies will be spending close to $1.3 billion, or perhaps even $1.4 billion, between them on the modernization of the rail system. In terms of my best estimate, that will create close to 4,000 jobs-

Member for Regina West should know enough about the railway business to know that when we go down from the shipping of 30 million tons to 23 million tons, due to weather and lack of cargo, it obviously takes fewer people to do it. I presume that is within the grasp of his knowledge.
The fact of the matter is that in terms of the basic objective, which was to unleash the type of capital expenditures which would bring the railway system into a modern, contemporary format, it is being fulfilled. It is providing a lead in terms of establishing a number of new transportation technologies as well. We would like to hear from the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski) with respect to whether or not it is being fulfilled and whether or not the types of powers which are within the Act to provide for enforcement of those requirements are being applied.
From the ostensible public evidence which we have been able to gather-and I refer to two reports published in 1985- the Canadian Pacific Railway will be spending something in the order of $600 million, as well as going ahead with its commitment on the Rogers Pass. According to the figures we have, the CNR will be spending $600 million this year in capital expenditures and it will be making purchases of more than $400 million. The jobs created will be something in the order of 2,000 in construction and 2,500 for suppliers. We are speaking in terms of 4,000 or 5,000 additional jobs being created by these major expenditures.
Because I can recall quite vividly the derision with which certain members of the Conservative Party treated the other side of our western grain proposal with respect to the encouragement of new investment on the part of western businesses through the Western Industrial Development Fund as a way of

December 4, 1985

diversifying the western economy, I would like to remind the House that these Members said that it would never work. They said that it would be nothing but a wasteful spending of money. I read with a great deal of bemusement, interest and, of course, happiness, the glowing public relations statements and releases put out by the Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer), the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens) and various Ministers from the western provinces announcing how, under their generous program called the Western Industrial Development Fund, they are now giving grants to groups of Hutterites to start pork-producing plants and money to this factory or that group of farm organizations. In other words, all of a sudden the Government has found out that that program has produced a very helpful and useful set of incentives to provide assistance to western businesses, farm organizations and farmers so they can begin to develop capital value and added value processing of agricultural products. I have some of the press releases and I will not take the time of the House to read them. For the life of me I do not see what it has to do with agriculture, but that Department is now administering that fund, and that is its business.
I know there is a great fondness among Hon. Members opposite to claim, of course, that everything the Grits did was terrible, but if that was the case, why do they take such delight and satisfaction in utilizing those kinds of programs which we had the foresight to put in place to help western farm organizations? I think it only worth noting-because I am sure we will hear from those Hon. Members in the course of debate about what a terrible thing this was-and I want to make sure we have it on the record, that the Government is sure taking full advantage of all of the expenditures and programs initiated by the Liberal Government.
I was quite amused the other day when we heard the Minister for the Canadian Wheat Board speak in the House. The Hon. Member for Portage-Marquette stood in his place and bragged about all the assistance which was going to western farmers. But what did he point to? He pointed to the Western Grain Transportation Act, the Western Crop Insurance Program and the Western Stabilization Program. These were all programs which had been introduced and passed by the previous Liberal administration. That was his record of assistance and it was all being delivered under legislation and allocations of money which had been brought forward by previous Governments. I do not mind his bragging. However, he was not quite charitable enough to mention that those programs had nothing to do with his Government, that those were all previous initiatives and pieces of legislation. But I suppose we can forgive the Minister for the Canadian Wheat Board for having certain lapses of memory from time to time. I believe it is useful to have this kind of debate so that we can at least set the record straight. We can say that, because of the foundation which was laid by the previous Government, the construction and development of a new system is in place.
This debate is far more important, however, than taking note of what has happened. I feel it is also time that the Conservatives in this House stood up and be counted. The time has finally come for Hon. Members of Parliament from Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba and British Columbia to get their act together. I went back with some degree of historical interest to read the debates which took place in this House. During those debates there were at least 14 or 15 different positions taken. I give some credit to Hon. Members opposite, they were very skillful in never making a decision as to where they stood on crucial questions such as methods of payment.

In the meantime, some very serious problems have occurred. While the Minister of Transport was whittling his time away, the Government of Alberta was bringing in a major top-up subsidy for its livestock producers in order to provide compensation, and that has created a very major distortion for livestock producers in Saskatchewan and Manitoba. That is a program which is creating very serious dislocations for the livestock producers. It is subverting what I believe those who are concerned about agriculture would try to achieve, and that is, to establish some basic national standard in these programs so that the benefits in the agricultural field do not just go to the wealthy provinces which have full treasuries and can afford additional top-up subsidies. That is what the Minister of Transport is allowing to happen at the present time. The Alberta program is creating a serious disparity in the livestock markets in western Canada. No one has seen any form of action, response or indication of how this Government intends to deal with that major change and dislocation in the livestock market.
Yet the answers are at hand, Mr. Speaker. The Minister could make changes at any time. He does not have to slough it off to another committee. He does not have to wait, as he said, and extend and prolong the period in which the reviews will take place and new legislation will be passed. He knows that there is a very serious problem. It is the kind of problem we saw two weeks ago when the Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster), I and other Hon. Members spent two weeks of our time in western Canada talking to farmers about the agricultural crisis. We spent two weeks travelling to every small community throughout the prairie Provinces and British Columbia. We discovered that those farmers see a number of serious transportation problems which are not being addressed.
In addition to the livestock problems produced by the Alberta subsidy program, there are major problems now being faced on the branch line rehabilitation program. The senior officials of the Saskatchewan pools are saying that the indecision of the Government of Canada on the branch lines is causing major uncertainty and, therefore, forestalling major investments by the pools in new facilities. I want to remind Hon. Members of this House that while we were still in Government, we established a totally and complete rehabilitation program for all branch lines which were in the system. ments with the railroads, the money had been allocated, and every branch line had a formula applied to it by which it would be upgraded. Members of the largest Wheat Growers Association in Western Canada are saying that the future of the branch lines is uncertain and unsure and that this is causing a major detraction. After the Government said it was dedicated to economic renewal and made all those bright promises and major commitments, why is nothing happening? What is the reason for the inaction in this area?
Let us look at the commitments made with regard to the ports of Canada which we use to provide an effective system for moving our grain. It is now December 4. It is obvious that the confusion exists not only in the farm circles, but in the mind of the Member who was the architect of this debate and of this legislation. We must go back to basics and talk about that which has triggered this debate.
The Western Grain Transportation Act is an Act to facilitate the transportation, shipping and handling of western grain and to amend certain Acts in consequence thereof. In Section 62 there is a requirement for a review. Section 62.(1) reads:
The Minister shall-
It does not say "may" but "shall". It continues:
-during the 1985-86 crop year, in consultation with such system participants and other persons as the Minister deems appropriate, carry out a comprehensive review of the operation of this Act and its effects on the transportation, shipping and handling of grain, including an evaluation of-
This is not willy-nilly. This is a statutory requirement. It continues:
(a)	the appropriateness of the provisions of this Act respecting the apportionment of cost increases between the Government of Canada and the shippers of grain in respect of the period beyond the 1985-86 crop year, having regard to trends in the incomes of the producers, the relationship between transportation costs borne by the producers and the price of grain and the economic position of the producers relative to other major sectors of the national economy and to any other factors that the Minister considers relevant;
We now come to the pertinent paragraph which reads:
(b)	recommendations referred to in subsection (5);
Subsection (5) refers to the Hall Commission report. Subsection (2) says:
The Governor in Council shall, on or before April 1, 1984, appoint a committee consisting of not less than three and not more than five persons who have expertise in matters affected by this Act and represent various regional interests.
December 4, 1985

Subsection (3) reads:
The committee shall examine all matters that, in its opinion, pertain to the method of payment in respect to grain transportation that would be the most conducive to agricultural development in Canada.
Section 62(4) goes on to outline the powers of the commission under Part I of the Inquiries Act.
We come to Section 62(5) which states:
The committee shall, on or before March 31, 1985, make a report to the Minister containing its recommendations pertaining to the method referred to in subsection (3) and the Minister shall cause a copy of the report to be laid before Parliament on any of the first 15 days that either House of Parliament sits after the report has been made to the Minister.
Section 62(6) provides the opportunity to trigger the debate on the recommendations of the Hall Report. However, here we have a situation where the Hon. Member has triggered a debate on the Hall Report while the mandatory review process is going on. There are many deficiencies in this piece of legislation and the Hon. Member has referred to them. This is clearly one of those deficiencies.
The Government, in its haste to pass the Bill, has drawn Parliament into this very difficult web. The slammer was laid on us on November 3, 1983. There were some 75 clauses in the Bill. During the report stage Parliament did not have a chance to consider Clause 33. So everything beyond Clause 33 was not debated by this Parliament.
I should also say for the benefit of the House that the Government moved closure after two days of debate at second reading and moved the Bill to committee. It was in a serious haste to ram the Bill through at all cost, without due consideration. Essentially, we are caught up in a process created by the legislative edict that was not clearly thought out. I am quite surprised that the Hon. Member would tread into this kind of debate given the fact that it is complicated by his own legislative measure. I must say that it really is a bit of a joke. The joke is on the Member who claims credit for this piece of legislation. He is also taking credit for triggering the debate.
The elements of the debate are enshrined in Section 62. That brings us to where we are today. Section 62(6) states:
Where, within sixty sitting days after a report has been laid before a House of Parliament under subsection (5), fifteen Senators or thirty Members of the House of Commons, as the case may be, by notice in writing addressed to the Speaker, request that the report be debated, the Speaker shall, as soon as possible thereafter, assign a sitting day of the House that is not later than sixty sitting days after the request is made, for the report to be debated and on the assigned day the subject-matter of the report shall be subject to debate without interruption . . .
That brings us to where we are today. It is quite obvious that the Hon. Member must feel very uncomfortable about it because he touched on the recommendations of the Hall Report in a very superficial way. I do not know whether he has read the report, but he did not even as much as tell the House what the major recommendations of the Hall Report were. I thought he would have done that.

For the benefit of the viewing public I thought it might be worth his while.
We have a report before us that recommends that the Crow benefit be paid to the producers in the form of a grain transportation refund, based on net grain sales. I believe the Hon. Member knows that some people in the agricultural community agree with it and others do not.
Members of the Hall Commission went out across the country to debate and obtain further views on their report. I had a discussion with them the other day. There are some major concerns about this proposal and some major concerns have been expressed about the workings of the legislation. Of course, this is compounded by the review process which is also currently taking place under the provisions of Section 62(1), which must consider, among other things, the recommendations of the Hall Report. That is a statutory requirement. It must consider the advisability of inadvisability, and whether these particular recommendations will work. It must consider what effect it will have on grain producers, what effect it will have to the value added, what effect it will have on agriculture across the country. It must consider Quebec's views and Ontario's views. That process is taking place now. How can we realistically engage in an enlightened debate when that review process is taking place and we are caught up in the mandatory legislative review process? The answer is that we cannot.
It is so typical of the Liberal half-baked scheme. It is due to this sort of half-baked philosophy that the Liberals are not in office today. The people of Canada became sick and tired of it. That is why they were kicked out of office. The Liberals are trying to recover some political losses through a political manoeuvre here today.
The ongoing review which I am talking about must be carried out. It is not discretionary but clearly mandatory as enshrined in the Bill. It must be carried out in the crop year 1985-1986.
The Hon. Member says that I am dragging out that process. I detect some negativism about the review by the Grain Transportation Administrator, and it is rather strange because we have engaged an appointee of the Hon. Member's Government to do the job. In any event, we have asked that the report be forthcoming as quickly as possible, hopefully in February or March and surely before the end of the crop year.
On August 2 we requested the Grain Transportation Administrator to conduct this review. The terms of reference include the provisions outlined in Section 62 of the Act. It includes the method of payment. It was stated in a letter transmitted to Mr. Horner that: "Section 62(1 )(b) requires that the review re-evaluate the recommendations of the Hall Commission of Inquiry into the method of payment of the Crow benefit". The letter goes on to state: "As you are aware, the Hall Committee established by my predecessor in 1984 submited its report to me in April and has recommended a pay the producer option". I asked that, in the context of the review of the WGTA and the possible future amendments, he evaluate its recommendations, guided by the need for the development of payment that is conducive to agricultural development

December 4, 1985
Crow Benefit Payment
across Canada. A number of additional items were included which emanated from various producers and producer groups about the deficiencies in the provisions of this piece of legislation.
Therefore, consistent with the legislation, we are not only exercising the mandatory authority, but some discretionary authority as well. A very important fact that the review Committee is discovering is that this is the first time that a review is being conducted in a public way. Invitations are sent out to individual producers. We are not dealing only with producer organizations and we are not dealing behind closed doors.
As a matter of fact, in the letter of reference, 1 indicated: "I want to advise you that I attach significant importance to providing adequate opportunity for public meetings and hearings, as well as informal discussions". Many farmers are surprised by this because they were shut out of the process during the Gilson and Hall committees. They said that it is the first time that they, as individual producers, have been able to come forth in the public way and talk to anyone about this legislation which has a very major bearing on their economic welfare.
Quite clearly they were left out of this process. The Hon. Member for Regina West is aware of the difficulty we had in extending the committee hearings to allow producers to come forth. The Government even put time limits on the committee hearings. Therefore, we are doing some of the dirty work that should have been done by that administration when it was taking the Bill through its stages.
Quite frankly, I believe that this process is not only needed but is very healthy because neither Gilson nor Hall provided this opportunity to allow individual producers to express their concerns and feelings about what this legislation should be doing.
Ten meetings have been held: two in Manitoba, four in Saskatchewan, three in Alberta and one in the Peace River bloc. Three public meetings have been held in each of the prairie provinces at Winnipeg, Calgary, Regina and Saskatoon. In British Columbia, there were private meetings with 11 organizations, including the Government of British Columbia, longshoremen, the Grain Workers Union, the Port of Vancouver, terminal operators, the Chamber of Shipping and B.C. Rail.
In Alberta, there were two public meetings, at which the Government of Alberta, the Alberta Wheat Pool and Unifarm appeared. Unifarm is one of the major farm organizations in Alberta. It held 46 meetings throughout Alberta to talk about the workability of this particular piece of legislation, and it reported to the ongoing review process. Also the NFU appeared. It was the first time that the NFU ever appeared before a body which was talking about the Western Grain Transportation Act. Also the Christian Farmers Federation, the Alberta Cattle Feeders Association, the Alberta Feed Grain Users Association, the Western Barley Growers Association, the Alberta Soft Wheat Growers Association, the Alberta Cattle Commission and the Alberta Grain Commission appeared.
The following appeared before the Manitoba public meeting: the Government of Manitoba, the CNR, Manitoba Pool Elevators, Manitoba Cattle Feeders Association, Dominion Malt, Canada Malt and the UGG.
They not only confined their meetings to western Canada. They held meetings on November 28 and November 29 in Toronto and have set a meeting for December 11 in Montreal. They are getting some excellent feedback from the grass roots as to what is wrong with the legislation and what needs to be done. There are many inequities and many anomalies. The Hon. Member outlined a number of the issues to which we took exception in 1983. We corrected some, and we will correct more. However, we dealt with a volume cap, with improved producer representation, with a freight rate ceiling and with the inclusion of B.C. Rail. All those things were not done when the former Government was in power. We are making progress. There is no question about that.
It is fair to say that more needs to be done. There still are anomalies. As I said, at the present time there is no clear consensus with respect to the method of payment. There is no clear consensus in western Canada. Certainly there is no clear consensus across the country.
The following organizations support payments to railways: Manitoba Pool Elevators, Alberta Wheat Pool, Saskatchewan Wheat Pool. Coop Federee, L'Union des Producteurs Agricoles, Saskatchewan Association of Rural Municipalities, Canadian Dehydrators Association and the National Farmers Union.
The following organizations support the grain transportation refund: United Grain Growers, Alberta Grain Commission, Alberta Grain Commission, Alberta Cattle Commission, The Grain Rate Reform Committee, Manitoba Farm Business Association, Government of British Columbia, agricultural industry groups in British Columbia, the Government of Alberta, the Government of Ontario, various Ontario industry groups and the Maritime Farmers Council. A number of organizations clearly support the producer option, whatever it might be. It has not been clearly defined, but there is no question that more needs to be done. There is discrimination in the way in which the Act is working now.
For example, to move grain into Vancouver for export, it costs producers $5.75 per tonne to ship it. However, if that same grain is going into the interior of British Columbia for the purpose of feeding livestock it costs $32.79 per tonne. That is a clear inequity and anomaly if we want to improve our ability to value add and to process more of those products in Canada.
There is concern about the level of the safety net, about inflation, about variable rates, about what improvements must be made to improve the system, and whether we should rationalize and consolidate more. We must control costs.
December 4, 1985

We are looking at a number of pilot projects in which we can experiment and innovate with regard to branch line operations, those branch lines destined for abandonment. Shortly we will be announcing a number of pilot projects such as off-line trucking, straight trucking, short-line railway options and road-rail option.
I am pleased to note that those people who are knowledgeable and part of the grain handling, producing and transporting industry recognize that we must take steps to improve the efficiency of the system and to bring down the over-all cost. Mr. Ted Turner was quoted in the November 21 edition of the Western Producer. When speaking to his delegate body, he said:
The many economic forces bearing on our present structure simply dictate that further consolidation is necessary if we are to maintain an economically viable operation and keep charges at reasonable levels.
Wally Madill, Chief Excecutive Officer of the Alberta Wheat Pool, is credited with stating the following to that delegate body on November 16:
It will be necessary for it to offer leaner and more variable services to its roughly 60,000 members to survive in the more competitive industry.
Of course he was referring to the Alberta Wheat Pool. I could not agree with those people more. The long-term future of the industry will depend upon a reliable and efficient grain handling and transportation operation. Of course, many people wonder whether the payment to railways option is the best way to go in terms of improving that efficiency.

I will be moving an amendment in a few minutes. He could have and should have moved a motion concerning the report, which is the object of this debate. The number one recommendation in the report was that the $658.6 million of Government contributions under the safety net provisions of the Western Grain Transportation Act should be paid directly to producers in the Canadian Wheat Board designated area. However, the legislation seen through Parliament by the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry indicates that the payments should go to the railroads. I would have thought that he would have moved a motion today indicating that the legislation which he brought before Parliament would continue to say that the payments should go to the railroads. That is not what he did. He, as was the case with the Minister of Transport, talked about everything else but the method of payment and what was in the report which is under debate. Mr. Speaker, if you are going to be something, be something, and if you are something, say so. The Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry is running away from deeds of his own doing. I cannot say a heck of a lot more for the Progressive Conservative Party. It was all for keeping the Crow rate. My goodness, they were so good about keeping the Crow rate in 1982, 1983 and even in 1984 until the election was over. They were for keeping the Crow, restoring the Crow, freezing the Crow, et cetera, ad nauseam. Both these outfits are like the girls at Jarvis and Queen. They work both sides of the street.
The issue is the Hall Report and the method of payment. There is a Hall number one and a Hall number two. He really is in second place. Hall number one states and I quote:
If once tampering with the statutory rate is accepted or condoned or as an item on the bargaining table, all will be lost. For once the subject is on the bargaining table, it will be only a matter of time until it is lost step by step. There is no position to take except to adhere through thick and thin that the Crow Rate is not bargainable.
That is Mr. Justice Emmett Hall, who can hardly be called a raving socialist. We have agreed with that from day one. We stick to it to this day and will do so for many more days to come.
If there is any change in the method of payment to the producers instead of the railroads, the complete undoing in transportation costs to western grain producers will have been accomplished. I listened to the spokesman for the Liberal

Party today. About the only major thing on which we agreed with him in the legislation in 1983 was the method of payment. The Hon. Member knows that we supported him on that. It was about the only major item. He had an opportunity today to say so and he had an opportunity to move a motion to that effect. However, he failed to do so. Me thinks he is chickening out.
Let us take a look at the pros and cons of the method of payment. I want to say something for the benefit of my livestock producing friends in Alberta. Because of all the difficulties they are having with regard to the price of their product, they continue to take it out on their neighbours, the grain producers. There is something about those who would beggar thy neighbour. The difficulty of the livestock producers does not lie with the grain producers. It never did lie with the Crow rate. However, it did lie with a lot of liars who were trying to blame somebody else for their own difficulties.
Cheap grain means cheap livestock. When you have cheap grain, you have more livestock producers. Livestock prices then go down even more. One would think that the Cattlemen's Association and the Alberta Livestock Commission would learn a little from history. Every time our grain producers have been in trouble and increased their livestock production, livestock prices fell. They were all in trouble together. It has happened repeatedly. I am sick and tired of those who say: "Leave us the tree and open market. Leave us to the market-place and market forces".
As soon as they are in trouble, as soon as market forces kick them in the head and the so-called free enterprise system lets them down, who is first to Ottawa looking for a hand-out? I remember the feedlot operators and the Cattlemen's Association coming here in 1969 and 1970. Who were the first with their hands out? They were the ones who wanted the free and open market. As soon as they got it in spades, who was the first to ask Parliament to bail them out?
The Crow rate was a part of the bargain for western Canada. It has little if anything to do with the price of hogs or cattle. It never has. It had to do with a bargain between the people of Canada and the railroads of Canada. It had to do with Canada and Canadian grain producers being able to export their grain and provide for their own needs. It took into account our geography and costs of transportation so that we could compete in export markets without transportation being a handicap and so that we could provide each other anywhere in this country with grain requirements, whether for human beings or animals, at a reasonable cost. The very essence of the statutory grain rates was to try to treat one another reasonably well and equitably, no matter whether you are a farmer or a livestock producer anywhere in Canada. Paying the producer instead of the railroads the $658 million means lower feed grain prices for our grain producers in western Canada. That might be nice in the minds of those on the Alberta Livestock Commission. However, it is not nice in the minds of the grain producers of the three prairie provinces. It might be nice for some big wheel ranchers in southern Alberta and southern Saskatchewan, but they are not that many in number.
What we have here in support of payment to the railroads and not the producers are the overwhelming majority of the grain producers in western Canada. The Minister of Transport recognizes that. It is not only the three prairie pools, but the Government of Manitoba, the Saskatchewan Association of Rural Municipalities, and the cow-calf operators in Saskatchewan. Something in the area of 80 per cent or more of the grain producers have decided and have said repeatedly how they want these payments to be made. Instead, we get a whole bunch of other outfits.
There is the Government of British Columbia, the coal association, the mining association, B.C. Forest Products and the Canadian Chamber of Commerce. There is a list as long as your arm. They demanded an end to the Crow rate and not a damn one of of them grows a bushel of wheat. They were great with their advice about what should be done to the other guy. The overwhelming amount of evidence in support for retaining the Crow rate and maintaining the payments to the railroads so that we would have some control over the operations and efficiency of the railways is endorsed in overwhelming numbers by those who produce the product, the grain producers of the three prairie provinces.
I appreciate that the Minister of Transport will be reluctant today to say whether he supports continuing the payments to the railroads or charging it to the farmers. I understand that. There is a terrible inequity in the price per tonne of export grain and feed grain in British Columbia. However, the Minister has the tools to cure that. There is no use getting up here and crying about it. I know that his problem is money. He needs the support of all his back-bench colleagues when dealing with the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson). We will back him up on that. He will have no problem with us. His problem is with his own guys. If he really wants to do something and if he wants to adhere to what he and his Party said prior to September of 1984, he will, during the next session of Parliament or sometime early in the new year, bring in legislation to repeal the whole damn Bill and restore the statutory grain rates. At the very minimum, he will give us a new statutory grain rate, which is the rate that is in effect for the current crop year. If he wants to do that, we will support him.
The method of payment is the crucial issue before us today. How much time do I have left, Mr. Speaker?

The payment to the railways exists for one main reason. It is a payment which has existed since 1983 to provide for the most efficient and best transportation system possible in Canada. That transportation system is not only for grain. To hear all the arguments against the Crow rate and all the arguments against payments to the railways, one would think that this is some kind of a hand-out, gift, subsidy, charity or welfare payment to the grain producers of western Canada. It is nothing more than a continuation of what was begun in 1881. It is a transportation subsidy, not a grain subsidy.
That transportation subsidy is not only for the movement of grain, it is for the movement of coal, potash, sulphur, lumber products, automobiles from Japan, automobiles from Oshawa and all the general commodities. We did not build a railway simply to move grain. We did not rebuild it, reduce grades and put in tunnels just on account of the grain producers.
Why are the grain producers being picked on and pointed out as being the villains in the piece? It is a transportation subsidy. Therefore the payments must continue to go to the railways. If they do, we have muscle to make the railways not only rebuild but perform. Sending the payment to the grain farmers leaves the railways with other choices. We could lose

another 2,000 miles of branch lines. The producers have to buy bigger trucks. In fact, within a matter of weeks after the passage of this legislation, Canadian Pacific bought four trucking companies in northwestern Saskatchewan in order to truck grain.

Today, I wish to inform the House of the Government's decision on the minimum tax which will take place for the 1986 tax year. In addition, I will be announcing other important measures to improve tax fairness.
In choosing an appropriate minimum tax design, the Government has balanced a number of important objectives. First, an effective minimum tax must ensure that high income Canadians will pay a fair share of taxes in each year.
Hear, hear!

Second, a minimum tax imposed in the name of fairness must itself be fair. It must also be consistent with the valid social and economic goals for
which tax exemptions and deductions have been created over the years. Third, a minimum tax should, as far as possible, complement the existing tax system and use familiar tax concepts. Finally, to limit the complexity inherent in any such measure, an appropriate minimum tax should minimize uncertainty by having as clear as possible a cut-off between those who are potentially affected and those who are not.
The Government has concluded that the minimum tax design which best meets these objectives is the option described in our discussion paper as the alternative minimum tax. I wish to take a few minutes to describe some of the key features of the chosen design.
All high income Canadians are potentially subject to the proposed alternative minimum tax, and it will significantly reduce the number who would otherwise pay little or no tax. In practice, however, the minimum tax will affect a rather small group of individuals, estimated at fewer than 100,000 of the more than 15 million Canadians who file tax returns. The vast majority of Canadians will not be affected by my announcement today. The minimum tax calculation can be ignored by almost all tax filers with earnings and other income of less than about $45,000 to $50,000, according to the number of dependants that person has. Likewise, for most individuals with incomes above $50,000 the minimum tax calculation will not be necessary because of the amount of regular income tax which they are already paying.

For those who are affected, the minimum tax calculation is straightforward. An adjusted income figure will be calculated for which some items will be deductible and others not. The taxpayer will then claim his annual minimum tax exemption of about $45,000 to $50,000.

Amounts exceeding the minimum tax exemption will be taxed at an effective federal-provincial-territorial rate ranging from 24 per cent to 27 per cent, depending on the province or Territory of residence. This is based on a federal minimum tax rate of 17 per cent, which is one-half of the top federal statutory rate. The taxpayer will always pay the higher of the alternative minimum tax or the regular tax.
This minimum tax will prevent high income individuals from using one or more tax incentives to pay little or no tax in any one year. I underline the words "in any one year" because available data suggests that very high income individuals have been able to avoid paying taxes for any number of years.
The Government is also aware that existing tax incentives were put in place for valid economic and social reasons. The benefits of these incentives should not be undermined by a minimum tax. Accordingly, the minimum tax will have a carry-forward mechanism to ensure that the value of tax incentive deductions and credits is not lost. Taxpayers will be able, in effect, to apply unused deductions and tax credits against their regular tax liability in future years. But in each and every year high income tax payers will never pay less than
December 4, 1985

the minimum tax based on a federal-provincial-Territorial rate ranging from 24 per cent to 27 per cent.
Hear, hear!

I stated earlier that the Government is concerned that any tax imposed in the name of fairness must itself be fair. Accordingly, a limited number of deductions and tax credits will continue to be eligible in computing the minimum tax. This will mean that certain Canadians whose incomes exceed $50,000 may still pay no tax in any one year, but only in a strictly limited range of situations. These include some items allowed in order to preserve fairness to individuals in extenuating circumstances, such as those with disabilities or medical expenses under the Income Tax Act. Alimony and maintenance payments will be deductible since they are already taxed in the hands of the recipient. As well, contributions to charitable organizations will remain deductible in computing the minimum tax. Also deductible will be the actual costs incurred to earn income. Examples include employment expenses, including union and professional dues, moving costs, premiums for unemployment insurance and the Canada and Quebec Pension Plans and interest expenses of business persons, farmers and investors. Business losses will also be deductible. Aside from this limited number of deductions and tax credits of the type which I have just mentioned, no other amounts will be deductible in computing the minimum tax.
Non-deductible items include tax shelter losses created by claiming capital cost allowances on films and multiple-unit residential buildings, so-called MURBs, or by claiming exploration and development expenses, either directly or by way of flow-through share or similar arrangements. Dividend tax credits and contributions to Registered Retirement Savings Plans and registered pension plans will also be non-deductible for minimum tax purposes.
In the May Budget the Government proposed a $500,000 lifetime capital gains exemption. As I said in the Budget, that tax measure is an important incentive to assist in promoting investment, risk taking and job creation. The minimum tax does not remove this incentive. It will ensure that capital gains eligible for the lifetime exemption will receive favourable treatment.

What the minimum tax does is to prevent high-income taxpayers from using the capital gains exemption, alone or in combination with other tax incentives, to avoid paying tax in any one year. The result is a balance between preserving the value of incentives that contribute to productive investment and reinforcing tax fairness.
Special transitional reserve provisions will be available for qualifying farm property in order to assist farmers realizing large one-time capital gains.
Statements by Ministers
The minimum tax will have a substantial yield. Although there is much uncertainty about such forecasts, I estimate that it will raise on additional $300 million in federal revenues in the 1986 taxation year. When provincial revenues are added, the total will be about $450 million. The new minimum tax should be viewed as part of a broad and continuing effort to improve the fairness and the effectiveness of the tax system. I want to speak briefly about this broader context of tax fairness.
There are some who have argued that a minimum tax ignores the real problem, the existence of significant tax preferences. I want to emphasize that I do not regard the minimum tax as a substitute for continuing efforts to re-examine the preferences which now exist in our tax system and, wherever appropriate, removing them. My record has been clear in that regard.
One of my first acts as Minister of Finance, together with the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. MacKay), was to suspend rulings on limited partnerships and similar financing arrangements which had the potential for major tax avoidance. Many of these arrangements involved a sale of deductions or tax credits from one taxpayer to another. They created benefit for only a small circle of taxpayers and they jeopardized the integrity of the tax system in the eyes of many others. [Translation]
In October of last year, in response to concern about abuses of the Scientific Research Tax Credit, I announced a moratorium on quick flips under this measure and ordered a full review. As a result, in my May budget I eliminated this particular tax credit and introduced more effective, better targeted provisions to support research and development. [English]
In addition, the Budget eliminated tax shelter financing of properties such as yachts, recreational vehicles and hotels. It also ended the long-standing advantages of splitting income between family members through low interest or interest-free loans, a practice primarily of benefit to upper income families.
The Government also acted to improve the fairness of tax administration. Limits to the powers of the tax authorities in the area of search and seizure, audits and demands for tax information, were clearly defined. Changes were made to ensure that taxpayers are not required to pay taxes in dispute until after a court rules on their appeal.
More recently, I moved to put an end to the so-called "carve-out" transactions whereby profitable oil and gas companies were temporarily transferring property to companies with losses in order to reduce their tax.
I am taking action to terminate the use of partnerships in corporate takeovers to increase tax deductions through so-called "partnership step-up" rules. I will be clarifying the law to ensure that the limits imposed on foreign property investments by pension funds cannot be circumvented by inter-

December 4, 1985
Statements by Ministers
posing a Canadian company between the fund and the foreign property investment.
I am tabling a Ways and Means motion with respect to the minimum tax and the two measures I have just mentioned. I am also making available detailed information for Parliament, taxpayers and their advisers, and for all Canadians. The legislation to implement the necessary changes will be brought forward as soon as possible.
In conclusion, I want to emphasize the Government's commitment to measures which will make the tax system not only fairer but more effective in encouraging productive economic activity.

In just over one year, this Government has brought forward a wide range of measures to strengthen the fairness and effectiveness of the tax system as an essential part of a comprehensive program of economic renewal designed to benefit all Canadians.

The minimum tax is an integral part of this continuing initiative. In a careful, balanced and effective way, it gives real meaning to the broad principle of fairness which underlies our efforts to build a stronger economy and a better life for all Canadians.
Pursuant to Standing Order 65(1) I wish to lay upon the Table, in both official languages, copies of a notice of Ways and Means motion to amend the Income Tax Act. And pursuant to Standing Order 65(2), I ask that an Order of the Day be designated for the consideration of said motion.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, this is another remarkable day in the life of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson).

If success were to be measured by incoherence, confusion and complexity, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) would be seen as moving from triumph to triumph. We on this side of the House are perplexed, as Hon. Members opposite are clearly perplexed. Even the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Nielsen) is blushing.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Never.

We are confused, we are bemused, but we certainly are not amused at what the Minister has brought us today. It is more tinkering by the greater tinkerer. He tinkered with the old age security indexation and, fortunately, we were able to convince him to back off on that. He has tinkered with the sales taxes. He has tinkered a little with the fuel taxes. He has tinkered with surtaxes. He has done all of this, I might say, at a cost of billions of dollars to Canadian taxpayers. But his greatest tinkering has been with the income tax system. The incoherence, the woolly thinking, and the lack of any
sense of direction, seems to grow daily with respect to the budget measures brought in by the Minister of Finance last May. The Minister knows. I know that he knows. We all know that he knows how ridiculous the position of the Government is by the juxtaposition of this minimum tax with the capital gains tax exemption which was introduced in his Budget.
The Right Hon. Leader of our Party recommended a minimum tax during the election campaign in August of 1984. In a speech he made in Chatham he recommended an alternative minimum tax of 13 per cent on upper income Canadians who pay less than that or nothing at all. Let us compare that particular recommendation with what the Minister of Finance of the Tory Government is presenting us.
The Budget proposed a $500,000 lifetime exemption on capital gains. We thought-and I think most Canadians who reflected upon it thought-that that provision would not see the light of day in a motion of Ways and Means in this House. However, unfortunately, it has. It has been tabled. In addition to that, the Budget proposed that a minimum tax of some form would be introduced in 1986. Of course, that is the intention of the provision introduced today by the Minister of Finance. Everyone in the country, except members of the Government, saw the dilemma that was created, a capital gains tax exemption to a very small percentage of wealthy Canadians on the one hand, and a minimum tax proposal intended to target those same wealthy Canadians on the other hand. One would have thought that having taken nine months to bring in a Budget, the Government might have identified the paradox in that situation. Indeed, it may very well be because of this dilemma that a further six months, or slightly over six months, has been taken before we are actually seeing the minimum tax proposal.
We know that the Government is inordinately sensitive to criticism although, unfortunately, not to that which it receives in the House. If the Government accepted some of the advice it gets in the House, it would avoid a lot of pitfalls with the public. However, it chooses not to do so. I need only remind Members of the great debate on the deindexation of Old Age Security. We were told by the Government that we were all wrong, we insisted that we were correct, and finally the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Minister of Finance had the good sense to admit that we were correct all along. It was not sufficient that Members in the Chamber made that point and it was not even sufficient that Members on the Government's back-benches made it. It had to be made by the public. The people affected had to march on Ottawa to make that point.
We told the Government that the capital gains exemption was wrong as well. Of course, it has now been told that elsewhere as well. Undoubtedly, the Minister of Finance has seen the comments in the November 30 edition of The Financial Post. Some of the comments with respect to the capital gains tax exemption describe the dilemma in which he finds himself today. One article reads in part:
December 4, 1985

The exemption runs directly counter to the spirit and intent of another Mulroney government proposal, the minimum income tax. This, to be launched in 1986, will reduce the impact of various tax shelter deductions claimed by well-off individuals.
All of which creates a no-win situation for Wilson. If the minimum tax is applied to the capital gains sheltered by the exemption, it will negate the beneficial impact from the exemption. But if the new tax doesn't go after exempt capital gains, it will be seen as a joke.
Donald Huggett, national tax partner, publications, with Coopers & Lybrand, sees the introduction of these self-cancelling measures as "an exercise in futility and stupidity".
Huggett suggests the Government write off the experience as "a terrible mistake" and scrap or delay both the minimum tax and the capital gains exemption.
Of course, faced with that kind of criticism, the Minister had to find some way out of this dilemma. He should have dropped the capital gains and put in the minimum tax. Of course, he did not. He has twisted himself and the Income Tax Act into a pretzel in order to try to accommodate both of these objectives. In his attempt to reconcile the irreconcilable, namely to have tax free capital gains for the wealthy on the one hand and a minimum tax for the wealthy on the other, he had decided to add back one-half of the capital gains exemption in calculating that minimum tax of 17 per cent. That, effectively, means a tax of 8.5 per cent on the tax free gain, but it is refundable at a later date, as the Minister just told us, because the minimum tax will have a carry-forward mechanism to ensure that the value of all these tax incentives, the deductions and credits, is not lost to the individual taxpayer. Effectively, it becomes a refundable minimum tax on high incomes and is not a real tax at all.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Big deal.
Quoting a great Canadian, the Minister should have opened his remarks today by saying: "A minimum tax if necessary, but not necessarily a minimum tax".
That sounds like a Liberal.

To save face he has simply added more complexities and compounded inequities. He has told us that there are some deductions. In A Minimum Tax for Canada he refers to the dividend tax credit and the capital gains exclusion which, of course, he effectively has not dealt with. However, carrying charges in excess of investment income which may be interest write-offs is the real problem, and he has chosen to skate that one off-side and not deal with it.
I learned from Mac-Eachen.
He says that he learned from the MacEachen Budget. The MacEachen Budget was intended to introduce some equity into the Act with respect to these exorbitant write-offs.

Why did you back down? You changed it all. Don.
Statements by Ministers

The fact of the matter is that what he must do is bring some coherence, clarity and simplicity to the tax system in order to avoid the necessity for this kind of exercise.
The Minister continues to drag us further and further into a swamp of fiscal incoherence and tax complexities. I know this is difficult in politics, especially for a Minister of Finance, but instead of admitting to the gross stupidities which characterize so much of the May Budget, he is wading further and further into treacherous quicksand and mud, praying that he will emerge on the other side of the swamp before he drowns.
Did he see MacEachen on the way?

We have asked him to turn back, to withdraw, to start again on solid ground, but he steadfastly refuses to do so. He believes that he will save some credibility by moving straight ahead and drowning. I fear that drown he must, unless he backs out of this quagmire.
I will now turn to some of the other provisions of which we heard today. The Minister now tells us that he is going to terminate the use of partnerships in corporate takeovers to increase tax deductions through so-called partnership step-up rules.

Mr. Speaker, I would remind you that it was a similar arrangement-an advance ruling, a tax interpretation-that made it possible to transfer the shares and create a tax haven with respect to the Gulf case, a famous case here in the House where we asked the Minister many questions. Why did he not overrule the advance ruling in those circumstances?

He tells us now, after the horse has fled the barn, that he is going to stop this famous little Egypt bump which has cost taxpayers, in that one transaction alone, perhaps as much as $1 billion. Now we are going to stop that transaction.
Why don't we tax nerve. We would make a fortune.

We are enjoying a little comic relief from the left. Mr. Speaker, during the great exchange over that Gulf transaction I recall asking the Minister why he did not simply refuse to give rulings on such transactions. We were told that it was in the law and that the law was there and that the law had been introduced by the Liberals and that they could not do anything about it and so on, all of which, of course, was just rubbish and nonsense. The Minister himself said today: "One of my first acts as Minister of Finance, together with the Minister of National Revenue, was to suspend rulings on limited partnerships and similar financing arrangements that had the potential for major tax avoidance". If $1 million is not major tax avoidance, I do not know what is. The Minister had the option to stop a ruling from issuing with respect to that Gulf transaction, as he did in the case of limited partnerships and other financing arrangements. I want to know why he did not do it.

You know it is a different type of transaction.

He says it is a different type of transaction. The fact is that it needed a ruling in order to proceed. He knows that, and there was no requirement whatsoever that that ruling be given.

Well, Mr. Speaker, it is indeed a difficult period for us. Hopefully, with the Government and our colleagues to our left, we are trying to improve the Canadian tax system. But every time the Minister comes up with a new project he makes the legislation ever more complicated.
Sure enough, the tax measures just introduced by the Minister simply confirm his reputation as an incoherent tax fiddler. [English]
If I may be nostalgic for a moment, Mr. Speaker, 1 picked up a document called A New Direction for Canada. In it, under the heading "Tax Simplification" I find these words: "The tax system is overly complex. It imposes on taxpayers and their advisers an unnecessary cost in time and money just to understand and comply with the law, and the more complicated the tax system is, the less effective will be the investment incentive contained in it". Need I ask Members of the Chamber, who uttered those words? It is our Minister of Finance. What has happened to him? I can tell you that there are many people in this country who are wondering what happened to that Minister of Finance.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I regret to interrupt the Hon. Member. I would ask him to conclude.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister had tax lawyers, tax accountants and fiscal advisers in this country worried when he made that statement last year. These well paid tour guides in the labyrinth of the Income Tax Act were concerned. They now know that they are safe and secure. They would be well advised, before they go to sleep each night, to thank God for the Minister of Finance.

Mr. Speaker, at the beginning of the election in 1984 we had a tax system that permitted special deductions for yachts, for club memberships, special deductions for rather spurious research and development schemes that were constructed and special deductions in the corporate sector that provided no concrete incentives for investment to create jobs. One of them was known as the little Egypt bump. All of these produced in Canada one of the most unfair tax systems in the western world and it was created by the Liberal Government that preceded the present Government.
I have just seen the ultimate act of nerve of a critic for the Liberal Party getting up and denouncing a system of taxation that his Party created just over a year ago when it was in
power. There are simply no limits to shame, as one of my colleagues has just said.
I will leave my Liberal colleagues-metaphorically and literally to the right-alone for the moment-

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: We are reformers.

Now that they are on this side of the House they are reformers, Mr. Speaker. They shift with location in terms of philosophic positions.
Unlike the Liberal critic, I want to deal with what was specifically announced today. Before doing so, I want to put it into some perspective. In the summer of 1984 there was a perception by Canadian men and women all across the country that they were indeed paying plenty of taxes. As the Minister has acknowledged, even before today, there were thousands of Canadians with very high incomes who were paying not a penny in taxes. That was perceived by Canadians even before the summer of 1984 to be unjust.
On July 25, 1984, in this city, as Leader of the New Democratic Party I was very pleased to repeat in that debate between the Leaders of the Parties the position of my Party, speaking out for Canadians across the land. That position, succinctly stated, is that as long as ordinary men and women are paying their share of taxes, it is time everyone in this country paid his or her share. I was pleased, as were all Canadians, to hear the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) say in that debate that if the Conservative Party formed the Government, in his view the rich would pay and, to quote him, "should pay handsomely".
After the election, we saw changes brought in by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) in his first statement in the fall of 1984, followed by the Budget. In those early provisions we did not see the kind of reform that was promised by the Prime Minister in that debate. We saw, along with other announcements, a package of tax increases on ordinary Canadians that amounted to approximately $1,000 per family, if one added the taxes together.
Oh, come on.

I would be happy to provide the documentation to my Conservative colleague. There were substantial tax increases affecting the ordinary family, but we did not see the promised minimum tax in the first year of the Conservative Government.
I say on behalf of my colleagues-and I make a distinction between righteousness and self-righteousness-that if there is something to which my colleagues remained faithful in that campaign it was that there ought to be tax fairness in this land. When we were elected in September, 1984, all NDP Members in the House plus many others in my Party across the country kept up our faith to work for tax reform.
We initiated a commission, under the chairmanship of our finance critic, the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis), that is under way now and will be hearing representations from Canadians across the country until the next Budget
December 4, 1985

from the Minister of Finance, because we intend to continue to address the important issue of major tax reform. Perhaps the Minister of Finance will know that the Prime Minister's Office acknowledged publicly some two weeks ago on Friday that, as a result of a campaign initiated by the NDP to mail out over one million pieces of literature throughout Canada, the Prime Minister's Office has received 1,000 pieces of mail per day in the past couple of weeks urging tax reform, a minimum tax in particular.
We have responded to Canadians' sense of fairness by carrying out our political obligation of maintaining pressure on the Government to do what it ought to do. 1 am pleased by what has been announced today. I see it as an important start. We now have a minimum tax, and I compliment the Minister of Finance for at last coming forward with that promise.
Hear, hear!

I also listened to him carefully when he said, with some emphasis, that this is a step and that he is committing himself once again to the process of continued tax reform, presumably leading right up to the next Budget.

However, Mr. Speaker, 1 want to emphasize that the policy introduced by the Minister today is just a starting point. This process must continue because all Canadians want to have a completely fair tax system. That is the objective of our Party here in the House of Commons.

I want to mention two specific items. First, of course, the minimum tax will provide some $450 million in additional revenue. That is important because $300 million will go to the federal Treasury and $150 million will go to the provinces. However, I would remind Hon. Members that the capital gains tax giveaway introduced by the Minister will mean a loss of $600 million a year. Therefore, the Minister has begun to retrieve a good part of that and we will be insisting that in the next Budget he retrieve the rest of it by abolishing that inequitable proposal.
Let the farmers hear that.
You forget about western Canadian farmers.

My Conservative colleagues know that we have made provisions in our approach to this to recognize that home owners and farmers are in a special category and ought to be so recognized. 1 say to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski) that if he will support our a special category we can have an interesting debate.
However, the Minister's proposal is an important and positive step. We question why the $40,000 in taxable income should be exempt and we will be very interested in discussing that proposal. I would also note that for some time our Finance critic and other colleagues in the House have criticized the little Egypt bump, this interesting tax provision that has no

economic benefit but has resulted in a great loss of revenue. Again, that was brought in by the Liberals. We were critical of that with the Liberal Government. We have been critical of that with the present Government. 1 compliment, unequivocally, the Minister of Finance today for removing that particular loophole.
In conclusion, I do not think the Minister took 15 minutes to make his announcement. The Liberal critic took 15 minutes to say nothing. I want to wind up my comments right now by saying that the Minister has made a good beginning. I do not qualify that. A good beginning has been initiated here today. He also said that it was step one in the process of taxation reform. On behalf of my colleagues in the House of Commons and New Democrats all across the country I want to say that we will continue with our mandate to fight for tax reform from now until the Minister's next Budget. We want the Minister, in that Budget, to deliver total tax reform on personal income tax and corporate tax. We will be watching.
Hear, hear!

Surely this is one of the most important economic issues in western Canada.
Also I was surprised that the Minister did not report more on the progress of the Western Grain Transportation Act, its

effects in western Canada, and his views with regard to the Hall Commission Report.
The Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin) seemed to complain a lot about the motion today. Although the Minister outlined those provisions of the Act which provide for the review committee, headed by the Hon. Jack Horner, a very good friend of the Minister, it seems to me that the Hall Commission has had massive resources at its fingertips. efficiency or practicality of feeding cattle in the West, with the Alberta Government providing $21 per tonne in transportation assistance for the feeding of cattle in that province. There will be some distortion compared with other western provinces with regard to the feeding of grain and finishing cattle.
Last week the Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer), in response to the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner), took great pride with regard to the benefit to be paid under the Western Grain Transportation Act, the $659 million. That is rather interesting because I do not recall hearing the Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board ever speaking in favour of the Bill or voting in favour of it at that time. The Minister responsible for the Wheat Board also took credit for the crop insurance, the western grain stabilization fund and all the other programs under which the producer pays a premium and, if he suffers a loss, he receives a benefit. That is analogous to any kind of insurance program that does not result in any great largesse from the Government of Canada.
The uncertainty in the agriculture field is greater than it has been since the 1930s. We recently spent two weeks in some 14 communities in the West listening to over 100 witnesses, farmers, farm organizations and community leaders. We certainly gained the feeling that there was incredible uncertainty in the West, not only among young farmers facing the loss of their farms because of the cost price squeeze, declining land values and low international prices. There seems to be no clear commitment by the Government to make any firm decisions with regard to agriculture.
This afternoon we are debating the Hall Commission Report on the Crow benefit payment. As far as we know, the Minister's position is that there will be a freedom of choice whereby the benefit can either be paid to the railroad or the producer based on his position in 1983. However, it goes beyond that. The Government made glowing commitments during the election campaign. When the Estimates of the Department of Agriculture came out, we noted that the Estimates for the previous year for the Farm Credit Corporation had been $494 million. This year they are $90 million. Obviously there was going to be no help or very little for the Farm Credit Corporation compared to the previous year.
Looking on through the Estimates, we see the Government making very significant demands on user-pay and inspection fees. At the end of the Estimates we noted that the Estimates were not going to be indexed. When we inquired of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise), we found that there will be a loss of purchasing power by the Department of Agriculture of some 10 per cent to 15 per cent in the coming year. In addition, there will be a straight cut of $50 million. We do not know whether that will be in meat inspection or research. Not knowing that has increased the uncertainty in western Canada as to exactly what the commitment of this Government is to agriculture.
In our task force hearings, we talked to many drought victims. We talked about the loss of farms by young farmers and farmers facing the prospect of asking the provincial and
Crow Benefit Payment
municipal Governments for welfare. We received the answer last week when the Government said it would provide assistance on an average of $5 or $10 per acre at a time when the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool and other wheat pools were asking for benefits of up to $50 per acre.
We see the uncertainty there and the prospect of the Minister paying the Crow benefit either directly to the purchaser or to the railroad, the choice being made by the producer. That creates great uncertainty. However, we could look at the other input costs which the Government has imposed upon the producers in the last couple of months. On September 1, there was an increase in the price of gasoline by 9 cents per gallon. That will cost many producers with large holdings $1,200 to $1,500 per year more. On January 1, a 1 per cent sales tax will be imposed, which will impact not only on fuel costs but on all the equipment a farmer buys.
There is great uncertainty as to the Government's priorities. Clearly the Government was not there for the victims of the drought. Clearly it is not there for the cost price squeeze. The Government is now increasing this uncertainty. The Western Grain Transportation Act was designed to improve rail transportation in western Canada and to provide funding to compensate for the benefit, and we are seeing some improvement. For instance, CP Rail reports that this year, it will have record spending of $600 million for locomotive cars, new rail tracks and mechanical facilities and $175 million will be spent this year on the Rogers Pass tunnel and on double tracking in the mountains. It claims that over 1,000 people will be working on those projects.
Clearly the Bill is seeing to the modernization and upgrading of western transportation. The response of the Hon. Minister of Transport was that the entire Bill should be put on freeze for three years. I would ask him where the improvement in rail transportation would have been today if he had had his way and the Bill had not been passed for three years.
There is great concern among groups like the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool. The Chief Executive Officer for the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool has said that the Government is sending out conflicting signals by not encouraging major cost reductions and efficiency gains on one hand while reactivating uneconomic rail lines on the other.
The international climate is very uncertain. The United States is putting in place a bonus program and the EEC has in place a massive bonus program. In Canada, the Government's commitment to agriculture is certainly in question. There can be no doubt that because of the input costs provided by the Budget, the cut-backs in departmental spending and the $5 or $10 per acre benefit for drought victims, the Government is sending out very confused signals as to whether or not it has made any commitment to the future of agriculture. That is sad because it is a very, very important part of our economy. It is important to western Canada. The Government should come clean and get its priorities straight.

As concerns the Canadian grains policy, the concept of equity between East and West is based on three components: First, a single domestic market for grains, which means a single price throughout Canada for grain users, except for differences related to transportation costs. Second, if there is to be equity, the balance has to be maintained between grain and meat transportation costs so that the meat production industry can develop in both Eastern and Western Canada based on production efficiency. Finally, the concept of equity also requires that any assistance or benefit given by the Federal Government to Canadian grain producers be available to all producers concerned, whatever their region.
Mr. Speaker, I hope nobody in this House will dare suggest the opposite, and I hope they will agree with me that equity is the fundamental and most important parameter to be kept
clearly in mind in order that the end result will not favour one part of Canada while harming another.

Mr. Speaker, the concept of neutrality of our resources is another basic and fundamental aspect that should be kept in mind in this debate. Although our country's economic complexity seems obvious to me, my hope is to attain, with all my colleagues, and as soon as practicable, some sort of neutrality in the interests of the country as a whole, and especially of Canadian agriculture.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is my pleasure to join in this debate with respect to the Western Grain Transportation Act. I wish to commence my remarks by complimenting the Hon. Member for Champlain (Mr. Champagne) on his maiden speech in the House of Commons.
