speechtext:
I rise to support the amendment which I had the honour to second, which states that this House rejects the transfer of the Crow benefit payments from the railroads to the producers as recommended in the Hall Committee Report. As I listened to the Hon. Member for Champlain (Mr. Champagne), I realized that so often we in this House, and I think people across Canada, see the Western Grain Transportation Act as something which only affects the prairie Provinces. Nothing could be further from the truth. It affects the three prairie Provinces, yes, but it also affects Ontario, Quebec and Atlantic Canada. It does affect producers in each of those provinces in terms of transportation. I, like my colleague, the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin), say that this

December 4, 1985
Crow Benefit Payment
is a transportation subsidy not an agricultural or grain subsidy, and we should look at it in that context. The movement of grain from the prairie Provinces through the Port of Thunder Bay-half of which 1 represent-is part of the backbone of the economy of a lot of eastern Canada. The grain which moves through Thunder Bay is upwards sometimes of 23 million tonnes for export. As we note how it flows through the transportation system, we realize how broadly the Grain Transportaton Act affects the economy. Twelve per cent of the grain handled in Thunder Bay is also handled in the Port of Montreal; 7 per cent in Sorel; 7 per cent in Trois-Rivieres; 15 per cent in Quebec City. Saint John and Halifax both handle 2 per cent of the export grains which move through my port. Significantly, 37 per cent of the grain which moves on those rail lines from Manitoba through Thunder Bay is transshipped through the two ports of the riding of Manicouagan- which is the riding held by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mul-roney) of this country-21 per cent in Port Cartier and 16 per cent in Baie Comeau. Clearly, whatever happens on the Prairies will be felt all the way through that system.
If there is a situation where more grain is moving in an easterly direction, then all of those communities will benefit both directly and indirectly. If, on the other hand, for some reason the movement of grain through the eastern leg of our export situation is reduced, then we hurt all the way through. We hurt in Manitoba in terms of rail jobs and services. We hurt in Thunder Bay in terms of grain handling jobs, marine jobs and the other spinoff jobs in the community. The same could be said all the way through the Great Lakes into the St. Lawrence River up to Atlantic Canada.
I rise in the House today to support the motion that we continue to pay the Crown benefit to the railroads rather than to the individual producer. There are a number of things which will happen out there in the grain industry if there is not a national policy in effect. With changes in pricing and rates, the individual farmer would have to make a very hard decision between supporting the Canadian economy on a broad base and recognizing the limitations of his own income and opting for an avenue of transportation which, while it would be beneficial to him, could be hurtful to other Canadians. It is no different from decisions individual Canadians make all the time about whether they buy a Canadian product or something which is produced in another country. It does not matter whether it is shoes or automobiles or a decision about which method to use to ship one's grain. If it is left to the individual, he will naturally look at his own finances and, of necessity, he would have to go with the lowest price.
But we, as a nation, have some responsibility. We provide a Crow benefit to ensure that our export grains can be moved to an export position in a manner which allows us to compete in the world markets. I think we have to stay with that concept, and the only way we can do that is by continuing to make the payments to the railroads. It is extremely efficient to do that. We only have to write out two cheques per year. If we pay to the producers, we will have to establish a very large bureaucracy, which will increase the administrative costs of providing
that same benefit. For that reason alone, I think this Government should reject the Hall recommendation and keep the legislation the way it is and pay the railroads a transportation subsidy.
Having said that, I would like to point out that there needs to be some changes in the kind of allocations and some provision for those improvements in the transportation system about which the Minister talks, so that on a national basis we can ensure that our grain products can continue to move to an export position and be able to compete in the world market.
A lot of the grain which Canada produces moves through the Port of Thunder Bay. In fact, historically, 60 per cent of that grain has been shipped eastward, primarily to customers in Europe, Russia and other countries in that general neck of the woods. But in recent years, the balance has begun to shift to a point where today less than 50 per cent of that grain is moving through the Port of Thunder Bay. With that reduction have come lay-offs, and not only in Thunder Bay, although we have suffered the greatest amount of lay-offs. This summer, for instance, we had over 1,200 of our people out of work. That was felt all the way down the Seaway system. We have seen unemployment levels of around 45 per cent to 50 per cent in some of the communities in Quebec which are involved in grain movement. Eighty per cent of the business of my port is grain movement, so you can appreciate, Mr. Speaker, why it is so important to me and my colleague, the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon (Mr. Epp), that we keep fighting to ensure that we continue to get our fair share. If the Government decides to accept the Hall Report and its recommendations, then we will no longer get our historical and fair share of the grain movement.
The movement of grain is under attack from many sources. In another place in this capital city of ours, we will be dealing with an Act which will allow the Government to charge for coastguard services. That will add to the cost of moving grain east and west. It will add to the cost of dredging and ice-breaking and navigational aids. That will make us less competitive. The Laurentian Pilotage Authority has asked for increases in excess of 60 per cent. The CTC has held hearings but has yet to report on whether it will allow those increases to occur. This summer the cost of weighing our grain which is charged back to the producer and the elevator operators has gone up. The S30 million dollar carve out, as proposed by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) in this past spring's budget to take $30 million from the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority, is going to force the tolls up.
Most recently a gentleman by the name of Esmond Jarvis from the Canadian Wheat Board proposed that we legislate geography, that we no longer say that the midpoint between western movements of grain and eastern movements of grain is somewhere around Saskatchewan but that we move it to the Manitoba/Ontario border. It would henceforth become cheaper to move grain from Winnipeg to Vancouver than to Thunder Bay, which is only some 400 miles away.

We are being attacked on all sides. If the Government accepts the Hall Committee Report it will be one more nail in the coffin of the port of Thunder Bay. We cannot allow that to happen. We cannot allow any of these things to happen.
We have to continue with our traditional balance of grain movements in this country to ensure that those jobs that exist today can be retained where they are and not shifted to another part of this country or to another country. That is what will happen if we become less and less competitive.
We are already fighting subsidies provided by the Americans and by the EEC to their grain producers. The last thing that we in Canada should be doing is adding costs to our own products.

Mr. Speaker, I believe today's debate is very timely, especially in the context of the current situation in agriculture. 1 had the privilege, together with a few of my colleagues, to go on a tour that brought us around Western Canada where we met with many farmers. Within 15 days, we visited some 15 communities from Winnipeg to Vancouver.
At each of these communities, between 8 and 12 briefs were presented to us, at the level of the national caucus of the Liberal Party of Canada, by farm producers' organizations, including the wheat pools, dairy producers, grain producers and in fact just about every commodity groups, and 1 was able to see first hand just how precarious the farm situation is in Western Canada, especially because of bad weather, including the drought and grasshoppers that devastated a significant part of the acreage, but also because of the cost price squeeze, the ever rising costs of production and the sharp reduction in the price of wheat resulting in an ever shrinking profit margin. So there is great anxiety in the agricultural sector.
Mr. Speaker, 1 would not want to digress too far from the motion we are debating; however, I suggest we cannot put this
Crow Benefit Payment
debate in its proper context without referring somewhat to the general situation in agriculture and without mentioning that the Hall report raises considerable concern and that farmers and commodity producers in Western Canada are anxious to learn about the position of the Government because of the impact it will have on their financial planning for the next few years.
I have noticed that most of the briefs that were presented to us, particularly by wheat producers in Manitoba and Saskatchewan, as well as by producers in British Columbia and Alberta, although the production is much lower in the latter Province, that most of the briefs that were presented to us in the Western Provinces insist heavily on the issue of wheat transportation and the manner in which payments or grants would be paid out.
I would not want to make a mistake or to risk quoting figures that could be misleading, but I would say offhand that some 75 per cent of briefs that were presented to us by various commodity groups and especially by wheat pools indicated a strong preference for maintaining the present legislation, that is, for continuing to issue payments to railways rather than to producers.
I must admit that in Alberta the reverse was true; however, when looking at the whole picture, it seemed to me that the view expressed in the briefs that were presented to us was, on the whole, abundantly clear. Moreover, on both sides of the matter, people are concerned because they cannot figure out what will be the position of the Government.
Turning now to the situation in the East, that is in Quebec, in the Atlantic provinces and also in parts of Ontario, there are also great concerns in these areas, and the motion introduced by my colleague from Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy) is certainly timely. Indeed, it could give the government the opportunity to reassure Western Canada producers, to bring them up to date on the issue while at the same time reassuring producers in the East. Obviously, significant amounts are at stake-some $650 million a year, as far as we can estimate. This is therefore a most significant amount in the overalll farming economy.
I listened earlier to my colleague the Hon. Member for Champlain (Mr. Champagne), and of course this was his maiden speech in this House, so it seems. It had not occurred to me that after a year and a half, there were still Progressive Conservative Members who had not not risen in this House. I apologize for that. We listened to many, many briefs. During the electoral campaign in Quebec some of the Conservative candidates were campaigning to keep the Crow as it is. I have been told that the Conservative candidates in the west were campaigning against the Bill. There comes a time when we should know the truth. That is why the farmers do not trust the Government.
There is an additional reason not to trust the Government, and that is the declaration made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) this afternoon. At page 4 of the documentation tabled this afternoon it states that those who have a capital gain will have to pay 12.5 per cent on it. The year that a farmer sells his farm with a capital gain of $300,000 he will have to pay a minimum tax. This declaration comes only a few months after the same Minister of Finance and all the Conservative Members were praising the capital gains exemption as the thing which will save agriculture. Now they are coming back through the side door and imposing a 12.5 per cent tax on capital gains on farms.

Mr. Speaker, I think it is about time the Conservative Members of Quebec and elsewhere should stop playing hide-and-seek and speak the same language instead of doing like the Hon. Member for Champlain (Mr. Champagne) who quotes from statements made by other people but fails to take position himself. I would tell them that it is time for a debate on this motion that will give the Government an opportunity to take a position and tell the farmers who are now looking after their books, because this is their slack season and they will be sowing in the spring, what decisions will be made. I urge the Government to take advantage of this debate and refrain from playing hide-and-seek and to let us know what will be the position of the Tory Government on the Hall Report.

Mr. Speaker, to begin with, I would like to congratulate the Hon. Member for Champlain (Mr. Champagne) for his fine speech.

I wish also, Mr. Speaker, to reply to some of the comments just offered by the Member for Laval-des-Rapides (Mr. Garneau). As happens so often with the Party which he represents, he has attempted to create confusion in many parts of Canada by spreading fear and apprehension. I know that the statement offered by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) today will be extremely well received by the people of Canada because they have been saying it is very important that all Canadians pay an equitable share of taxation. I believe that in the end the statement offered by the Minister today will meet a desire of Canadians.

I want to remind you, Mr. Speaker, other Canadians, and members of the Official Opposition, that Canadian farmers well remember which Party introduced the capital gains tax, and they will also remember very clearly which party nullified the capital gains tax for Canadian farmers.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext:
The debate today is not on capital gains or on the minimum tax. The debate today is required by legislation dealing with the operation of the Western Grain Transportation Act at this particular time. Today we are taking a very important step in that process, a process which involves consultation with Canadian farmers and farm organizations. The process requires than an impartial committee be struck which is representative of the industry in Canada. It requires that committee to report to the House, and that the report, having been made to the House, be examined by Members of the House and then be presented to the Minister for his consideration.
The members of the Official Opposition have contributed a considerable amount of confusion to the debate this afternoon. I wish to stress that right now we are in the midst of this very important process. It is very appropriate that the Government should come before the House today and participate in this debate on the motion presented by the Official Opposition. Let us remind ourselves of that process and how it is unfolding. While we may be aware of it, I suspect that many Canadians are not. Unfortunately, if they only listen to the speeches by members of the Official Opposition I believe they will become more confused.
I remind Hon. Members and all Canadians that the legislation required that a committee be struck to examine the Western Grain Transportation Act and its implementation. This was done according to the statute. That committee was struck in 1984 and began its process of hearings as required by the legislation. The legislation required that it make a report to the Minister on or before March 31. Those recommendations were presented to the Minister and, as required by the legislation, were tabled in the House. There is provision within the regulations for Members of the House to request a debate, under certain regulations, and that is the debate which is taking place.
Let me point out that there has been a substantial change in the way Parliament operates. Our Government is in the midst of a process of consultation with farmers and farm organizations.

That is required in the legislation. Indeed, it has been carried out because the Government is committed to consultation. With all due respect to members of the Official Opposition, it seems that they have not realized that a change occurred over a year ago with the election of a Government that was committed to a process of consultation.

December 4, 1985
Crow Benefit Payment
Therefore, we do not enter into this process with preconceived decisions. We do not enter into this process under a facade of consultation. We genuinely have sought and continue to seek the input of farmers and farm organizations from all regions of Canada, as pointed out by the Member for Champlain (Mr. Champagne).
We are also extremely fortunate that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski), unlike his predecessor who spoke earlier this afternoon, sincerely believes that the way to good Government is to work in co-operation with the provinces, the organizations, individuals and all Members of the House. Such a process has not existed for a long time. I speak as a historian as well as a Member of Parliament. I have been here for two and a half years but as a historian in Canadian politics I know that such a process has been lacking for the last two decades. Therefore, perhaps it is understandable that members of the Official Opposition are confused that we have no preconceived position on this extremely important issue.
The issue we are concerned with today has been of immense importance to western Canadians since 1897. Unfortunately, those listening to the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin) may have come to the conclusion that the Crow's Nest Pass Agreement came into effect in 1881.
This agreement was very much a fabric of western Canada. Canadians will know that in 1897 the railways received certain benefits from the Government of Canada to construct the line through the Crow's Nest Pass, which is so much an integral part of British Columbia. In return for that financial compensation and acreage compensation which the railways received in 1897, the farmers of Canada were guaranteed a certain concession with respect to freight rates into the future.
A couple of years ago the Government of the day-the Official Opposition today-decided to change what had been a perpetual agreement up to that time. I will not repeat the debate which took place at that time, when we debated this issue into the early morning hours.
The point is that the legislation under which we are operating now was passed as a result of the decision by the Official Opposition, which was the Government of the day. It is important to understand that the so-called Crow gap, what is now called the grain transportation refund, was part of a package that was put together two years ago to compensate those western Canadian farmers who were injured as a result of that policy change. Many western farmers would have preferred that that policy change never took place two years ago. Indeed, they would prefer that we never became involved in the question of the Crow gap involving some $650 million or the question of how it should be paid. Nevertheless, we must live with that decision because it is the law of the land. It is an irrevocable change.
We are now concerned with a review of how that policy is operating. Let me stress that we are not talking about a new policy of subsidy implemented some two years ago. We are concerned with compensation for a policy that was enunciated some 80 years ago and changed two years ago.
The difficulty we face with this issue is that we are attempting to govern during a time of real financial crisis. Canadian farmers are suspicious about any policy change, the suggestion of a change or, indeed, any suggestion that would raise doubts about the future.
I say with all confidence that our Government has done more for agriculture in 15 months than any Government in Canadian history over a comparable period of time. However, despite what we have done and will continue to do there remains a financial crisis among farmers which must be addressed, as well as a tremendous suspicion within that farm community.
With all due respect to members of the Official Opposition, I believe that that suspicion which has been growing in western Canada is part of the legacy left to us when we came to office some 15 months ago. I am pleased to see that my hon. friend, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie), agrees with me for once. We regret that this legacy exists and that there was cause for such suspicion, but it is a fact. Therefore, when we address a question as important as this we must proceed with all caution so that we do not add to the suspicion or cynicism that exists.
That is why our strategy of consultation is exceedingly important. Philosophically speaking, I believe that this should be a strategy followed by any Government. However, it is particularly important at this time.
The Hon. Minister is reassuring Canadian farmers and I do not believe that there is another Minister in the Government or previous Governments who is better suited for the task with which he is appointed than the present Minister. I have every confidence that the Minister will proceed in such a way that he will reassure those various farm organizations that do not agree on this subject that their sensitivities and fears are being carefully considered.
The Canadian Federation of Agriculture was in Ottawa some three weeks ago to attend meetings. One of the highlights of that week was their meeting with the Prime Minister and 18 Cabinet Ministers. I believe that is an event such as has not taken place in recent times. I asked the Canadian Federation of Agriculture what they felt about the method of payment issue. It was not that they did not have any attitudes. Of course they had many, but they had no position. We recognize the issue which we are addressing as being extremely important for many reasons.
As I have said already, people are very apprehensive about anything which would work to their financial disadvantage. It is an exceedingly complex issue which is not well understood in various parts of Canada. Perhaps it is fair to say that it is not well understood by farm organizations in any region of Canada. There is still a considerable amount of confusion.
What we have is a report of an inquiry which tried honestly and sincerely to listen to farm groups and to alleviate some of their fears. It has tried to come up with a reform which is "resource neutral", in its own words. The committee of inquiry
December 4, 1985

went in that direction and sought a solution which would not injure any particular sector of the Canadian agricultural community.
1 remind the House that there is a recommendation in the Hall report that compensation should be paid to any segment of the agricultural community, should it be established through due process that indeed there was injury. The fear that there might be injury and the possibility of dealing with that injury are recognized in this report.
Also there was an attempt in the report to alleviate some concerns about the previous recommendation of acreage payments. This report abandoned that particular proposal and talked about net grain sales. I think that is a step forward in that regard. However, there are some remaining problems in that particular part of the report, as I see it and as was expressed to me by farmers. There is a fear remaining about the difficulty of monitoring sales between farmers. Also there is some fear that farmers who are feeding their own grain might divide into a grain enterprise and a cattle enterprise and try to take advantage of the proposed changes. These types of concerns remain and stress the importance of the process of continued consultation.
I am sure Hon. Members of the Opposition realize that this is an ongoing process throughout this crop year. In essence, it began some 12 months or so ago. However, the Minister is required, by the end of the crop year, to have considered these recommendations. That is why the debate is occurring today. I am sure there will be other opportunities in the future for it to be continued. This is an ongoing process. I think we are looking at some seven additional months, and 1 hope within the course of that seven months that there will be adequate opportunity for various farm organizations to reach a definitive position. Also I hope there is an opportunity for farm organizations which fear some of the implications of the report to speak directly with each other.
It seems to me, as political scientists and historians have said, that Canada is a very difficult country to govern because regionalism, which is so much a part of us, tends to be divisive. One way to lessen that regionalism is for those people who represent the different regions of Canada, whether they be Members of Parliament or part of the farm community, to have a chance to come together and perhaps informally meet on common ground to discuss their differences.
The Hon. Member for Champlain made an exceedingly important point today. He stressed that under the new Government, which has been in place for 15 months, he felt perfectly comfortable in rising as a representative of his province, on behalf of his constituents, and expressing their concerns. He felt that he could do that in an atmosphere where such debate was welcome. Other Hon. Members feel equally comfortable in the process. I believe I may be followed by one of my hon. friends from the Province of Alberta. I know that he, too, feels equally comfortable entering into this debate. The essence of the parliamentary process is that those of us who represent varying constituencies which sometimes have conflicting points of view must have the opportunity to express those points of
Crow Benefit Payment
view. In fact, later this evening we will be discussing parliamentary reform as a result of the "McGrath" report which is before the House. If I understand that report correctly, that is one of the main principles in it. The parliamentary part of the process which began today is an important step in the direction of parliamentary reform.
I want to conclude by saying that a great deal of discussion must yet occur. Although many of the farm organizations are not yet in agreement, whether they be in western Canada or elsewhere in the country, what we are doing today is setting the stage. We look forward to being a part of that process. I compliment Hon. Members who participated in this debate. Even though in western Canada we see this as being primarily a western Canadian issue, for historic and economic reasons, I am delighted that all Hon. Members of the House feel comfortable in participating, and I congratulate them on their contributions today.

I understand that there cannot be a vote. I know that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski), except on occasions when he disagrees with me, is very seldom wrong. I will take his word for that. However, on this occasion I want to reflect upon what happened to the statutory grain rate and to remind Hon. Members of the great things which were predicted by both railways if the Crow rate were to be changed.
In particular, I refer to something which happened this year as a result of an arbitrary action taken by one of the railways. I understand that a great many Hon. Members are concerned about it. I am referring to the arbitrary action of Canadian Pacific in depriving its pensioners of their pass rights. Many Members on all sides of the House have expressed concern about this matter. I am not aware of anyone in the House who supports the CPR in that action. I am sure almost all of us have CPR pensioners in our ridings and will therefore know how much of an insult this was to them, even though many of them may not use their passes. The amount of money which it costs CPR for those who use them is a very insignificant one indeed. However, that was the generous corporate response of a company that got its way with the change in the Crow rate and received $300 million per year which it otherwise would not have received. What was its response? Its response was to act in a mean, stingy, cold-hearted way toward its pensioners. I just wanted to put that on the record.
The other railway in the country, Canadian National, along with CPR, has responded in general through a systematic reduction in its employee levels. It has responded by trying to do away with what we regard as important processes for worker and public safety, such as the preservation of cabooses on trains. I do not have time to go into the record of the railways and their responses to getting what they wanted in terms of the Crow rate, but it has been an abominable one.

December 4, 1985

They have not shown the generosity one might expect from a recipient of this largesse from the public purse. They have not proceeded to deliver the kinds of jobs which they promised their employees. Many people in railway shops across the country were called in and showed nice movies about all the jobs that would be created. Since then we have had nothing but lay-off after lay-off. In fact, I was informed by CNR just yesterday that another 93 positions are to be eliminated at the Transcona shop. This is the kind of response we have had. Also we have had an unwillingness or a reluctance, shall we say, on the part of the Government to go ahead with other related programs, such as the boxcar rehabilitation program which came about as a result of a federal-provincial agreement. We have seen a third of that program implemented at Transcona. We have another two-thirds to go. That two-thirds is not happening yet. Instead, what do we have? We have more lay-offs at the shop.
I just want to put on the record that I think the behaviour of the railways following the change in the Crow Rate has not lived up to the promises they made to the Canadian people, and to a certain extent the Canadian people and Parliament itself, at least those who voted for the change, were hoodwinked by the railways.

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (for the President of the Privy Council) moved:
subtopic: REFORM OF THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: That this House take note of the matter of reform of the House of Commons.

speakeroldname: Hon. James A. McGrath (St. John's East):
subtopic: REFORM OF THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. It will be one year ago tomorrow since this House established a special committee on reform. In so doing, Sir, it embarked on the most ambitious and comprehensive reform ever undertaken by any Commonwealth Parliament. This is the first opportunity we have had since that time to discuss the committee's reports, although much has taken place since the committee was struck.
We already have in place the recommendations of the first report on a provisional basis. Before dealing with that, though, I want to take this opportunity to thank my six colleagues on the committee who gave so selflessly of their time and who put so much effort and energy into the work of the committee. I want to thank especially my two Opposition colleagues, the
Hon. Member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet) who served as first vice-chairman of the committee and the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie), who was the second vicechairman of the committee. They, Sir, together with my colleagues on this side of the House, the Hon. Member for Argenteuil-Papineau (Mrs. Bourgault), the Hon. Member for Peace River (Mr. Cooper), the Hon. Member for Prince Edward-Hastings (Mr. Ellis) and the Hon. Member for Surrey-White Rock-North Delta (Mr. Friesen) were able to rise above narrow partisanship and take the broader view, thereby taking up the challenges presented to them by the Government and this House.
They brought to the task a personal commitment, a commitment to make this a better and more effective place to deal with the business of the nation. Critical to this was their commitment to enhance the role of the private Member. 1 want as well to acknowledge the work of the alternate members of the committee and the 83 Members of this House who made submissions to the committee.
We brought to our task almost 100 years of parliamentary experience. As well, we had the professional support of the most able people who serve us in this place. I mention this because of the many new Members of this House who came here 15 months ago full of high hopes and great expectations. 1 can say to them that the frustrations that they experienced are well known to us who were already here. They expected great things from us and their ongoing interest served as a constant reminder of the importance of our mandate and the challenge inherent in it.
The House will be interested in knowing that in the 55 formal meetings of the committee, which included visits to the national Parliaments of Great Britain, France, the Federal Republic of Germany and the United States, there was not one single division. There were no heated partisan exchanges. As a consequence, the committee was able to reach consensus on the 82 recommendations contained in the three reports. The result, in my opinion, is a package of reform which would change the way this place functions in an important and fundamental way-change the way it functions in an important and fundamental way for the benefit of all Canadians.
Therefore, tonight I express the hope that this will not be a partisan debate. Were we to engage in such a partisan exchange we would destroy not only the letter but the spirit of these reforms. We are not here to score partisan points in this debate. We are not here to discuss the benefits or emoluments accruing to Members. Nor, Sir, for that matter are we here to cater to the complacent and the self-satisfied.
The fundamental question that each of us should ask ourselves tonight is what do the people of Canada expect of us? Are we who are here on their behalf satisfied with the way we conduct the business of this nation? Are we satisfied with the procedures already in place to hold the Crown accountable for the way it spends the taxpayers' money? What you have before you tonight are the efforts of seven private Members who attempted in the recommendations of the committee to address these important questions.
December 4, 1985

I would like now to pay tribute to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) for it was the commitment of the Prime Minister to the people of Canada to reform Parliament that resulted in the setting up of the special committee. The first priority of this Government in the Speech from the Throne called for the setting up of this special committee. I quote directly from the Speech from the Throne of last fall:
The central focus of this task force will be the enhancement of the role of the Private Member. From that prospect the task force will examine and make recommendations concerning the powers, practices, organization and resources of the House of Commons.
The Prime Minister never once wavered in that commitment. Not only that, he publicly supported the work of the committee throughout the life of its mandate. That commitment to this House by the Prime Minister can best be summed up by his words which, consequently, I found at page 823 of Hansard for December 3, 1984, one year ago, and I quote:
-what is emerging is a conflict between Parliament and the executive. 1 stand fully for the rights of Parliament.
Never in the history of this place has a Government, and I pay tribute to the Government House Leader, moved so quickly and so positively to implement the recommendations of a committee of this House. The recommendations of the first report which are now in place are dramatic testimony to that fact. When the Prime Minister agreed to give the committee the broadest possible mandate, he was by his vision challenging this House to reform itself. I hope, Sir, that we as Members of this House are up to that challenge.
Let me say that if we were to identify a philosophic thrust to the findings of this committee, it would have to be its attempt to enhance the role of the private Member and to provide for greater accountability by the executive to this House and its committees. That is the heart and soul of the committee's recommendations. That is what we at least attempted in our reports.
We have already set up legislative committees arising out of the recommendations of the first report. Let me say to my friend and colleague, the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Hnatyshyn), that I believe it was a mistake on the part of the committee to recommend a floor on the size of those committees. In retrospect I believe that was a mistake. That would have been better left as a question to be negotiated by the Leaders of the House, through the work of the Striking Committee. I do not say that to address the configuration of this House because that would be a mistake, if we were to address the reforms to this Parliament. I say that because I think that is much better way to go about the business of the House. However, I would like to say this parenthetically: when we made that recommendation, we never envisaged a situation of having more than six or seven Bills before a committee at any one time, as that had been the record of the House up to that time. I would say to the House and to the leadership of the House that neither was it our intention that these legislative committees be struck after first reading. They were to be struck after second reading and that is clearly explicit in the
Reform of the House of Commons
recommendations of the committee. 1 hope the House will take that suggestion seriously.
I would like now to move on to the specifics of the Government's response to the committee's second and third reports. Time will not allow me to deal with all the recommendations, all the changes that have been made as a result of some of these recommendations, or every response of the Government for that matter. Rather, I would like to highlight some of the areas that the House may wish to reconsider, and indeed the Government House Leader in a spirit of reform may wish to reconsider.
To its credit, and to the credit of the Government House Leader, the Government is for the most part in the process of moving toward implementing many of the recommendations of the second and third reports. However, I am concerned about a number of areas and I will refer now to two recommendations contained in the second report.
The first concerns new voting procedures. I would like to have some explanation in this regard, that the 30-minute bell proposed in the Government's response would only be an interim measure in place until the House installed electronic voting devices. Otherwise, it would make no sense. After examining the experience of the electronic voting system in the U.S. House of Representatives, one would see that to have the machines activated for 30 minutes would really make no sense. What we are recommending here is that for the 15 minutes while the bells are ringing, the machines would be open and Members would come to vote. This must be taken as well in the context of the attitude of the House toward the convention of confidence, something which I believe has to change. We made no recommendations there but we addressed the matter in narrative form. The Minister has dealt with that as well.
I am also worried by the proposed changes in the Standing Orders as they relate to the new voting procedure. Paragraph 4 of the proposed Standing Order 13 seems to indicate that either the Government or the Opposition could delay any vote while the bells were ringing for a period of one day. I hope 1 am reading that wrong. This proposed change would certainly make the job of the Party Whips easier, but I think it would dramatically alter the accepted principle of the House and how it votes. It would be a backward step. For example, any contentious vote could simply be delayed until the Parties were satisfied they had the numbers here to deal with it. That is not reform.
In the committee's recommendations concerning the precincts of Parliament, we recommended an intendant. We did that because we were concerned that we had lost control over this place and its precincts. We acted from evidence presented to us by former Speakers and present Speakers. Things are happening here that do not have any reference to Parliament at all. Just a few months ago, they put a marquee tent on the grounds of Parliament, something which had no reference to this place. We had the sound and light show learning up the

December 4, 1985
Reform of the House of Commons
grounds of this place to turn the front lawn into a carnival without any reference to this place.
Surely we are responsible for this place and not the Department of Public Works or the bureaucrats from the National Capital Commission. I would plead with the Government not to tamper with that recommendation so that the proposed parliamentary intendant would become merely a co-ordinator between the Department of Public Works, the National Capital Commission, the Speaker of the House and the Speaker of the Senate. We want him to be in charge of this place, to execute our wishes on behalf of the people of Canada and to enhance and preserve this important part of Canada's national heritage.
Other than that, 1 am satisfied that the Government has moved with regard to the implementation of the recommendations of the second report. I hope the Minister or the House will reconsider those points, because the Government to its credit has not presented its response in a partisan fashion. It wants to hear from the House. I congratulate the Government House Leader and his colleagues for arranging for this debate.
The third report was tabled in the House on June 18 and is the basis for new provisional Standing Orders which will take effect next month.
One of the series of recommendations that we made in the first report was that all questions relating to confidence be removed from the Standing Orders. We did that because we felt that this was not the role of the Chair. It is not for the Chair to say when a Government should resign, when it has lost the confidence of the House or when it should not. That judgment and the responsibility for that judgment must be taken by the Government. Yet we have references to confidence restored to the Standing Orders by defining what is a free vote.
How can the Chair define what is or is not a free vote? How will the Chair be able to enforce the Standing Order if a Government is defeated on a measure which is defined in the Standing Orders as confidence yet the Government of the day decides not to resign? What happens then? The Chair is then left in the position of having a Standing Order that it in fact cannot enforce. I hope the Minister will give some thought to that.
We talked at great length about the myth surrounding questions of confidence that has grown up in this country. Governments should not have to resign when they are defeated on a Bill. All Parliament is saying is that we do not like the Bill, bring back a better one. If the Government gets defeated on a Budget, obviously it cannot function as it cannot get its Supply and it must resign. If it is defeated on a specific, explicit vote of confidence, then clearly it has to resign. But surely we should put in place reforms that will give the House an opportunity to express itself on legislation.
We know just as much if not more than those faceless people in the PCO who draft these Bills. Surely we should be given the opportunity to improve them. I would hope that the Government will take to heart the words of the eminent
constitutional expert, Senator Forsey, who produced a 323-page paper for the committee on the convention of confidence. He said: "Questions of confidence and their definition are best kept out of the Standing Orders altogether".
If we adopted the attitude necessary to restore to the House a new approach to the so-called confidence convention, we would by that very fact be restoring to the House an important role in the legislative function, a role which I do not believe it now has because there are no surprises in this House any more. We know how we are going to vote on every Bill that comes before the House because the Whips are on on every Bill. We asked a representative from Britain about the three-line Whips. He said that they have used the three-line Whip there so often that it has become a feather duster. We have used the three-line Whip in this country on every Bill. It is about time we changed that.
If I want to vote against a Bill because it is not in the interests of my constituents that should not mean that I have no confidence in the Government I support; nor should it mean that I am a maverick who makes the headlines and the national news that night. When we in the House reach the stage that that fact no longer makes news, we will have achieved one of the greatest reforms in the history of this Parliament.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext:
There are two other areas on which I wish to touch very briefly. We as a committee working with consensus felt that the heart and soul of parliamentary reform and the enhancement of the role of the private Member could best be done through a new committee system. We recommended a new Standing Committee system, and in order to ensure the independence of that committee system we recommended it be given its own budget, have its own ongoing mandate, be better equipped to hold the Government accountable during the examination of Estimates, and that Parliamentary Secretaries be excluded from membership on the committees.
There is a very important role for Parliamentary Secretaries to play and that is in piloting Bills through the legislative committees. In my view, they have no role on the Standing Committees. They may observe the proceedings but they should not in any way attempt, as surrogates of the Government, to interfere with the process of concensus and collegial-ity that will hopefully emerge from that new Standing Committee system.
Finally, I hope that the Government will accept our recommendations regarding Private Member's Business. Surely, that is something the House can deal with itself. My friend, the Hon. Member for Peace River, took the lead in putting those reforms together. It is one of the area, apart from the new committee system, about which we are most excited as members of the committee. We hope that the Government will give us a chance to function as legislators. The only way we can truly and fully function as legislators is if a new system with
December 4, 1985

regard to Private Member's Business is brought in. In this way, Bills will have a chance to become law. The last Private Member's Bill which became law in this place was a Bill establishing the beaver as Canada's national symbol. Who will take us seriously if we conduct ourselves in that fashion?
1 will not indulge myself on the time of the House. This is a special debate by Special Order. I have 20 minutes and my time is up. I wish to say to the House, the Government House Leader the Prime Minister and his colleagues in the Government how grateful I am for the opportunity which was given to me as one member of the committee to be a part of what I consider to be this exciting process of reform.
I hope in saying this that the Government will not lose the spirit which prompted it to start this reform process in the first place because if there is one thing this Government will be remembered for, among all others, it will be its determination to reform this place in order to make it more meaningful for the people of Canada.

subtopic: REFORM OF THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in this special debate tonight and I would like, at the outset of my remarks, to congratulate the chairman of the special committee on the reform of the House of Commons, the previous speaker, for the speech he just delivered, but especially for the outstanding work he has done as chairman of that special committee. In my view, he was an inspiration for all members of the committee and he prompted us to work in a non partisan fashion. Our job was excessively difficult in some regards but I believe the results have been well received and even applauded like no other report from a Parliamentary committee has ever been before.
The media unanimously paid tribute to the hon. member who presided over that committee and unanimously expressed the hope that the Government will implement as soon as possible the recommendations contained in what is commonly referred to as the McGrath report.
That explains why I was somewhat surprised, Mr. Speaker, when I read the response to the recommendations contained in the second and third reports from the special committee on the reform of the House of Commons, response which has been submitted to us last October by the Government House Leader.
I suggest the recommendations made public at that time by the House leader can be viewed in two different ways. On the one hand, one can say that the government seems to be prepared to accept almost all recommendations suggested by the special committee. This approach, this reaction is of course that of an optimist. On the other hand, a pessimistic or partisan member of Parliament could react in an exactly opposite way because when one examines very carefully the response of the government, one realizes that only one of the
Reform of the House of Commons seven recommendations made in the second report is in fact immediately accepted by the government and that the six remaining are to be subjected to additional studies, consideration and discussion within the new Board of internal economy.
As for the third report from the committee, the government is telling us that it only accepts one third of the recommendations, that it wants to see further discussion about another third of the recommendations and that the last third is not accepted at all.
Well, Mr. Speaker, I am not sure whether, when rising tonight, I can consider myself an optimist or a pessimist. But 1 want to say this to government members, that we, as members of Parliament, every one of us, collectively, have a unique opportunity to operate a major, meaningful reform benefiting the institution of Parliament and all members, whether they sit on your right or youi left, Mr. Speaker. And 1 suggest it would be unfortunate if, through misunderstanding or hesitation on the part of the government, we were to miss the boat on parliamentary reform.
I am prepared to accept the word of the Government when it says it is in a favourable frame of mind about this. However, I believe that this report which results from the assiduous work of all members of the special committee must be accepted in its entirety. The fact of the matter, Mr. Speaker, is that we have worked in a spirit of consensus, in a non partisan fashion. 1 am sure that the representative from the New Democratic Party who was sitting on that committee alongside with me would agree with me that we have agreed to some things in the best interests of Parliament even though we knew that for us, in the opposition, for the Liberal Party as well as for the New Democratic Party, some of these recommendations would not necessarily be well received by all our colleagues from the opposition. We accepted these compromises because, on the other side, the Government Members sitting in the committee were also willing to make certain compromises and non-partisan suggestions in the best interests of the Canadian Parliament.
The Government cannot now pick and choose in the document which has been presented to us and accept only those recommendations which it might find more interesting and reject other recommendations because they seem to favour the Opposition.
I believe that the balance which we have been able to maintain through the work of the Committee Members is a delicate one, and that it is essential that it be respected by the Government. Otherwise the package of recommendations made by the Special Committee on the Reform of the House of Commons will make no sense.
If we were to accept only the recommendations which favour the Government, it is obvious that the objective of parliamentary reform would not be reached. Essentially, Mr. Speaker, what our Committee tried to do is to bring to bear an

December 4, 1985
Reform of the House of Commons element of freshness, a new approach to Parliamentary procedure which puts more emphasis on the individual Member of Parliament. This does not mean the Ministers, Parliamentary Secretaries or Members of a political party, whether in the Government or in the Opposition, but the Members democratically elected by the public to represent their views in the Canadian Parliament. Throughout our work, we always kept one thing in mind, namely the obligation of parliamentarian to reassert the value of our institution in the eyes of the Canadian public. We should not delude ourselves. We have to face the brutal truth. Many Canadians have lost confidence in politicians. Many Canadians no longer see the Member of Parliament as someone with an important role in Canadian politics. If we want our democratic institution to have some meaning and usefulness, it is essential that we give back to the population a minimum of confidence in its representatives in the Canadian Parliament. 1 believe that this is still the fundamental purpose of parliamentary reform.
I would like to say that the first report to be approved by the Committee chaired by the former Member of this House who is now Senator Tom Lefebvre included a series of recommendations which were nearly identical to the recommendations accepted unanimously by the three political parties in the previous Legislature.
However, 1 have to say with some regret, Mr. Speaker, that three of the recommendations contained in this first report are not being rigourously applied and followed by this Government. The first of course concerns the legislative committees. We had recommended that legislative committees be created after the second reading stage, but that the Government also be able to decide after second reading that a bill would be referred to a Committee of the whole for consideration.
The Government obviously had a choice in dealing with bills. They could be referred either to a Committee of the Whole, to a legislative committee or even to a Standing Committee of the House. However, at the present time, there is a proliferation of legislative committees, much too many compared with what we had envisioned at the Special Committee on the Reform of the House of Commons, and certainly also with the views of the Lefebvre Committee, which had never recommended such a proliferation of legislative committees.
Yet, there are now 13 legislative committees, although seven only are active. Why were six other committees struck if they are not to meet and do worthwhile work? It is my view that something went wrong with respect to the spirit, if not to the very concept of the use of legislative committees.
Secondly, we had mentioned appointing Members of Parliament, Private Members, back-benchers to the Committee on Internal Administration, because as suggested earlier by the Hon. Member who spoke before me, the Hon. Member for St.
John's East (Mr. McGrath), it is important that Members of Parliament should control the administration of their own institution. Of course we have no objection to House Leaders from the three parties sitting on that Committee.
However, it may happen that they will not always be as nice and civilized as the three present House Leaders, and the spirit of cooperation now prevailing between House Leaders could also deteriorate. It would be too bad, and most unfortunate were the Committee on Internal Administration to become just another forum for discussion between House Leaders. 1 simply wanted to point that out, because we believe it is very important that the other committee members besides the two Ministers, the Speaker and Deputy Speaker who play an important role on that Commiteee, be actually Members of Parliament, not necessarily Officers of the House, but actual Members of Parliament.
Finally, the provision concerning Ministers' statements is something we wanted, but on this side of the House we have been somewhat amazed to see to what extent the Governement can take to the letter of the new procedure. What I mean is that Ministers' statements must be delivered in an orderly manner, and the least we can expect is that there should be some advanced notice because, as you know, Mr. Speaker, Ministers' statements are made after the oral question period, and proceedings go on after normal hours at 6, 6:30 p.m. We ask for advanced notice at least on the day before such Ministers' statements are made-I am not asking Ministers who will be making statements to send their documents, but at least to notify the Opposition that there will be a Minister's statement the next day-in order that on this side we may, at least prepare for the debates for a period somewhat longer than after 6 p.m. Those are the comments I wanted to make concerning the second report.
I want to commend the Government for deciding to proceed with parliamentary reform. The fact that they accepted the first report is a very clear signal that they wish to implement parliamentary reform, but one thing I woud like to suggest this evening is that in order to have a genuine parliamentary reform, the second and third reports have to be implemented almost entirely. Failing this, we of the Opposition will have been somewhat gypped in the co-operative effort made at that non-partisan committee to arrive at a series of recommendations which in my view are most fair to all Members of Parliament, whether we are Government or Opposition Members.
My major concern is with some proposals made in response to that report by the Government House Leader. I cannot understand in particular why he does not accept the suggestion concerning the in-depth consideration of the estimates. We believe-a view that was shared by all Members from both sides of the House-that the consideration of the estimates is practically a farce. The way it is done leads to a minimum of scrutiny in the discussion of the estimates of various Depart-
December 4, 1985

merits. And it is our view that strengthening the MP's role depends on the opportunity for that Member to make a more thorough study of the various expenditures of Canadian Government Departments. What we have suggested, in view of our parliamentary tradition and precedents .. . We did not want to change completely this review of budgetary estimates, but we thought that Committee Members who will look into these estimates should not only have the right or the privilege to put questions for a few minutes to civil servants or ministers, but also to ask a series of questions to officials concerning the activities and spending of their Department, and to obtain a written reply in time to make it possible for Committee Members to carry out a better informed and more useful study of a particular Department.
I cannot understand why the Government has not accepted this recommendation. 1 can assure the Government that this suggestion had been made not only to benefit Members of the Opposition, but also in response to the wishes expressed by Government Members. I dare hope that we can find a formula which will satisfy the Government so that these questions which could be tabled with the Clerk of the House in an appropriate form may be accepted and answered before consideration of the estimates.
Mr. Speaker, I see that unfortunately my time is just about up. To conclude, I should simply like to say that 20 minutes to describe the great experience which I have lived with my colleagues on the Special Committee on Reform is not enough. I want to thank all of them for their co-operation, understanding, and I hope that the Government will remember that this document is so valuable that it should be accepted in full, not just in part.

subtopic: REFORM OF THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I want to begin this evening by expressing my congratulations to the Government House Leader for instigating this debate before any resolution of the recommendations made to the House by the Committee on the Reform of the House of Commons took place. I am glad to see that this is indeed happening.
I also want to congratulate the Hon. Member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) with whom I have had the pleasure to work in two special committees dealing with parliamentary reform.
In that respect I want to say that tonight we are nearing the end of a stage which really could be said to go back to 1979 when the Hon. Walter Baker, the predecessor of the current President of the Privy Council (Mr. Hnatyshyn), brought in a position paper on parliamentary reform of the Government at that time.
Since that time of course we had in the last Parliament the Special Committee on Standing Orders and Procedures chaired by the former Member of Parliament, now Senator
Reform of the House of Commons
Tom Lefebvre. I had the opportunity to serve on that committee as the vice-chairman and as well in this Parliament as vice-chairman on the Special Committee on the Reform of the House of Commons.
I recall these things because I want to be clear that what we are talking about tonight is the accumulated consensus of the opinions of many Members of Parliament from all sides of the House. If I understand the history of parliamentary reform correctly, we are nearing the end of what has been a truly remarkable process. Going back to the last Parliament, leading up to this very moment, we have seen a remarkable process whereby consensus rather than division and partisanship has been the rule of the day. I feel that 1 as a Member of Parliament have been privileged to be a part of that process for as long as I have. I estimate that I have probably attended about 95 per cent of all of the meetings that have been held on parliamentary reform since the bells rang for 16 days.
During that time I have had the privilege to see the best side of many Members of Parliament and the best side of what Parliament can be. I say that tonight because 1 am, as I hope it can be said of me throughout the process, not out to pick a fight with anybody. I do not want what I say tonight to be understood in that way at all, but I want to say some things in what I hope will be a strong and convincing way about how I think this process should come to a successful end. It needs to be nursed to a final conclusion consistent with the spirit that has imbued the process from the very beginning.
The Goverment has a special responsibility in this respect because if the process is to end as it began with consensus then the Government must not flinch as it faces the final stage of parliamentary reform-or at least the final stage in this stage of parliamentary reform, because we know that the process of reform is ongoing. The Government must not falter in the respect it has previously and consistently shown for the consensus arrived at by the Special Committee on the Reform of the House of Commons.
It can fairly be said that the Progressive Conservative Party has demonstrated a consistent interest in and support for parliamentary reform. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), to his credit, as was said by the Hon. Member for St. John's East, has made it a centrepiece of his claim to represent a new era in Canadian political life. I say to the Prime Minister, through you, Mr. Speaker, do not back off now; reconsider some of the ways in which the Government's response to our final report needlessly tinkers with some of the recommendations, with little or no reason offered for doing so, in many cases; reconsider the ways in which it significantly violates both the letter and the spirit of our reform particularly as it pertains to the question of the confidence convention, and to the matter of parliamentary secretaries sitting on standing committees. I will elaborate in more detail in just a few minutes on those two matters.
But first I want to say a word about something that has arisen more as a problem than as a principle, and that has to do with the way the recommendation on legislative committees has unfolded. We know there is a problem with the legislative

December 4, 1985
Reform of the House of Commons committees, that people feel Members are overloaded with work and that there are too many committees. I think we have to acknowledge a couple of things here, and make a few suggestions about which I think can be easy consensus.
First of all the committee, in its imagining of how legislative committees would work, always imagined the legislative committees working simultaneously with smaller standing committees. I understand the mechanics of what the Government wanted to do, and rightly so; to introduce our second report. So they did, and that brought about legislative committees. Our smaller standing committees were in the third report fully, so there was a chronological difficulty there. Let us keep that in mind when we are critical of the existence of legislative committees, as some Members have been. Hopefully it is only a matter of time before they exist alongside smaller standing committees. That will help to ease the problem.
It will also help to ease the problem if, at the same time as we initiate the next stage of reform, we also more to make the number of Members required on legislative committees more flexible. I do not want to second guess the work of the committee, but I think that we should have recommended more flexibility for the size of legislative committees. We did not, but I think there is a consensus in the House that it will be possible to have smaller committees for noncontroversial legislation and larger ones for legislation which is seen to be politically controversial.
I think there is also a consensus that there should be some kind of traffic control on the creation of legislative committees. There should be only a given number of legislative committees sitting at one time. There are various ways in which we could do that and I will not use up my time suggesting them. However, I think it is important for Members to realize that the problems with legislative committees are solvable and that we should not allow transitional irritants to lessen our enthusiasm for reform. My concern with legislative committees to this date has not been with the possibility of them working as we intended them to, but that in the short run they have made some Members skeptical about the reform process.
I will now turn to the two elements of the Government's response to our final report which I find to be the most troublesome. The first and the most troublesome has to do with parliamentary secretaries sitting on standing committees.
As you know, the committee recommended that there be smaller standing committees with seven members and the Government responded by recommending standing committees with eight members and parliamentary secretaries. We recommended that the committees have a form of tenured membership with Members selecting their own alternates. This will, hopefully, develop a sense of collegiality that will provide better scrutiny of and accountability for the various departments which these standing committees will mirror than we have seen to date.
I say to the President of the Privy Council that what all Members and the public imagine for these committees and, falsely, for present committees, is an independence from the Government which will be impossible if parliamentary secretaries are allowed to sit on those committees. I say that with no disrespect to persons who are presently or may in the future be parliamentary secretaries. It is just in the nature of the beast that this will be the case.
The Government argues that parliamentary secretaries will play an important role in liaising with the Minister. Mr. Speaker, if we get these new committees and if they are as important and as meaningful as we want them to be, the job of liaising with the Minister can easily be done by a capable chairman of a committee. The chairperson will still be appointed by the Government rather than by the Speaker as is the case with legislative committees. That chairperson can work with the Minister and the Minister will have more inclination to keep channels open with these new committees than he may have had in the past with former standing committees.
As long as there is a parliamentary secretary sitting there feeling, quite naturally, some obligation to defend Government policy, the Minister, or the department, and to report back to the Minister about what has been going on there will be inhibition of the free, frank and independent collegiality that we want to have developed on committees. It just cannot happen if parliamentary secretaries are allowed to be on committees.
Imagine a standing committee coming to a unanimous decision that a judgment or an action of the Government or a department is to be criticized. A parliamentary secretary could not very well make unanimous a recommendation of a committee which was critical of his Minister or department. Let us think about that recommendation because I believe it goes to the heart of reform. If the Government does not change its mind on that it will be very, very difficult for me to be supportive of any conclusion we arrive at. However, I will do my very best because I want this to result in consensus, if at all possible.
I would now like to speak about the issue of confidence. The whole gist of our recommendation up to and including the final report was to deproceduralize confidence. That is the reason we recommended that the language of confidence be taken out of the Standing Orders, and presumably that is the reason it was accepted. That has already been done. We did that because we wanted the question of confidence to be explicitly political rather than a procedural maze in which Members could find refuge when they wanted to as was often the case, and Members of all Parties were guilty of it.
Motions of supply on Opposition days were procedurally matters of confidence so people said that they had to vote with the Government even though they were really against testing the cruise, for example. That is one example. But people in all political Parties were guilty of using that procedural reality in a number of ways which debased the coinage, if you will, of what Parliament is all about, that is, standing up and being
December 4, 1985

counted for what you really think about an issue and being answerable to your constituents for that.
What the Government proposes is not only a violation of what the committee recommended, but if the President of the Privy Council moves ahead with this he is asking for an incredible number of problems just in terms of trying to define what confidence is. As has been suggested before, having that in the Standing Orders and putting the Speaker in the position of having to rule on Standing Orders that deal with whether the Government will stand or fall is an incredible position in which to put the Chair. That is certainly quite the opposite of what we contemplated when we recommended that all reference to confidence be taken out of the Standing Orders and that only those motions that are explicit motions of non-confidence in the Government be so regarded. The Government will continue to have the freedom, at the political level, to say what is confidence and what is not.
The idea is to give the Government the flexibility to say that it pays attention to Parliament and because a particular Bill was defeated, either in the House or in committee, it will go back to the drawing board and have another look at it rather than being caught up in a codification of what confidence is all about.
I say to the Government House Leader, who I know has great respect for the common law tradition, that he should not try his hand at any other tradition at this point. I would refer Hon. Members to various studies conducted by Doctor Forsey and Doctor Norton for the special committee in which the case for this is outlined at great length and quite convincingly.
With respect to the question of recorded divisions, I could be satisfied if what the Government has recommended is seen as an interim measure and that it intends to go ahead with our recommendation of conducting a vote while a 15-minute bell is ringing. When that recommendation is finally implemented, we will not have the possibility of House Leaders deciding to defer a vote during the time it is being taken. That is possible in the Government's response. It may not be significant in this Parliament but one can imagine the problems that might occur in a minority Parliament where pressure could be on people overnight if a vote could be delayed by people interested in the outcome once the vote had started.
The Government's response with respect to the precincts of Parliament is a half-hearted acceptance of our recommendation for the establishment of a Parliamentary Intendant. I do not understand why the Government could not have accepted our recommendation to establish a Parliamentary Intendant and that we gather to ourselves all the various and confusing jurisdictions that now exist with respect to how Parliament Hill is administered. We would then have some control over our own lives. We would be accountable to the Canadian people for what is seen to be related to us. Too often we have been put in a position of not knowing what is happening. An example which was already mentioned is when construction was taking place about which we knew nothing.
Reform of the House of Commons
If time permitted, I would comment on many other questions. However, 1 believe I have spoken to the two issues that are most important to me. They are the ways in which 1 believe the Government is tempting itself to set itself against the momentum which has been created for some years now. We have done so much and made so much possible that it would be a shame to fail in this eleventh hour. It would be a shame for the Government to fail by backing off in crucial ways as it is tempting itself to do. I hope that as a result of the debate tonight, and as a result of whatever process remains before there is final agreement, the Government will reconsider those very important areas that are now at variance with what the committee recommended.
