speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, thank you for giving me this opportunity to participate in this debate. 1 must say that this is a very special evening because in the six years that I have been in Parliament this subject has become a love of mine. It is a subject that is important to me and one that I think is extremely important, not only to this institution but to the people whom we represent throughout Canada.
Tonight I want to begin by acknowledging the Chairman of the Committee, the Hon. Member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath). He is a tenacious, demanding task master and 1 think it is very much to his credit that we as a committee were able to come forward with these recommendations. He pushed and worked us hard. I often remember getting off an airplane after a hard weekend in my riding only to know that there was a phone call from the chairman with a message that we were about to go back to work. It was a tough ongoing process and 1 pay him the greatest compliment I can by saying how much we appreciate his work. It was because of his work that we have what is before us tonight.
I also want to pause for a moment to mention the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney). When this debate began and the committee was given this job, I recall frequent comments that the Prime Minister, although new, would never go through with this change. It was said that he would pull the rug out from under us so that this would not happen. As stated by the chairman, the Prime Minister supported us throughout the process. He listened to our concerns and I believe he has responded to our report.
I also want to mention the Government House Leader who has made this debate possible. That in itself is a reflection of the kind of work we were doing in committee. We believed that when important reports came to the House there should be some discussion of those reports. Tonight we are seeing that in a real, intensive debate that gives each of us an opportunity to express our opinions.
I must also thank my colleagues from both sides of the House who worked with me on the committee. When we look at the membership of that committee we see a quite unlikely group to arrive at a consensus on a report. It is an unlikely group that would go through some of the discussions and

December 4, 1985
Reform of the House of Commons decisions which we made without a vote to arrive at a consensus.
If one considers the structure of this committee, it is no accident that it arrived at many of the reforms and recommendations it did. For example, it is no accident that it was recommended that there be seven members on standing committees. We picked seven members because our committee was made up of seven members from all sides of the House who were able to get together to confront an issue that we all believed was important. Therefore, I want to say a very special thanks to each of those members.
I also want to mention the staff who worked with us, some of whom are watching the debate tonight from the gallery, some of whom are at the Table, and some who are watching on television. They gave their all to make this evening possible.
I want to mention one final group. As we went through this reform process, people talked about the responsibilities of the Government, the responsibilities of the so-called McGrath committee and the responsibilities of the House Leaders. However, throughout the whole report there is the responsibility of Members of Parliament.
Reform, no matter how wise, how effective and practical, will not work unless Members of Parliament have the courage and the desire to make it work. My concern is that once we move from this stage into practising some of the recommendations we have put forward on a provisional basis, the success of those recommendations will very much depend on the understanding and demonstrated concern of all Members of Parliament from both sides of the House.
Let me move to the issue on which I want to focus tonight. In many ways, I think this question personifies what we in the committee were trying to accomplish. The area I want to talk about concerns Private Members' Business. It deals with the whole issue we were trying to address in terms of parliamentary reform. I came here in 1980. Since then I have watched the process of Private Members' Bills and Private Members' motions. I have found it one of the most humiliating, frustrating and perhaps most useless processes in which any Member of Parliament can engage.
In his remarks, the chairman of the committee referred to the last private members' Bill that was passed concerning the symbolism of the beaver for Canada. That is a picture of what has been happening with Private Members' Bills but, more important, I think it is a picture of what has been happening to private Members in the House of Commons of Canada.
I have chosen tonight, in the few moments I have, to focus my remarks on this particular area and to put forward my concerns and ideas about why we have to proceed with the reform of Private Members' Hour. A Private Members' Hour with teeth and with opportunity for private Members would change the way that we as Members of Parliament look at this institution. It would change the way that the Government looks at private Members. As well, it would change the way Canadian people look at their own Members of Parliament,
the role of MPs, the institution called the House of Commons, and the Government as well. It is crucial to come to grips with that.
For a few moments I should like to talk about some of the fundamental elements which I feel are absolutely essential in a proper and effective Private Members' Hour. The first element is that any subject an Hon. Member wishes to bring before the House has to have at least the chance of a vote. Otherwise, it is nothing more than talking in the wind, nothing more than speaking for the record, nothing more than rhetoric. It has no chance for action; it has no chance to demonstrate a concern, and it has certainly no chance to make a change to the country.
We have recommended that any Private Member's Bill which comes forward should go before a committee of selection, comprised of our peers, to discuss whether or not the Bill should have the opportunity to come to a vote. That is absolutely fundamental and essential. If that is allowed to happen, then all of a sudden there is a reason for those of us who are private Members in the House to take an interest in a subject, to seek a solution and to go out to try to achieve some action. That is the first element which I think is important.
The second one which I felt was important was the whole idea of other Members of Parliament being able to say "I support" the Hon. Member from whatever riding it may be. Then, as we begin to work, not only individually but collectively as Private Members of Parliament, we begin to impact on this institution and ultimately on the nation. My dream and my ideal would be to see an Hon. Member come forward with a Private Member's Bill, have some seconders sitting around him, but also someone from the other side seconding his or her motion. It would then demonstrate that private Members are trying to take control of some of the responsibilities given to them by their peers and by their constituents.
Another area about which we talked in this reform was that a Private Member's Bill, once introduced in the House, must have an opportunity for thorough debate. I have sat through Private Members' Hour here; all of us have. We have watched what happens. Hon. Members rise to speak on subjects which are important to them, only to have two or three speakers come after them often filling time, because if they manage to talk the clock out, the Bills die and the potential for opportunity or change is finished. Thus, all we have engaged in is an exercise in frustration. However, if we had the ability to vote, the ability to attract others to demonstrate their support for what we are working on and a designated time for debate, then Private Members' Bills would take on a whole new dimension.
I see you signalling, Mr. Speaker, that my time is coming to an end already. It is difficult, after the work we have done in committee, for those of us who love this institution and feel that the work we are doing here is important to express it in just a few moments. In closing, I believe that if we change the way in which Private Members' Bills and Motions are viewed in the House of Commons, we will change the way that Canadian people, our constituents and we, as Members of Parliament, view this whole place. Then we will have a House
December 4, 1985

of Commons which relates to, brings dignity to and really accomplishes what the Canadian people dream about, talk about and hope for.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) and those who worked with him on the McGrath committee stand in the company of a determined and dedicated few who continue to believe most fervently that Parliament, this greatest of democratic institutions, stands always in the need of reform. 1 believe the Hon. Member for St. John's East, himself an outstanding parliamentarian and a reformer, knows that the road to parliamentary reform is not one that is well travelled.
It was in the year 1830 that the Prime Minister of England, who was so out of touch with reality and with the demand for parliamentary reform in his country, was able to say in the House of Commons: "The legislature posesses the full and entire confidence of the country", and he was wrong. Two years later he was out of office and, in 1832, the Parliament of Great Britain got its first reform Bill.
I simply mention that because I believe that the citizens of Canada today know that their Parliament is not serving them as well as it should or could. This institution today, to a significant degree, lacks public confidence. It desperately needs to be changed. It needs to be reformed. If we do not understand that and do not believe that, then we too are out of touch.
The report of the McGrath committee is a radical report, but it is radical in the very best sense of the meaning of that word, that is to say, it goes to the root of the problem. This report does not merely tinker and dabble and rearrange our Standing Orders. Of course, the procedures and rules of our House are vital to orderly and democratic disposition of the nation's business. Our orders ensure as much as possible the smooth operation of Parliament, enabling the Government to govern but to do so under the close scrutiny of the peoples' representatives.
More than just procedural reform, the McGrath committee calls for attitudinal changes on the part of Hon. Members, Ministers, party Leaders and Whips.

speechtext:
Of course the McGrath committee saw the need for more effective committees to monitor carefully the performance and spending of government departments. As much as we look to the Auditor General as one of our allies, we cannot rely upon him entirely to do everything for us. We, too, every one of us, have been elected as watchdogs of the public purse. We have a responsibility to do as good a job as we can and to be allies with the Auditor General to see that taxpayers get the best deal for their dollars.
With rare insight, however, the McGrath committee saw what is a central and persistent problem with the Canadian parliamentary system. Our parliamentary system is dominat-
Reform of the House of Commons ed, controlled, manipulated and at times even suffocated and exploited by a far too powerful executive branch of Government. The legislative branch in our system is alarmingly weak. There is in Canada a serious and extreme imbalance between the executive branch and the legislative branch. That is our essential problem.
What is the result? It is that we have a parliamentary system in Canada which is underdeveloped, immature, retarded and defective. For example, in what other Parliament of the world are Members referred to as sheep or trained seals? Can we imagine one of those appellations being applied to a Member of the United States Congress or even to most Members of the United Kingdom House of Commons? Certainly not. Among most MPs there is a prevailing sense of frustration. Ours is a full-time job to be sure, yet there is such limited room in which to manoeuvre as one seeks to serve his or her constituents. Around here, to have an independent mind, to have one'w own thoughts on some public policy issue, to buck Party disciline is to be what, a maverick, a loner? In our heart of hearts, do we not admire those who display such courage?
Just the other day magnificient words of respect were paid to our late colleague, Max Saltsman, a man who fought for himself, a man who acted and spoke always in the best interests of his constituents. Would not every one of us be proud if those kinds of words could be uttered about us when we are no longer active in this place or no longer present on this earth?
From the very outset the McGrath committee defined the problem as it saw it. I quote:
The purpose of the reform of the House of Commons in 1985 is to restore to private Members an effective legislative function, to give them a meaningful role in the formation of public policy and, in so doing, to restore the House of Commons to its rightful place in the Canadian political process.
With this in mind, the McGrath committee examined the principle or the convention of confidence; that is, that every vote in the House of Commons is in some way a direct threat to the credibility, to the acceptability or even to the right of the Government to govern. What a ridiculous convention that is.
The McGrath committee concluded that Party lines would become more flexible if there could be a change of attitude on the part of MPs, the Government and the Party Leaders. That is the way to essential parliamentary reform rather than by simply changing the rules of procedure. The McGrath committee has argued very effectively and convincingly that it is up to Members themselves to prove their independent spirit and the Government should avoid raising the question of confidence at every turn. It does not serve it well, it does not serve Parliament well.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, the ball is in our court. It is up to us as Members to reform this institution that I think most of us respect and even love. I wonder how we are going to respond.

Reform of the House of Commons

subtopic: REFORM OF THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to say at the outset that I will be eternally grateful for having had the opportunity to serve on this committee. I would echo the words of the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie) that it has been an opportunity to see the best of the institution and the best of the other Members of this House. I believe it is worth mentioning again that we brought together recommendations that should bring about sweeping reform, almost radical reform of this place, and we did it without a vote. It was a committee that represented all Parties of this House and we did it without a vote. If that, does nothing else, it ought to prove that we can get a lot of work done here without confrontation, argument and bickering if only we will get close enough to other Members to establish some kind of trust. We can set aside some of our ideological differences for the betterment of the institution and the country if only we will put some trust in other persons, get close enough so that we know them and have confidence in them. We can do away with the confrontation, accomplish a lot more and work for the welfare of our country.
There are three reasons I was interested in working on this committee. I want to say how pleased I was that the first working statement in the Speech from the Throne by our Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) was the statement calling for the establishment of a task force that would enhance the role of the private Member. You cannot enhance the role of the private Member unless you free him. What you have to do is emancipate the private Member.
The private Member gains his authority from the people who elected him. When we come together as a House of Commons representing all of our Parties, representing the entire country, we become the aggregation of the voice of the people. However, to come here as a private Member and find that legislation and policy has already been drafted by people who were not elected and find that you are supposed to give the stamp of approval to something over which you had no voice is unsavoury. We need to emancipate him.
Therefore, it is central to any kind of reform that we deal with an ocean of confidence, as other Members have already said. We cannot free the private Member if at the same time we enslave him to the work of the bureaucracy. We cannot free the private Member if he is made to feel that he has to obey slavishly the Party line and thereby neglect the wishes of his constituents, the particular part of the country that he represents, and overlook the mandate that his people have given him in some cases. Therefore the notion of confidence is central to the emancipation of the private Member.
What will happen the first time a private Member or private Members vote against their Party? There will be first of all a psychological rupture within that particular caucus. Imagine what the press gallery will say the day after that vote has been taken. "Aha, there is a split in the Party ranks of the Government", or "The Liberal Party is split again", or "The New Democratic Party is fractured". If we are not careful, we will allow ourselves to be pistol-whipped by the press because we are afraid of the image we will create. Therefore, we will fall
back into the chains and the slavery to which we have become so comfortably accustomed.
We will have to overcome that psychological slavery. There will have to be some political will on the part of private Members to take the initiative on a Bill on which they feel strongly to vote against the majority of their colleagues and their caucus. Some day that will happen and we will have to suffer the fall-out. We had better have the courage to do that.
I say to my colleagues that it is easier to accept the status quo. It is more courageous to adopt a change that will free us all. I would urge, as other Members have, that the notion of confidence be adopted in such a way that the Government or the opposition Parties will have to take the initiative to declare what is a matter of confidence in that instance. Therefore, my first concern on becoming a member of this committee was the motion of confidence, the opportunity to free us all and be able to represent our constituents in a much more accurate way than we have been able to do in the past.
The second reason I was concerned about this work was the whole notion of Orders in Council, the practice and use of Orders in Council, otherwise called delegated legislation. I remember several years ago talking about what we call the emergency planning orders and how easily the Government of the day slipped massive powers into its hands by an Order in Council which is not fair to call secret, but which was quiet, easy and had the force of law. There was no way in which the House at that time could overcome those Orders in Council. Now to find that we have the means of neutering those massive powers that the Government has accumulated, over the years, and the means of giving back to the Members the opportunity to negate some of those powers which the Cabinet has taken for itself, it is very important that when the Committee on Regulations and Statutory Instruments meets that it take the initiative to nullify those Orders in Council it finds offensive to the freedom of the private Member.
The third issue to which the committee addressed itself that I think is important is the matter of private Members as has been so well stated by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Peace River (Mr. Cooper). We must have a guaranteed vote. I can tell Hon. Members that I worked for six years on a private Member's Bill. I flogged the House with it. It was a Bill dealing with the matter of parental abduction. The former Government did adopt it as part of its legislative package back in 1982, something for which I am grateful. However, why should it take six years? Why should children in those six years have had to undergo the threat of abduction simply because the legislation referring to abduction happened to be a private Member's Bill?
If a private Member sees a need and wants to reflect a need, that is not a matter of Government policy but reflects a concern expressed in his constituency or in a narrow constituency across the country, why should he not have the opportunity to do so? I say to Hon. Members that the biggest problem that we in the House have had to face has been a commitment
December 4, 1985

to the status quo. We need a commitment to changing the past. We cannot afford to be defensive about the flaws that we will continue to see in the Standing Orders we will bring forward. There are going to be mistakes made. The Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie) has already pointed out the flaws in some of the changes we have made. That is a human institution. It is a human committee. We will need to make further changes. We cannot afford to be defensive about the flaws in the system. We must take the initiative. We must have the courage to change the flaws before we get accustomed to them.
The greatest danger that 1 see is the commitment to the status quo. It is easier to stay the same. I would like to commend the Government and the Government House Leader for adopting the measures that the committee has presented through recommendations so that sweeping reform is now possible. I would urge that we not be committed to the present as it is, but that we continue to look for ways in which the role of the private Member can be enhanced so that he can be emancipated in order to represent the people of Canada in a much more accurate and wholesome way.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to have the opportunity to speak on this debate this evening. At the outset, I would like to extend my congratulations to the Hon. Member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) for the tremendous amount of work and effort he along with his committee has put into this report for the benefit of the House and all Parliamentarians. I would like to let him know that I as an individual appreciate it very, very much.

subtopic: REFORM OF THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: REFORM OF THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
I know one member of the committee a little better than I know others and that is the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie). He has been a champion within our own caucus for parliamentary reform and has studiously apprised the caucus of the work of the committee as it went through this process. Individual members of my Party were kept aware of what was going on. I appreciate that as well as do other members of my Party.
If I may be permitted to do so, because it is key to the remarks I want to make this evening, I would refer to one of my first experiences on a standing committee of the House after I was first elected in 1980. When I was elected, like most Members of Parliament, I thought I was coming to the House of Commons in Ottawa to participate in great debate. I thought 1 was coming here to act as an individual Member of Parliament not only on behalf of my own constituents but in the best interests of Canada generally. I hoped in that role to do something to better the lot of all citizens around the world. I must say that that impression was rapidly savaged.
My clear impression of the first several years I spent in this place was that it was one long, continuous, all-candidates' debate, such as the ones we see during election campaigns. I saw very little evidence of Members of Parliament working together in the common interests of the people of Canada. We
Reform of the House of Commons seemed to be much more interested in adopting positions as political Parties rather than as a group of people working in the best interests of Canadians, with one exception. There was one saving grace to that and it occurred on the Standing Committee on Health and Welfare.
My first meeting of a standing committee was of the Standing Committee on Health and Welfare. Stanley Knowles took me to that committee. Stanley had to leave and he said to me: "You keep an eye on things". So I said that was fine, but what I was supposed to keep an eye on I had absolutely no idea.
The then Minister of National Health and Welfare came before that committee and made a broad, general statement on policy. The Hon. Member for St. John's East decided to ask the Minister some questions; he did so. Then the Chairman said: "Mr. Young," and I said: "Yeah?" He said: "Would you like to ask questions on behalf of your Party?" The Hon. Member for St. John's East leaned over to me and said: "You're supposed to ask questions, Scotty".
I dreamed up some quick questions to ask the Minister which were promptly ruled out of order because 1 was not discussing some particular vote of which no one had ever heard except the Clerk of the Committee, and perhaps the Chairman of the Committee. So I got into a dispute with the Chairman and decided I should exercise my authority as a Member and challenge the Chair. The Hon. Member for St. John's East leaned over again and said: "It's not an NDP convention, Scotty. You can't challenge Chairs around here". The Hon. Member for St. John's East jumped in there because he knew I was a new Member and he argued for my rights as a Member of Parliament to ask the Minister questions. The committee agreed and I appreciated that. It was an example to me of how this place should operate. Every one of us should be supportive of each other, regardless of political Party affiliation.
Having said that, I would note that since the last election there have been some 100 new Members elected to the House of Commons. I think it has made a difference. It has brought a fresh point of view to this place, and certainly to Standing Committees. I have found the standing committees to be somewhat less partisan merely because people have minds which are more open than they were before. That is no reflection on the previous Parliament or the previous Government, because I do not think that had anything to do with it. It was the tradition and the history of this place that had led to the stifling of debate.
I have found that the newest Members of this place are less likely to fall into that trap. Certainly in committees on which 1 have sat Government Members have been more willing to go after the Minister involved if they did not like what that Minister was doing. They would question the Minister just as strongly as members of the Opposition were likely to do.
On the question of parliamentary reform, 1 had the opportunity to serve as chairman of a legislative committee which examined a Bill referred to it. That was a great experience. It

December 4, 1985
Reform of the House of Commons
is a refreshing approach to the way we do things in this place. I must admit that when I sat in the chair and called the meeting to order a few members who have been around the Elouse for a long time looked at me in wonder as if to say: "What is he doing up there?" Eventually, one of them finally said it: "What are you doing up there?" I said: "Under parliamentary reform and the changes which have taken place in the House of Commons, the Speaker has appointed me as Chairman of this committee". "Yes?" they said. And I said: "Yes". I explained what was happening in terms of parliamentary reform. I have to hand it to those Members, it took them about ten minutes, but they finally accepted a member of the NDP chairing a legislative committee. As we went through the Bill a strange thing happened. Members of the committee no longer looked upon me as being a member of the New Democratic Party caucus. They started to look upon me as the Chairman of the committee. To people outside this place that may sound strange, but in here it is extremely important. Members from all sides of the House must participate in all functions of this place as equal and responsible Members.
The reforms which we have initiated thus far have taken us a long way down the road to achieving that end. A number of different Members have been appointed to chair committees. That does not mean to say there have not been problems. Of course, there have been problems. Change does not take place without creating some problems. That is so because what is happening is changing from something which is old to something which is new. In many cases that newness creates a resistance on the part of some people because they do not want to accept it.
That is not to say that some of the problems have not been real-they have been real. Personally, I think the size of legislative committees is far too huge. They are too unwieldy. I do not know why we need 20 Members to discuss a piece of legislation. There is an obvious lack of research capability in these committees. I would much rather see a committee have an independent reserach capability of the Members' choosing as opposed to the way it is done now. It would make the committees much more effective. What I mean to say is, put in place a reserach capability which is permanent, as is the case with standing committees, as opposed to having different researchers at different times depending upon the subject of debate.
I see some problems with respect to the matter of research and with the size of committees. The difficulties we have at the present time are the result of an overabundance of committees. This places tremendous pressures on the time allocation of individual Members. I think that will be straightened out when the second or third report of the committee is adopted.
I see that my time is up. I thank Hon. Members. I hope we can get on with it.

subtopic: REFORM OF THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am particularly pleased indeed to speak tonight on the subject of parliamentary reform as I was appointed as a new Member
of Parliament to sit with my colleagues on that Special Committee on Parliamentary Reform, and I wish to take this opportunity tonight to express my thanks first and foremost to the House Leader who gave me the opportunity to be a member of that committee, and also to thank with all my heart my colleagues, and in particular the Hon. Member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath), the Hon. Member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet), and my colleagues here on the Government side who supported me at all times, because as you know, Mr. Speaker, I joined that committee as a new Member of Parliament with great expectations ... and I had another problem: I was not very fluent in English.
The committee therefore was a tremendous school of parliamentary procedure for me as a newcomer to the House of Commons. I did not know at the time that I would become so deeply involved in parliamentary reform and procedure. That committee also gave me the opportunity, Mr. Speaker, to get a free English course so to speak. I therefore thank my colleagues for their co-operation and help at all times so that 1 might become a full-fledged member of that committee like the rest of them.
In looking at this House tonight, Mr. Speaker, it is interesting to see that so many Members are present at 8:30 p.m. on a Wednesday night, and the reason is that they are interested in parliamentary reform. Not only are those Members interested, Mr. Speaker, but also all the Members of provincial legislatures in Canada. Other countries are also interested, as shown by the fact that the main debate at the 25th Annual Meeting of the Commonwealth Association which we hosted last summer centered around the Special Committee on the Reform of the House of Commons. The private sector is also interested in parliamentary reform. The Hon. Member for Papineau and myself were invited not very long ago before a group of Montreal businessmen who are very concerned with the reform process, and who asked us to tell them about our experience; they asked us: What is in fact parliamentary reform, and what is it going to mean for us, as citizens, as business people? Most of those individuals come from time to time as witnesses before our committees and, with the advent of television in Parliament, those groups were not sure that their views, their suggestions were really considered by the Government, when they came before a committee.
So I was pleased to meet them, and of course, we told them about our experience with the work of the Committee.
My colleague from Peace River (Mr. Cooper) was ahead of me, Mr. Speaker, because it was important for me too to raise the matter of the Private Members' Hour, between 5 p.m. and 6 p.m. I had myself the opportunity to experience recently the fact that after that one hour, after 6 p.m., it is over, it is gone, I do not know where . . . Mr. Speaker, one day, I would appreciate if you would show me the boxes of papers you must have in the anterooms of the Government. I would like to know what you do with all those documents, what happens to the
December 4, 1985

incredible work done by Hon. Members to bring forward a notice of motion, to debate it, and to know how many hours our staff puts in to enable us to have an interesting debate, to get our bill passed. I am interested in the volunteer sector. I have another motion, Mr. Speaker. As long as I sit in this House, I will put forward motions to enhance the role of volunteers in our society, every six months, as long as that matter is not passed at a certain time somewhere, at the first or second reading stage, in a committee ... I don't give up easily.
Now, I echo what my colleague from Peace River said about bills. So, in order not to repeat myself, because as you know, ten minutes is a short time, and I would have so many things to say .. .
Mr. Speaker, you know, according to an English saying, "You will never get another chance to give a first good impression." You will understand that. Well. When one comes to this House as a new Member, one is in for quite an experience. Now the biggest ceremony ... Of course, the Clerk is a charming man who welcomes us with the usual courtesy, except that we are sworn in almost in secret. And when the Speech from the Throne, the most important part of our Government... here we are, we poor ordinary members, behind the curtains of the High Chamber of the Senate, trying to see what is going on inside, that is our first impression. You know, one feels pretty small in such large surroundings and our Government has agreed to the principle, for which I am very greatful, that collective oath taking ceremonies would be interesting for new Members of Parliament and even for those who have been around for a long time, and then the people of my riding would see me. The next morning, I got some phone calls: Mrs. Bourgault, I watched television, how come I did not see you, you were not sitting next to the Speaker, nor beside the Prime Minister. Where were you?
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, 1 did not dare tell them that I was at the back, trying to get a glimpse of what was going on inside the Senate Chamber. I could not tell them. It seems to me that I would have offensed them somehow.
I have too much respect for my constituents, and I am therefore very happy that in future, my colleagues, those who will follow us, the new Members of Parliament, will at least feel they are part of the big family and that together, we are sworn in for the good of all.
We have also dealt, Mr. Speaker, with the issue of the convention of confidence. Well, I do not want to repeat myself either. I share the views of my colleagues but I would like to add a few personal views regarding the concept of confidence. I have checked and since our proceedings are broadcast on television, a dramatic change has occurred. 1 was speaking today with the Hon. Member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle), because we happened to visit my riding together and he told me that he missed those happy times when there were substantive debates, heartfelt discussions, when Members were rising
Reform of the House of Commons and reacting on the spot. Now, some people are watching us on television. We now have the American C-SPAN Network that broadcasts our proceedings as well as, of course, Mr. Speaker, the great national show, Question Period.
Our constituents are always asking the same question: "What are you doing? How is it that when I visited the House of Commons last week, Mrs. Bourgault, you were not there?"
I tell them this: "Listen, I sit on committees, but committee proceedings are not televised". Therefore, ordinary citizens do not know .. . There is in Weir, in my riding, a constituent who watches the oral question period every day hoping to see me doing something. So it is important, Mr. Speaker. Leaving aside the principle of trust, I will say that the TV broadcasting of committee proceedings would make it possible for Hon. Members to tell their constituents: "If you want to know what I am doing, just watch me tonight, at such and such hour, because I will be sitting on the Agriculture Committee, which is of great interest to my riding".
The fact is that, outside of Parliament, there are the committees. People do not know well enough how Parliament operates. There are people who come and see us, and they are astounded. Perhaps there should be a system which would make it possible for these people to say: "Well, that is what a Member of the House of Commons does in his or her everyday life. When the House opens its doors at 10 o'clock in the morning, he or she is sitting on a committee." Well, if some committee proceedings were televised, we could at least tell our constituents that we are working.
Mr. Speaker, I see that you are trying to cut me off. 1 must regretfully say that I had a great many other things to say but I thank again the Government for allowing me to sit on that committee, and I hope that the Parliamentary reform . . . Mr. Speaker, I urge all Hon. Members to push for this Parliamentary reform, because it is far from being over. This process will certainly continue. Let us all try to sell this reform and make sure that the House becomes the major forum which all our constituents expect it to be.
Hon. Warren Allmand (Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine
East): Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to take part in this debate. I regret Hon. Members have only 10 minutes because there is so much in this report to comment upon. It would take much longer than that to do justice to the recommendations. Although I was not with the Special Committee on Reform, chaired by the Hon. Member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath), I was with the Committee on Reform in the last Parliament. It is a subject with which I have been struggling within this House for many years.
Before we consider what the role of this House should be, 1 believe we have to come to some decision as to what the goals of this Parliament should be. It is only by having some idea of

December 4, 1985
Reform of the House of Commons
what the goals of Parliament are that we can construct rules of the House to achieve those goals.
In considering that matter, I think the first thing we must deal with is that the rules of this House cannot be evaluated in terms of how they best serve Hon. Members here. They must always be looked at as to how they serve the Canadian public. What is the Canadian public interested in? First, we must have rules in the House of Commons that enable Canadians to believe that we can do the job for them, that we can deal with public issues and develop public policy and pass legislation. We must have credibility in this institution. I am afraid that at the present time, many Canadians do not believe that this institution is doing the job for them which they want done. In fact, many Canadians hold this House in disdain, and that is regrettable.
I believe Canadians want to see a parliamentary institution where all of the issues could be raised, not only national issues, but local and regional issues. They want those issues fully discussed and finally resolved. They also want an institution where Hon. Members can keep in touch with them. For that reason, of course, we should not be sitting all the time. Because if we sat too long and too often we would become a ghetto here in Ottawa and would lose contact with the people we are supposed to represent. We have to consider that aspect in developing our rules. We must have an opportunity to keep in touch with the people we represent, and we should do that not only on a personal and individual basis but through our parliamentary committees, subcommittees and so on.
It is my belief that Parliament should seek to accomplish three goals. It should be a legislature, a watch-dog and it should control the public purse. As a legislature, it usually deals with legislation prepared by the Government. As the saying goes, the Government proposes and Parliament disposes. However, in order to do that in an effective way we should be able to deal with legislation as we really believe it must be dealt with. If there is something lacking, we should be able to amend it or defeat it without fear of defeating the Government. Unfortunately, that is not the case at the present time. As many Hon. Members have already said, at the present time all Parties vote in unison without any consideration of their personal feelings with respect to Bills or measures put before this House.
Our role as legislators has to be improved. As watch-dogs, we try to keep the Government accountable and responsible and we do that through Question Period and through Motions for Production of Papers. We also do it through Opposition days. That system can be improved as well. In Parliament we can control as well the spending of money by the Government. We do that through the Budget debates and Budget votes and by supply days and our votes.
To accomplish all of these tasks this House has to be an effective forum where we can discuss those issues and put forward all the pros and cons, the majority and minority views. Sometimes the debate becomes hot, and sometimes it becomes unruly. I do not believe Canadians should be shocked when that happens. I say this because people come to this House
with strongly held views and policies. They come here with passion, in many cases. This is a place where those strongly held views result in confrontation. This is a place where we resolve those conflicting views. How fortunate we are that we have this House, when we consider that in countries like Lebanon, El Salvador, Ireland and Poland, and I could name many others, the great political issues of the day are not resolved in parliamentary institutions, but in the street and mountains with guns and bombs. So when things get a bit passionate here let us compare that with what we find in other parts of the world. Remember that of the 150 countries in the United Nations only 25 are democracies. Only 25 have forums like this where representatives can come together and fight out issues on the floor of the House in a very moving and passionate way. Once these issues are voted on and resolved here we accept them. We do not resort to terrorism, bombing or shooting it out in the streets.
I think that Canadians should understand that no matter how good our rules are, and I believe we need reform and 1 am going to get to that in a minute, there will always be partisan debate and strongly held differences.
Mr. Speaker, of course there have to be clearly understood and well defined rules, and we are dealing with that in this report. There has to be a balance between the Government and the Opposition, even when the ratio is 282 to 70. There has to be a balance between the front benches and the back benches so that the front benches are not in a dominant position all of the time. There has to be fairness to the third and fourth Parties. We have to consider, when we are adopting rules for this House, that there will not always be a majority Parliament. I have lived through three minority Parliaments. In one of those minority Parliaments there were four Parties in opposition. So when we are making the rules for Parliament we cannot just consider the stereotype that we have before us in 1985.
With respect to some of the specific recommendations in the report, I fully agree with the additional powers given to the committees, allowing the committees to commence investigations and studies and work on their own without references from the House. I fully support the fact that they are given independent research resources and so on, but I am not convinced at all that we need legislative committees. That is one proposal in the report about which the members of the committee will have to convince me.
At the present time the 282 Members of this House are spread so thin that we are not able to do the things that we must do as Members of Parliament. One must remember that as Members of Parliament we must be available for debate in this House. As well, at the present time we must be available to deal with 22 standing committees, nine special committees and, at last count, 15 legislative committees. We also have our caucuses and the responsibility to meet with lobby groups and groups coming here to make representations. We must return to our constituencies from time to time. We have Party
December 4, 1985

responsibilities. We have many things to do as Members of Parliament and this proposal to add on legislative committees in my opinion is not well founded and is not reform. I am willing to listen to more debate, but I am not convinced that it is reform. It is almost as if those who made that proposal felt that over here we would have one group of Members who would serve on the standing committees and there would be another group over here serving on the legislative committees. In fact, Mr. Speaker, it is the same Members who are expected to do both.
There have been days in the last few weeks when at nine o'clock in the morning we have had standing committees; at eleven o'clock we went to legislative committees that went on until five or six in the afternoon, and then we went back to standing committees again. I would like to hear more discussion on that.
Mr. Speaker, with respect to confidence, I fully agree with the measures that are put forward in the report on confidence.
I wish I had more time to discuss them.
With respect to voting procedures, I like the electronic voting but I cannot accept the fact that the vote must take place in 15 minutes. That would never work in a minority Parliament.
My final word, Mr. Speaker, is that there are some good things in the report, but we need a lot more discussion in this House before we reach a consensus among 282 Members on what that reform should be.

subtopic: REFORM OF THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to have this opportunity to say a few words in connection with the report of the Special Committee on the Reform of the House of Commons, and also on the Government response to this report. Many important issues and recommendations are dealt with both in the report and in the response. To begin, I would like to congratulate the special committee itself and the chairman of the special committee, the Hon. Member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) on the outstanding job they have done. I would like to congratulate as well the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) on being prepared to recommend the establishment of this committee and the adoption of the recommendations coming out of the committee. I would like to congratulate the House Leaders on their efforts to date in putting these recommendations into effect, and I hope that all three House Leaders will actually concur so that the recommendations can be put into effect.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: REFORM OF THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
I am a new Member of this House, as you know, Mr. Speaker, but two of the areas that have been dealt with by the committee particularly stand out in my mind. The first is the right of the private Member to speak out on behalf of his or her constituents in this House, and I might say, particularly the right of the Government supporters to do that. That may be of a concern to Opposition Members but it is certainly of much greater concern to Government supporters.
Reform of the House of Commons
As a new Member of this House I came here not knowing what to expect. I had great visions that we would be having new rules, that we would be having reform and that private Members would be able to speak out and speak their minds. 1 find, as we all have, that there are a number of barriers to this that prevent us from speaking out on behalf of our constituents as they expect us to do.
First, of course, is the whole concept of confidence itself, that parliamentary tradition and convention that says that every vote in this House is a vote of confidence, that if you vote against the Government the Government might fall and if you vote against the Government that is an indication that you do not have any confidence in the Government. That certainly is the number one barrier to a private Member speaking out on behalf of his constituents.
The second is perhaps the Government itself, and a number of the Hon. Members tonight have spoken about that. There is what I guess you would call a subtle pressure on the part of the Government to make sure that all of its Members speak with a common front. That is an understandable concern on the part of the Government because it has a legislative program, it has Government policies and it wants to see those policies and that program put into effect. So it is quite understandable that it wants to see them supported as unanimously as possible.
A third barrier to this whole process of speaking out on behalf of our constituents is in fact the members of one's own Party. There is within one's own Party a team spirit and a feeling that if in fact one speaks out and goes against the team that is breaking faith. So there is a group pressure, a peer pressure, if you will, to restrain particularly the private government Member from speaking out on behalf of his constituents.
A fourth barrier of course that has been mentioned also tonight is the press and the media. As soon as a private Member does speak out on behalf of his constituents, if it is in any way, shape or form in variance with the Government's position, right away the media seize upon those remarks as an indication that there is a division or a split and that perhaps that Member is a maverick. I myself have been referred to in the press in those terms and I undrestand what that means and what a potential barrier that is.
I guess the final barrier in my mind is the inhibitions of the individual Members themselves. I think when you add up all of these other barriers, the convention of confidence, the Government's feelings about private Members speaking up, their own colleagues' feelings about them speaking up and the press and the media, it is no wonder that individual Members have certain inhibitions about speaking their own minds and actually representing the true feelings of their constituents.
I have struggled with this problem since my arrival in the House of Commons. There have been a great many issues about which 1 have had some concern, and about which I know my constituents have had some concern. There have been a great many issues on which I have wanted to speak out. I did

December 4, 1985
Reform of the House of Commons
speak out on some of them and I felt the censure of the various barriers to which I referred as a result.
However, whether there are these inhibitions and barriers or not, it is clear to me that the people of the country, and certainly my constituents, expect me to speak out in their behalf. They expect me to speak up if there is a problem which affects them. If I do not, they do not understand. They do not know why I am not speaking out and representing their thoughts and feelings. They feel that perhaps I do not understand them. They feel that I am not sympathetic toward their concerns and views. They feel that I am not representing them properly and, at the bottom line, they feel that Parliament as an institution is not working.
I hope that this report and these recommendations are part of the answer to a great concern of the people of the country. They want to see their Member of Parliament, whether or not he or she is a Government supporter, speak out and represent their feelings and problems. That sort of thing can be answered in part by this report and by the Government's response, but it must be answered as well by the Parties in the House. It must be answered by the House Leaders. They must agree if we are to put these reforms into effect. I have heard a lot of comments tonight about how wonderful the recommendations are and how wonderful the Government's response is. However, the proof of the pudding is in the eating; it all depends on whether we actually adopt these recommendations. I trust that we will, after all is said and done.
There is one other thing in addition to that, Mr. Speaker. After we adopt these recommendations we will have to put them into effect-not only the words on a printed page but the spirit of them. Individual Members will have to be prepared to speak out to ensure that this works. I have with the existing rules and this is not very easy. I suspect it will not be very easy with the new rules either. If an individual Member speaks out he will feel the response from the Government, his Party and the media. All of the individual inhibitions which I mentioned will come out to stifle the spirit of these recommendations.
I am hopeful, Mr. Speaker, that we will be able to break out of those inhibitions, that we will have the courage of our conviction, that we will have the courage to utilize the rule changes which I hope will come. We must not do this in the way the Soviet Union does with its constitution, but in the way we in Canada and other western democratic nations have practised those things that are in black and white.
There is one other area which I think is very important, Mr. Speaker. I would like to commend the committee and the Government for the recommendations with respect to the parliamentary review of Order in Council appointments. I think that is very, very important. It was an issue in the election and has been an issue since. On September 9 the Prime Minister indicated that he was adopting those recommendations. I think it is essential that they be adopted as well as the other recommendations in order that, to use the Prime Minister's words of September 9, "We can revitalize the faith of the citizens of the country in their institutions and their government". Mr. Speaker, that revitalization is long overdue.

Mr. Speaker, I do not propose to take very long, but there are some things I want to say. First of all I would like to congratulate the members of the committee for the work they did. Although I do not agree entirely with every recommendation, without exception I would be prepared to see all the recommendations tried in the form in which they were recommended. I entrusted that committee with the job of reviewing the procedures of Parliament. Having been a part of the committee at one point, I know that it worked diligently to come up with recommendations which seemed to fit the changing times. Therefore, from my point of view, that which they recommended should be given a fair trial. I think that on balance that is in fact what is going to happen.
The one aspect that is always difficult when dealing with recommendations for change is the diverse nature of the change and the need to co-ordinate and to understand how one change impacts on another aspect of political life in order to ensure that we do not unnecessarily add to the burden in one area in an effort to cure what may well be a problem in another area. That falls, in some ways, to the House Leaders, myself and my colleagues.
I want to deal with another aspect of parliamentary life which I believe is necessary to be dealt with now, and that is time allocation but not time allocation as we see it on an irregular basis when the Government and its predecessor bring forward a motion designating a day or two to complete deliberations on a Bill. That kind of time allocation inevitably leads to political confrontation.
It is not that about which I am talking. I am talking about the allocation of the time of Parliament and of the time of Members of Parliament. How can we best utilize the hours that we have available to us? How can we, as Members of Parliament, both in Government and in opposition, establish a system that will allow the various and many agendas which we establish from time to time, either on a partisan or individual basis, to be met and the results to be fruitful?
I want to set out a challenge. Time allocation is the responsibility of every Member of Parliament. It is not simply the responsibility of Government; neither is it the responsibility of the collective opposition. It is everyone's responsibility. It is our time that is being allocated.
I suggest that there are two areas in which self-discipline will bring about time allocation. The first is in the process of dealing with Estimates. I recall when I served in another place. We developed a process whereby, knowing how many hours were available for the consideration of Estimates, we set out the priorities of each of the three caucuses. We decided on an annual basis which Estimates we wanted to go into in some detail and which Estimates we were prepared to pass with less investigation. This meant that over the life of a Parliament all of the major Estimates received careful consideration in some detail and certain of the less major, although not necessarily minor, Estimates received lesser consideration in terms of the time allotted to them.
December 4, 1985

We did that in the following way. We submitted our priorities and a group chosen from Parliament sat down and in turn priorized. If the first choice was that of the Official Opposition, that was put down as the first Estimate to be considered, followed by an Estimate chosen by the Government and then by an Estimate chosen by the third Party. This process was continued until we had gone through each of the Estimates. We then decided how much time was required to give fair opportunity for careful scrutiny, while at the same time recognizing that it was not open-ended and that each Estimate had to be given some review. I must say, in all fairness, that this system worked.
I would like to suggest that in the new year we consider a system that would allow that kind of consideration. In return for doing that I would expect, however, that the Minister, the Deputy Minister, and the officials requested by the Opposition would appear before the appropriate committee for the duration of the time agreed upon for those Estimates. There would, in fact, then be an opportunity to discuss, not only the details but also the political decisions relating to the details. I would commend that to the House for its consideration in dealing with Estimates. I have only touched on it but I think it bears some careful thought. I believe it would add to the public's sense that we are indeed requiring accountability in expenditures. It would follow in some ways the model that has been used by the Auditor General in conducting in depth reviews in certain years and somewhat less in depth reviews in other years.
Let me turn to legislation, which is the next major problem. I believe that the chairmen of the committees that have now been established should, in themselves, form a chairmen's committee. When legislation is referred to a committee, the chairman should meet with the steering committee of that legislative committee and work out a time frame within which the deliberations can be concluded. The chairman should then sit down with the other chairmen and together work out the schedule of work, taking into account that certain Bills will take longer than others. Then, in the process, committees will be assigned some heavy work and some lighter work so that they will be able to proceed in a more orderly way.
I say to the Government House Leader in the most friendly way that it ought not to be necessary for the Government to move time allocation, except in the most extraordinary circumstances. I believe that we should be able, together, to look at legislation and determine how long is reasonable time for dealing with it at second reading. We should be able, without fear of criticism publicly or otherwise, to determine within the time frame that we know is the parliamentary calendar how much time can reasonably be allocated for dealing with a piece of legislation at a particular stage. If 1 may say so, I do not recall when I made this point some years ago and got the wholehearted support of the then Official Opposition. I might get it now, since the then Official Opposition is in Government, but I may not get it from the present Official Opposition. However, I believe that in the interests of Parliament we
Reform of the House of Commons should seek that kind of understanding. The time we are talking about is not endless. The responsibility is to point out the flaws in the legislative program. However, the responsibility is to also deal with it.
1 suggest that when these new legislative proposals come into effect, albeit on a trial basis, together we should consider the three suggestions I have made and make every effort to live by them. It should not be a practice to breach them; they should only be breached as an exception.
Having said that, I look forward to the trial period. It will not be easy. We have to be patient and we must understand that not everything will work exactly the way we anticipated.

subtopic: REFORM OF THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be able to participate in this debate tonight on parliamentary reform because I believe it is one of the most important issues that will be dealt with in the House. 1 want to commend particularly the committee and the chairman of the committee for producing what I believe will be important wide ranging reforms.
Each of us brings his or her own perspective in the House. I have had a rather checkered political career. In a very short period of years I have been in opposition, a Government Member in a minority Government, I have been out of office and 1 have been a Government Member in a majority Government. I think I have just about covered all the bases in a very few years. I have come to some conclusions about the necessity of parliamentary reform as a result of seeing Parliament from the different aspects I have experienced in those few years.
I want to deal with three issues that are in the report and one issue that is not in the report but that 1 believe is important to parliamentary reform. I believe that parliamentary reform is necessary to have an effective Parliament and effective Members. The first issue was dealt with earlier, but I believe I can put a different perspective on it. It concerns votes of confidence.
I do not want my remarks to be misunderstood by the Opposition, my fellow Members or the press. I am proud of the record of our Government. I think we have had a solid economic performance, with good legislation. However, let me say quite frankly that I think the record could be improved with respect to legislation we have presented.
In some cases, 1 think legislation should have been amended in committee. I am not quite sure that I am ready to say that legislation should have been defeated, but I certainly see some cases where Government legislation may warrant defeat. I am not out to end my political career in martyrdom by trying to pick a Bill with which to defeat my own Government, but I think we are talking about an important principle. Members of a Government Party or indeed members of the Opposition should feel free be able to vote against a Bill if they feel strongly about it. It is important to recognize the pressure that can be put upon Members both by their own Party and indeed by the opposition Parties.
The Member for Cochrane-Superior (Mr. Penner) said earlier tonight that the onus is on the Government to free up its

December 4, 1985
Reform of the House of Commons
Members. Well, I would argue that if the system is going to work, the onus is equally on the Opposition. The onus is on the Opposition because the first time a Government Member breaks ranks, the temptation will be there in the Opposition to talk about the Tories being divided again, to say that they cannot stay united and so on. It is in their interests that we not go back to that old system. That will force the system back into the rigidity which we have had in the previous years.
I do not believe it will be the end of the world if a Government measure is defeated. Margaret Thatcher has a majority Government comparable in numbers, at least, if not percentages, to that of our Government. However, she has lost a number of Bills since she has been Prime Minister. No one is suggesting that Margaret Thatcher is weak because one of her Bills was defeated. Perhaps it is a reflection of a strong Parliament and strong individual Members of Parliament.
If and when a Government Bill is defeated, let the Opposition not use that to point out that it is due to a weak Prime Minister. It may not be our Prime Minister. It might not happen until another Parliament. However, let the Opposition recognize that it is the way Parliament should function if parliamentary reform is going to work.
The second issue dealt with by the committee is the issue of smaller standing committees with broader powers which can produce wide-ranging reports. Something which has struck me since I have been in Parliament-I have been in three-is the high quality of Members from all Parties. I have had the opportunity to work on many standing committees. Recently in this House, I worked on the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs when we were producing a report on child benefits. I also worked on the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs when we were working on the investigation of banks, trust companies and insurance companies.
I could list the members from my Party who impressed me, but perhaps I could make my point better by saying that on the Health, Welfare and Social Affairs Committee I particularly enjoyed working with the Member for Vancouver East (Ms. Mitchell) and the Member for Sudbury (Mr. Frith) because I thought that together we were able to produce something that was useful. Similarly, in the Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs Committee I enjoyed working with the Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) and the Member for Trinity (Miss Nicholson) to whom I never even had a chance to talk let alone get to know and find out how valuable and hard working she was as a Member.
The point I want to make is that I think we have a tremendous amount of talent in the House which, with parliamentary reform, can be used for the benefit of the country. As I see it, smaller committees with much more power can investigate matters that may not be that important to the Government of the day but can be important national issues on which there can be consensus. Just as the reform committee
was able to produce some pretty revolutionary ideas, I see the same thing happening under the new standing committees.
The third issue about which I want to speak briefly is the matter of Private Members' Business and allowing some of it to come to a vote. The system we have now where basically the Government decides which measures come to a vote is wrong. It should be a committee of private Members that decides what measures warrant coming to a vote. There are many Members bursting with ideas here which could be accepted. Perhaps they will not bring in the wide-ranging Bills a Minister is expected to bring in, but they could bring in measures which are important for the country and improve the quality of life of many people, regions or whatever. Allowing Members to designate which Private Members' Business comes to vote is a very important part of reform. I hope we can approach that issue in as non-partisan a manner as we have the reform committee itself.
I indicated that I wanted to speak briefly on a subject which was not covered by the report. 1 think it is an important subject when it comes to dealing with the effectiveness of Members and of Parliament. It concerns recognizing that Members have different responsibilities which in some ways are reflected by the size of their ridings. I happen to represent the most populous riding of the country, which is now some 10 times to 12 times the size of the smallest riding in Canada. The Hon. Member for Nunatsiaq (Mr. Suluk) represents a riding which I think is a little bigger than Europe. He has special responsibilities as a result of that. While those different demands on him are recognized in a very small way through the moneys available to Members, they are not adequately recognized. I do not think his ability to function as an effective private Member is really available to his constituents because of the constraints placed upon him. Certainly I feel the same, representing the largest riding in Canada.
I talked briefly about supporting or not supporting a Bill. I happen to support a Bill which is before the House right now dealing with redistribution. I also recognize that the new redistribution Bill cannot be brought into effect before 1988. I am somewhat terrified by the prospect of representing, not a quarter of a million constituents when the average is 85,000, but some 350,000 to 400,000 constituents by that time. In order to make Parliament effective, the House has to address the problem of what should be done for Members who represent very large geographic or remote ridings or Members who represent enormously growing ridings, so that they can be effective Members of Parliament, representing their constituents adequately and also representing their views adequately in a national forum.

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian Tobin (Humber-Port au Port-St. Barbe):

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise to participate in the debate on reform this evening. First let me say, "Amen and me too" to the last words uttered regarding the size of ridings and the facilities available to Members of Parliament, given various kinds of ridings-some of them are large and rural and others are heavily populated-and the current disparity which exists. That matter was not addressed in the report. I believe the
December 4, 1985

House can address it by way of the Internal Economy Commission, if we have the political will to do so.
Perhaps I represent, in some sense, the majority of Members of Parliament in respect of this reform exercise. I am one of those who did not pay a lot of attention to the exercise. I am one of those who did not participate by taking the time to come before the committee to understand what it was about and to make my views known. I am one of those who very nearly was not here tonight because I thought that what would happen was esoteric and would not make that much difference.
A few days ago I read, from beginning to end, the report of the reform committee. I really read it, rather than quickly look at the major recommendations and not give much thought to the exercise. I became excited about the reform process when I read the report. When I came here in 1980, like many new Members I believed, contrary to that famous quote by someone or other who said that parliamentarians 50 feet away from Parliament Hill were nobodies, that to be elected as a Member of Parliament was a great honour and privilege and was quite a serious responsibility, by the very nature of the fact that my constituents saw fit in an election campaign to send me here. 1 truly believed that my voice would count for something and that 1 could in a substantial and real way, as could every Member of Parliament, make a difference. I believed that my being here would count for something and that 1 would have some input if I was prepared to work hard. I discovered that it was not the case that parliamentarians were nobodies 50 feet from Parliament Hill, that the opposite was true, and once we got within 50 feet of this place we became nobodies. In our ridings the understanding of the mandate given to us was fairly clear. It was to speak in the House of Commons, to participate in the decision-making process and to exercise, bearing in mind our constituents' views, our best judgment in the final analysis. As a member of the Liberal Government of the day-and I am sure it is no different whatever Government is in power-I discovered that in order to get along I had to go along. I discovered that if I exercised an independent point of view or judgment, I would be considered a rabble-rouser or a rebel because I would be bucking the carefully laid plans of the executive branch of Government, and there were no rewards for that kind of attitude.
What does that teach Members of Parliament? What does that tell us? It tells us that the House of Commons-and this is somewhat of an exaggeration-is a little like Beirut. There is a green line running down the centre carpet, and a Member in his own caucus and in his own Party is best rewarded when he aims his gun across the way and pulls the trigger, irrespective of whether or not in his own best judgment his energies are truly being well spent and in a way which represents the best interests of his constituents.
There is a real opportunity for all of us, as a result of the report, the excellent work of the McGrath Committee and all members who served on it, to make a change. That is not to say that we will function in a parliamentary system where we are all chums, where we agree all the time and where we always operate with a consensus. That will not happen. There
Reform of the House of Commons will be times when we agree and when we disagree strongly. That is as it should be. However, we ought not to be disagreeing just for the sake of establishing Party lines and undertaking our responsibilities as Party people versus parliamentarians.
I have a couple of concerns to which 1 would like to see a positive Government response if the reform process is to work. One of those, and 1 believe the most important, is in the committee process and having parliamentary secretaries taken off those committees. I was a parliamentary secretary for three years. I will tell you what my job was. It was to understand the Minister's point of view, to understand what the Minister wanted to happen, to rally the majority of Members on the Government side, and I did that effectively, and to get the Bill through in exactly the manner in which the Minister proposed it or with the least possible change.
What happens when you set up that kind of system? Government Members initially resent being told how they should vote, what is acceptable and what is not. However, after a year find they cannot fight the system or, if they do fight the system, they are not rewarded. To the contrary, they become rabble-rousers in this place. They learn to come in, be a warm body, find out which way the Party is going and vote accordingly.
That is not because parliamentary secretaries have an inherent desire to run a dictatorial regime. It is not because the Government or even Ministers have an inherent desire to run a dictatorial regime. That is the system we have had. If we are going to continue to have parliamentary secretaries, and this is very important, sit on these committees, there must be an opportunity for Government Members and Opposition Members to reach a real consensus. Consensus means give and take. It means you do not get everything you want. However, you expect to see some sensitivity that at least people are listening to your ideas. Even if your ideas are rejected, there is some satisfaction in knowing that you at least had the opportunity, starting with the first clause of the Bill, to make your views known. Hopefully, people on all sides are listening to your point of view, accepting it or rejecting it for rational reasons.
I say to the Government House Leader that there is nothing more important, in my judgment, on the matters on which he reserved that needs to be corrected than this question. If this is not corrected, we will have changed the structure, but we will have presented a factor in the committee work that will make it impossible to have any kind of serious, objective consideration of government proposals.
It is strange when all of us realize that caucuses, which are the place where Parties should come together to develop policy, do not work that way. We all know what caucus is primarily used for, particularly if you are in Government. 1 have been there. Caucus is the escape valve where Members who cannot speak their mind because of the current make-up of the system go behind closed doors and let off steam. It is not only the escape valve but a red light indicator for the execu-

December 4, 1985
Reform of the House of Commons tive. The executive discover from time to time when matters are building up and the pressure is becoming extreme. That works in all caucuses, Opposition and Government. There is no better indicator that it is not just a minority of Members who feel the desire to operate as more independent agents or as agents of their constituents and their conscience in this House.
Tonight there is almost a magical mood in this House. I find it a fascinating experience to listen to parliamentarians on all sides. I sense the desire for real change. When the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria) was in the chair, he did a fine job, enjoying the confidence of Members on all sides of the House.
I close by simply saying that the majority of Members of this place are not here. I suppose most of them are like me. They are either late coming to the reform process, they have not paid much attention, or they are so cynical about the current structure that they think nothing can make any difference. We must address the question of parliamentary secretaries, the question of confidence, and address something which is terribly cloudy in the reform process. People are venting their frustration in the wrong way. Legislative committees have got out of control. They are too big and too numerous. That must be addressed immediately.
