speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it must indeed be a magical evening when I can stand up after the Hon. Member for Humber-Port au Port-St. Barbe (Mr. Tobin) and say I agree. For several years that has not been my experience and it is indeed a pleasure.
I sat here this evening remembering my sense of deep anguish during the constitutional debate and in the constitutional committee. My sense of anguish about the constitutional committee was that we had probably collected in that room from among the Members of the Senate and the House of Commons almost as good a group of Canadians in terms of their background and concern as was possible. We were able to call as witnesses the most informed group of Canadians in the country. When it came to amending that piece of legislation, the power did not lie with the Members who sat in that room. The power lay outside the room. We did not know who it was, but we knew that whoever it was, they did not have the time to listen to the witnesses, to share the sense of anguish or the sense of hope, whatever was there, and then use their judgment to produce a basic law for this country that would work.
What the parliamentary reform committee is proposing to this Chamber is not reform of the Chamber. It is a revolution for the Chamber. As is the case in all revolutions, you can espouse the cause, fire the guns and achieve the revolution, but there is a delicate period which follows as to whether the revolution will stick or disappear.
This evening I would like to direct by remarks, perhaps in a somewhat critical fashion, at some of the Government's response to some recommendations of the parliamentary reform committee. If we are really going to use the talents of the Members of this Chamber, and I concur with previous speakers who say that the notion of confidence and its use or
abuse lies at the very heart of the reform process, we must not have the tendency to think of that sense of confidence simply in terms of votes in this Chamber. In reality, the useful work which Members will do is more often in committees. The executive branch of Government must have confidence in those committees and in the wisdom of those committees to do a lot of the work.
I was sitting here this evening wondering if I am ever going to see a Minister come before a standing committee or legislative committee and say: "Here is a piece of legislation which represents the best thinking of the executive branch. What 1 want from you is a lot of hard work to see if you can make it better. Do not come back to me and ask me about my judgment. Simply call your witnesses, hire your experts, sit in dialogue together, take that piece of legislation and make it as good as you can".
If that were the set of instructions to a standing committee or a legislative committee, it would make the world for all of us a great deal more satisfying. More important, it would make legislation better. Legislation would be more sensitive to the reality of all parts of this country. What we have had in place up to this point is a set of bureaucrats who live in Ottawa. They may be in Justice and do the actual drafting or they may be in a policy analysis part of Government. They live here in Ottawa, they are captives of the Ottawa television stations, radio stations and newspapers. They do not understand the reality of Canada. It is Members of Parliament who were sent here to reflect that reality. Whatever we can do in this new revolution to free those Members up to do their jobs will work in the best interests of all parts of the country. That delicate situation relies on the political leaders. The risks are greatest for the Government and less so for the Opposition, but the leaders of all three political Parties and the sub-leaders within those Parties must demonstrate in the things they say and the ways they act a commitment to the processes that are possible within this place.
The part of the report on parliamentary reform about which I have thought the most and about which I know the most is the part about the role to be played by committees in the future. I was pleased to see that the Government simply agreed with Recommendation 4.1 which sets out the role of standing committees. However, the Government then began to deal with the structure of the standing committee system, and there we begin to disagree. I would like to suggest to the Government House Leader and the House Leaders of the other two Parties that they think about that a little more.
The biggest deviation from the philosophy of the reform committee's report as it affects standing committees is the decision by the Government to go to eight-person committees rather than seven and to include the parliamentary secretaries as the eighth person. When the Hon. Member for Burin-St. George's (Mr. Price), who had that kind of experience with the previous Government, laid out his concerns about it, I found myself nodding my head. I think he was dead on. There
December 4, 1985

is a role conflict, and that is what the committee told us and what our experience has told us. I hope that the Government will reconsider that in what is an experimental year.
There is nothing that stops a committee from co-operating with a parliamentary secretary and nothing that stops a committee from bringing the parliamentary secretary forward as a witness. However, having a parliamentary secretary as a member of the committee creates a problem regarding the issue of confidence. That is its biggest flaw. There is as well a secondary flaw. Any time there is a committee with an even number of members, more pressure is put on the committee when it comes to creating a quorum. It is easier to get four out of seven members together than it is to get five out of eight. I would hope that the Government would reconsider and return to seven-member committees as recommended in the report of the reform committee.
The other major area of disagreement I have with the Government is in its comments regarding the review of delegated legislation. All of us know that we are in a situation in which 3,500 to 4,000 Orders in Council are passed per year. All of us who have served on the Regulations and Statutory Instruments Committee know that the impact on people's lives from the publication of regulations can be and frequently is absolutely enormous. The regulations are more important in terms of impact than the actual legislation itself in most if not all instances. To leave the job of reviewing those regulations to one committee, a joint committee of the two Chambers, is to ask that committee to do the impossible. With the new setup for standing committees, if the Government were to go along with the committee's recommendation that standing committees be given the responsibility for reviewing the regulatory environment related to their areas of responsibility, I suggest that possible mistakes could be avoided and certainly regulations would be better promulgated.
I would make a brief comment on legislative committees. I would like to see them have from 10 to 30 members rather than thee present 20 to 30 members, and I would like to see their composition cut across committees. Someone from the Justice Committee should sit on every committee, as should someone familiar with finance. That way we could put a screen across a piece of legislation containing all of the different emphases Members might have.
I sent a letter to the committee recommending that we bring back evening sitting hours. I did that because I believe that if the House were not so sit until 2 p.m. four days per week, the sense of push and rush that all of us are feeling would be relieved. I know the committee did not accept my view, but it is my feeling, having experienced both systems, that one of the reasons Members do not have the time to think carefully, consider and learn enough about much legislation, is that we try to put too many things into too few hours in the course of a normal week.

subtopic: REFORM OF THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hope a few of the members of the public who watch the House of Commons during Question Period and see us as being the most undisciplined day nursery in the country will have had a
Reform of the House of Commons
chance to listen to this particular debate. I think it reflects Parliament at its best and gives us a chance to talk about some very serious concerns.
We are trying to reform this place and we are trying to ensure that the momentum for reform which built up in the last Parliament is continued. I do commend the members of the committee for their leadership and I also commend the Government, not for all of its responses but certainly for the fact that it is prepared to go a substantial way toward indicating its support for the recommendations.
I would like to talk mainly about committees tonight. Certainly in recent weeks we have experienced overload because of the overlap between the legislative committees and the larger standing committees which have different timetables. We now know that it is possible for an Hon. Member to begin his day at nine o'clock in the morning and wind it up at 10 o'clock or 11 o'clock at night and to have been in the House or committees continuously during that time. Frankly, that is exhausting and is not good in terms of the quality of work we can do. I do not think we can sustain it. That is why I would like to talk in some detail about some of the specific recommendations and ideas that I hope will be taken seriously by the House Leaders and the Government.
First, it is important that the new, smaller standing committees be independent. I happen to feel that to have only seven members on a committee with a permanent attachment may not be sufficient. My experience on the Public Accounts Committee and other committees on which I have played a part is that it is a bit like tag-team wrestling. Members do have many commitments in their ridings for speaking engagements and those sorts of things. Therefore, it seems to me that in addition to seven members on the standing committees, we should have a permanent alternative group of another seven who have some greater privileges and access to the committee minutes and agendas than other members. It should be expected that those members keep in touch with those committees and work very closely with the members to whom they are an alternative.
I do not think that a parliamentary secretary should be a full member of a committee. If the Government wants to assign a parliamentary secretary to sit in on meetings of a standing committee, exercising the right of any Member of the House to be there, I think that is fine. However, to have parliamentary secretariess on the steering committee and giving guidance to committees will, it seems to me, essentially undercut the independence of the committees. I certainly endorse the comments of the Hon. Member for Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes) and others on that particular question.
There is a danger in the fact that the legislative committees, because they are ad hoc and have no history, will not have give and take between Opposition and Government Members, something which I think makes a committee work particularly well. I am concerned over the fact that some of the committees on which I have sat have seen an effort by Government Members to guillotine debate and shut down the amount of time in which consideration of an important matter could take place.

December 4, 1985
Reform of the House of Commons Since there was no appeal, we wound up wrangling with each other and playing the kind of games that I think people are anxious to try to avoid.
While allocation of time is becoming more prevalent and the Government seems to have chosen to use closure on an almost continuous basis, there must be in committees some recognition of the rights of the Opposition as well. Given that there is no give and take because legislative committees are temporary, it seems to me that there should be some right of appeal so that Opposition Members may go to House Leaders and dispute decisions of legislative committees which seem to have been too rigid in terms of their allocation of time. It seems to me that we should not have a situation in which the Government is all take and no give in terms of the way the committees work, in terms of the witnesses they hear and in terms of the amount of time which is given to ventilate concerns over important pieces of legislation, such as the divorce legislation or the legislation dealing with family allowances. These issues will come up again and again.
I endorse the comments which suggest that the size of legislative committees should be made much more varied depending upon the importance of the issue and also upon whether or not an issue is controversial. Given that the committees have to work very quickly, consideration should be given to having research support on legislative committees and, occasionally, on standing committees, allocated to caucus, that is to say, on a partisan basis and not just allocated to the committee as a whole. With respect to particular Bills, there are times when we in the New Democratic Party, or members of the Liberal Party and maybe even Government Members want to develop a particular line of thinking. We do not have the resources in our offices to carry that out. Our caucus research staff is limited and cannot focus on these committees. Sometimes the hearings of a committee may go on for a long period of time and we need to have access to either partisan researchers, who are also attached to the Library of Parliament, or perhaps even people who come in on an ad hoc basis for particular considerations.
My next point deals with the question of timetabling. It is a long way from matters of principle. However, it is very germane to all of us who have experienced a meeting at 3.30 p.m., a meeting at 6 p.m. and a meeting at 8 p.m., have gone home exhausted and in a bad temper without having had a decent supper and not having been able to do a particularly good piece of work.
When the legislative committees began it was decided that they would sit when the House sat but the standing committees would not. 1 think that decision is wrong. At times standing committees took place on a very artificial schedule. They were blocked in to two meetings, one a 6 p.m. meeting and one a day-time meeting. They have important work and yet find it impossible to fit within that particular strait-jacket. We have had situations in the Public Accounts Committee, on which I sit, which needed to meet for three hours but was told
it had to quit at 11 a.m. to make room for legislative committees, even though on certain days no such committees were scheduled after that time.
I suggest the balance has gone too far. 1 suggest too much day-time has been allocated to legislative committees and not enough to standing committees. I suggest something which is a great deal more simple and perhaps more manageable. 1 suggest that the mornings be given to the standing committees and that the afternoons be given to legislative committees exclusively, that is, outside of the time for Question Period. Then, in the evenings, when committees will only meet if they are particularly preoccupied with a subject, standing or legislative committees should be allowed to spill over into the evening hours, whether it be 6 p.m. or 8 p.m. We could see how that would work after a trial period of one year.
Some flexibility is in order because certain committees, such as the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence, need a lot of time for their considerations. The Finance Committee, which is considering the Green Paper on financial institutions, needs a lot of time and should not have to be subjected to artificial limitations.
I am also concerned about the allocation of administration costs of the House of Commons to the committees. At the moment the cost for staff alone is estimated to be something more than $1,000 per committee meeting. That enters into the budget of a committee. That will make heavy costs which could be misunderstood and even discourage committees from meeting frequently, despite the fact that most of these costs are fixed costs of the House of Commons and not variable costs, as is the case with the cost of printing committee minutes and other matters which can probably be costed and charged to the committees. I am glad to see the Government House Leader (Mr. Hnatyshyn) nodding his head.
With respect to the question of costs, we should look at ways by which committees can reduce the costs of travel, possibly by having a stripped-down form of reporting and of translation or other means by which it is flexible enough for committees to travel without the feeling that it will cost $5,000 or $6,000 a day, a sum which is felt to be intolerable.
In the limited time I have available to me, I also suggest that we should be looking at ways by which committees can communicate what they are doing to the public and call for witnesses without the need to spend $30,000 or $40,000 to advertise in every major daily newspaper across the country. That could well come into part of the public relations effort within the Speaker's office. Perhaps there should be a weekly journal of Parliament which is easy to understand and which could include notices of committee meetings calling for witnesses or informing the public about consideration of particular pieces of legislation. We could then make that journal available at a low subscription cost to every public library and newspaper in the country. Something in that respect could be part of an effort which should be made in order to find means to communicate what Parliament is doing.
The suggestion that the parliamentary channel be expanded and turned into a sort of Canadian version of C-SPAN is a
December 4, 1985

good one. The suggestion that committees be televised but that those televised versions of committees be run at night when the proceedings of Parliament are no longer on is also a good one.
The suggestion which I make now is that parliamentary notices with respect to committees seeking witnesses and so on should be on the parliamentary channel every morning between eight o'clock and nine o'clock. In this way people would know to look at the channel at that time. That should be encouraged.
The suggestion with respect to interpretive material on Parliament being televised on the channel and also in a Museum of Parliament, perhaps where the Postal Museum used to be, should be considered. The suggestion that we should try to find ways to interpret what this place is doing to visitors who come to Canada is something which is also a good idea.
Perhaps these ideas stray somewhat from what is contained in the report of the committee. However, I think they are all part of a desire that many members share, which is to make Parliament relevant and ensure that Parliament is seen to be relevant.

subtopic: REFORM OF THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a great pleasure for me to participate in this debate with respect to the reform of the House of Commons. Since I became a Member of this House approximately 17 or 18 months ago it gives me particular pleasure to take part in a debate in which we are talking about reform of the institution which represents the people of Canada.
With respect to the proposal regarding the reform of the House of Commons, I would like to restrict my remarks to the recommendation of a standing committee which suggests that there be a standing committee on human rights established. I think it is important in 1985 that a standing committee on human rights should be established. I would like to elaborate on that point.
In 1982, the Charter of Rights and Freedoms was passed by the House of Commons. There was a delay experienced with respect to one section of the Charter. I refer to Section 15. This section of the Charter refers to equality, that is, that every individual is equal before the law, has the protection of the law and receives the benefits of the law. This section of the Charter came into force on April 17, 1985. When it came into force, the previous administration had done little to prepare for this three-year delay. Of course, the delay was facilitated to change programs and laws in order that they could comply with Section 15. When my Party took office in September of 1984, very little had been done in terms of preparing legislation and changing programs to comply with Section 15 of the Charter. Thus, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Crosbie) brought in an omnibus Bill which changed minor items. In addition, he established a parliamentary committee formed by members of all Parties of the House to review programs and legislation.
Last summer and spring I had the opportunity to serve as vice-chairmen of the subcommittee dealing with equality rights. As all Members know, this committee was charged with
Reform of the House of Commons the responsibility of reviewing federal laws and statutes in order to determine if they conformed with Section 15 of the Charter of Rights. The work of our committee was crucial in helping develop a practical and sensible approach to equality issues under the Charter. Our report Equality for All covered a wide range of issues which demanded immediate attention.
I believe it is important for the work of the Equality Committee to go on, and it is important that that work go on here, in Parliament, carried out by parliamentarians. Therefore, I propose, consistent with the recommendations in both the McGrath Report and in the Equality for All Report, that a Standing Committee on Human Rights be established to deal with the important equality issues surrounding Section 15. The Equality for All Report listed three key reasons for an ongoing assessment of federal laws in light of Section 15 by a standing committee. First, a mechanism for public input into the process of addressing Section 15 to the wishes and needs of the community is very important. Under the current committee system, that mechanism does not exist.
Second, future Government policies or programs which are introduced into the House as legislation, may not conform to the Charter and, therefore, that legislation would merit scrutiny by a Human Rights Standing Committee.
Third, an all-Party committee would be in a position to review the Charter conformity of federal laws, providing the opportunity and enabling the examination of that legislation with input from witnesses attending that standing committee. That, in my opinion, would assist the Ministers of the Crown who are often consumed with the details and intricacies of the legislation. The standing committee would give us the overview representing all the regions of the country.
If there is one important message which came through loud and clear during the cross-country hearings of the Equality Rights Committee, it is that Canadians are very interested about how their Charter will affect their lives. Those concerns will continue to arise as our legal system grapples with the details and complexities of Section 15. Therefore, it is most important that Parliament deal with these issues as opposed to putting these issues into the hands of the lawyers or the courts. It is most important that we as parliamentarians continue to work toward practical application of the Charter which will fulfill the great principles of equality, justice and fairness for which this country has always stood.
The issues raised in the Equality for All Report represent only the beginning of a long and exciting process of clarifying our Charter and applying it to Canadian society. Let us make Parliament a part of that process by establishing a Human Rights Committee which will address the fundamental equality issues this country is now facing and those it will face in the future.

subtopic: REFORM OF THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I take some pleasure in participating in this debate, mainly because the wisdom of whoever drafted the motion that this

December 4, 1985
Reform of the House of Commons House take note of the matter of reform of the House of Commons has given us all a chance to address the issue of reform in the House, and many other matters.
Since the end of June of last year, we have been operating under a different set of rules. We adopted, I believe, on June 27, some modifications to our rules which were inspired, in part, by the special committee of the House chaired by my friend, the Hon. Member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath). These were supported, I believe by most Members of the committee-at least all those I have come in contact with-in the spirit of trying to make this place more relevant to the issues of modern society and more understandable to Canadians.
I do not want to address all of the issues because none of us could do that in just 10 minutes. But since we have been operating since June under certain rules, I would like, as Party Whip of the Liberal Opposition, to make a few comments on how we have done with the new rules since September. I do not believe we can operate without a foundation of trust among the House Leaders of the Government and of the opposition Parties. I believe there have been some elements of difficulty which have arisen from the fact that some rules were either misunderstood or applied unequally.

What in French, Mr. Speaker, would be referred to as "demi-mesures". I do not think that in this Chamber we can tolerate that when a parliamentary committee makes recommendations, Members only go along with what suits them and drop what does not.
This evening, there has been some discussion about the legislative committees. I believe there is a problem. We have 282 Members in the House, and two weeks ago I counted 51 committees including standing, legislative, special and joint committees, task forces and sub-committees; add to these the task forces of political parties that travel across the country and all the work that has to be done in committee and in the House. Members each have to do their share of a very impressive workload, something which I think is at times frustrating because we are not always able to work in the manner we would like and to see exactly where we are going.
Mr. Speaker, not long ago you sent me to England to see how legislative committees were handled over there. I appreciated this opportunity because I found that with 650 Members and a very impressive legislative menu, the people over there had managed to set up eight legislative committees, which they refer to as standing committees, and each committee receives the legislation which is sent by the House of Commons, and there is a line-up and people wait their turn to be heard. I think that is eminently sensible.
We did not do that. Every Wednesday, I sit down with the Government Whip and the New Democratic Party's Whip and we have to appoint Members to legislative committees, when the House has adopted a bill on first reading or the Member has presented a Private Member's Bill in his name. That is not
what was recommended by the Committee on Parliamentary Reform. Somebody failed to understand what the Committee's recommendation was and this caused some problems. We are now stuck with an incredible number of committees and that has caused problems as well.
The other question I wanted to raise-and I realize I don't have much time-concerns Ministers' comments or statements. Ministers' statements are usually made on very short notice, and the Official Opposition and the other opposition have the right to reply, but the time spent on these statements is made up at the end of the day. Sometimes this may cause problems. A statement may take five minutes or half an hour, and this time is added on at the end of the day.
The point 1 wanted to make, Mr. Speaker, and I think you know what I am referring to because I already brought this up two or three times this week, or at least in the last few days, and that is that the provisions of Standing Order 46(7) provide that normally, the hour set aside for Private Members' Business ... If I am a backbencher and I want to have an adjournment debate because I asked a question and was not satisfied with the reply, I have the right to ask for an adjournment debate, a late show.
I can request that a question be dated on the "Late Show", and at certain times it is allowed. Standing Order 46(7) says when there is a vote the "Late Show" shall not take place unless there has been a statement by a Minister and Standing Order 19(4) applies-then there is a "Late Show". Yesterday we had a typical example of that. I cannot understand the logic of that. I do not know who came up with that, that sometimes, when there is a Minister's statement of five minutes, we have "Late Shows", and other times when there is no statement there is no "Late Show". I do not understand that. Somebody must clarify for us some day why a private Member is entitled to a "Late Show" if a Minister makes a statement, in certain circumstances, and at other times he is not. This does not make sense, and these are the things we have to clarify. I hope the Government House Leader will take that into consideration when he comes in with his package, if he has one to present.
I just want to make a few comments during this opportunity we have at this time to address the question of reform. I have been here for 13 years, Mr. Speaker. Every time we have talked reform in this House we have had difficulties, because the opposition is too strong or the Government is afraid and we do not move. This time I think the Government has the proper atmosphere and the proper timing, and it should move. But, very importantly, we must be entirely satisfied that we have debated this question thoroughly.
Speaking for the members of my caucus, I do not think we can accept that some deal will be made somewhere, that it will come in a package at whatever time in the evening, and we will say we have agreed to these changes of our House rules. I
December 4, 1985

think the Government has to come in with a package, and that the package must be debated in this House as it is tonight. 1 think it is a matter of eloquence, Mr. Speaker. The speeches I have heard tonight have been very eloquent and very interesting. 1 really must say that I have been here for some years now and I have heard some very, very nice statements and some very good ideas put forth by Members.
The point I really want to make clear to the House Leader is, and I think his little distrust comes from his misunderstanding of this point, that we want debate. Tonight 10 minute speeches are too short. 1 would like to have put questions to the Member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath). I would like to have put questions to the Member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet). We could not do it because of our constraints tonight.
I hope that if the Government House Leader intends to come in with a package of new reforms, these reforms will be inspired by this committee work, and that indeed the Government will read it properly, digest it properly and come forth, not with half measures but with full measures. Surely it is time we moved on reform, and that we created that type of atmosphere in which we all participate in a debate-not a monologue as we see tonight. I think it is good, it is interesting, it is eloquent, but 1 would like to have some real debate with some Members of the House. Those of us who cannot attend all of these committees need to have this debate in the House. We have to be able to discuss with our colleagues in the House the pros and cons, for example, of electronic voting versus manual voting versus lobby voting versus a whole system of improving the way that we vote.
I would like to see us debate these questions at the appropriate time, and I leave it in the House Leader's hands to arrange that. I repeat that the trust is his to take and to go with, and we will certainly work with him in the interests of House reform.

subtopic: REFORM OF THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is a very interesting discussion we are having tonight. I do not believe it can be tainted by any acrimony or any accusation of political binding. It has been in effect a free-wheeling, freespeaking debate.
I think we are attacking in this debate tonight some symptoms which we cannot get at by the reforms that have been suggested in the remarks of the Member for Humber-Port au Port-St. Barbe (Mr. Tobin) and to the Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. Allmand). Their emphasis was not on the difficulty within the House, but rather was on the failure of the Parties concerned to allow input from backbenchers to obtain the consensus we are now seeking to obtain by parliamentary reform, when in fact what we need is an element of caucus reform which does in fact accommodate the opportunity for the individual to represent his policies, his principles, his own interests with Canada as a whole.
There has been some discussion as to what is a free vote and when should it occur. Let us suppose that we introduce into this House an opportunity for a free vote. Let us take some examples of legislation that has been dealt with in this House
Reform of the House of Commons of Commons since it has been my privilege to represent my constituents.
Let us assume for the moment that we adopted the pattern of the United States Government where there is in fact a free vote, in principle, although I submit to you that most Members are bound by the principles they have espoused in their own constituency, that they are as bound in their voting by their own constituencies or their own districts as is any Member of this House bound in his vote as a result of his association with the Party and the constituency which he represents. It is a myth that it is totally free. There are a few people with stature who can in effect vote freely to their hearts' content, who will be returned to the Congress or the Senate of the United States, but there are only a handful of people who really have at their disposal a totally free vote.
I am going to make a suggestion here tonight which will not be acceptable to a great many people. I may get ruled out of order by some, or they might wish I would be. We have a bicameral system, and if ever there was need for reform it is that we reintroduce the intent of the bicameral system which was brought in with Confederation. There is an opportunity for the Senate to be given Green Papers, White Papers- whatever papers-for study and reference. 1 can think of no better work than that done by the agricultural committee when it studied soil erosion and prepared a report. I think that is typical of what it could do, and what it should do. This would relieve this House of those onerous duties that are beyond the capacity of most Members. It has been pointed out many times by many speakers on all sides of the House that the overload of committee work, plus constituency work, does render us to a degree incapable of serving all the purposes for which we are here.
We have heard some talk about what should happen to private Bills. I have had a little experience in this area. Let us be honest about private Bills. Some private Bills are introduced on principle. I think the Hon. Member for Surrey-White Rock-North Delta (Mr. Friesen) who spoke earlier in the evening, espoused a principle in a Bill that he pursued for six years. I think it should have had the opportunity of a vote in this House-not a Party vote, not a vote on the whip at all.
I want to cite an example of a mischievous Bill which was introduced by one Ralph Ferguson who later became the Hon. Ralph Ferguson and the Minsiter of Agriculture. If ever there was a Bill intended to incite discontent in this nation it was that private Bill.
How then, Mr. Speaker, do we delineate between the mischievous Bills and those of principle which should have consideration? To say that private Bills should automatically be accepted by this House and go to committee is saying that every mischievous act of every mischievous Member, and there are many of us here who could be mischievous in opposition or in Government, should indeed be referred to committee for study. The Bill introduced by the Hon. Ralph Ferguson is an example of why, under no circumstances, should there be a carte blanche for private Bills to hit committee or the House in

December 4, 1985
Reform of the House of Commons
debate. How then do we sort out the mischievous from the sincere in principle?
1 say to the Hon. Member for Surrey-White Rock-North Delta, through you, Mr. Speaker, that his is an honourable case, but all cases are not honourable. How many of us have participated in the preparation of private Bills which were intended to be mischievous and embarrassing to the Government? That was their purpose and there is no question about that.
Before I arrived in Ottawa as a Member of Parliament I had the privilege of sitting in a provincial Government. I think that Government had the answer to some of the problems which have been voiced directly and indirectly or insinuated. That Government allowed Party members the opportunity to participate and influence the consensus within their own Party and before virtually every piece of legislation was introduced in the House it was vetted in principle before the caucus or the caucus committee. That would remove a great many of the problems which have been voiced here. But it has not been the principle of the executive of the Party, let alone the executive of the Government, to vet its policies, legislation or principles before its own caucus or caucus committee with a particular concern of interest.
If a free vote had been introduced I believe there are two or three pieces of legislation which the Members from the Atlantic provinces would have rejected out of hand during the last Government. I do not see any other Maritime Members here. Oh, there is one at the far distant corner of the House, the Hon. Member for Annapolis Valley-Hants (Mr. Nowlan), and there is one behind me from Prince Edward Island.
The health Bill introduced by the then Minister, Madame Begin, was one which deprived Atlantic Canada of badly needed money by virtue of its phraseology. Had the Atlantic region had a free vote in the House the Government of the day could not have passed that Bill in the form in which it did. Therein lies the difficulty of an area getting consensus in its own caucus, because had that area been able to achieve consensus and express the needs of Atlantic Canada that Bill would never have appeared in the House as it did.
One could go further than that and refer to certain pieces of legislation related, for example, to the fishing industry, a very major item in Atlantic Canada. The Member for Southwest Nova and I moved and seconded a motion for information in the fisheries committee. The results of that motion never came forward because the then Miniser of Fisheries blocked the information we requested. We should indeed explore what information can be obtained in committee. There is reform required.
However, let us not consider that we are part of a republican system. Before we go too far with the reform of the Hosue we must consider whether we are indeed trying to adopt republican principles in a British parliamentary system, there is room for changes. The Auditor General was mentioned tonight, and, as he said, it is impossible for a self-respecting member of the
Committee on Pubic Accounts to nail down the information which gives rise to the allegations of the Auditor General. He made a charge with regard to the Dairy Commission of Canada. Unless we had a leaker within the Dairy Commission-one who would give us confidential information-we could not ask the right questions to learn why he made the charge, who was the culprit, and who should be dismissed. The Act, as it presently exists, does not serve the House of Commons or Canada.
These are areas which require reform, Mr. Speaker. I thank you for the opportunity to speak on this debate. However, let us not dream that we are a republican system-we are not. Until we change the minds of the Opposition Parties, the people, and the press, the free vote will depict split Parties, whether NDP, Liberal or Conservative. Let us face reality.

Mr. Speaker, I really had not intended to say anything tonight, I had not even intended to be here, but I happened to walk into the parliamentary lobby and, not only did the sandwiches look good, the debate on TV was excellent. I am very glad I stayed. I join with other Members to say that it has been a most enjoyable and worthwhile session. We must have more of them.
I would just like to add a couple of things which I do not think have been covered. I also want to say something for my colleague, the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy), who wanted me to mention one point he did not have time to raise. He feels that we should have an on-going review of this institution and that once a year we should have an open session such as this to allow people to speak in a very non-partisan way and to share feelings, ideas, and inspirations.
One of the things which bothers me, and probably bothers most Members of Parliament, is the perception that most people have of politicians. I am sure there are many reasons for this. Most of the politicians whom I see here day after day work very, very hard and are pretty serious minded. We do not always think alike, but that is part of the system as well. However, the perception of the public seems to be that we are pretty irrelevant, perhaps opportunistic, and somewhat shallow and manipulative. I must say that I do not find that. I think we are a pretty noble bunch, on the whole.
I think that we need to show this kind of a session to the public occasionally. This is kind of an in-House meeting that we are having tonight. I do not imagine many viewers in the outside world are as interested in parliamentary reform as we are. However, surely there is some way in which we can get this kind of mood projected into some of our other sessions so that the public will see us a little differently. So many of the people I speak with think that Question Period is just a squabble. Every time I return to Ottawa my niece asks if I am going back to the "funny farm". I find that it is people who enjoy theatre and politics who really enjoy Question Period. An awful lot of people do not understand what we are getting at. Perhaps the commentators on TV could help us to explain that the Opposition has an important role to play in democracy by criticizing. Many people do not understand that. We must try to change perceptions a bit.
December 4, 1985

The point I really want to make has to do with the role of Members of Parliament other than in the House. I always feel that my first responsibility is to represent my constituency, to create a two-way flow between Ottawa and my constituents and make Government and Parliament come alive. 1 am wondering why the Committee on Parliamentary Reform did not deal with any of the responsibilities we have and the reforms that are needed in our roles in the constituencies. I imagine it did not have enough time.
We all tend to say that our ridings are all different; some are close to Ottawa, some are very distant, some are rural, and some are urban. I personally feel that we do not have enough common standards to follow. I would like to mention two or three things.
I think we would all agree that the MP in the local constituency office has a responsibility to provide accurate information about federal programs and legislation. Yet we do not always have the necessary tools to do this. 1 would like to have a regular report on what is going on in the House that we could make available to our constituents. We all do our own things in our householders which are slanted to our own perspectives. However, I think that something quite factual and direct is needed. I have had ethnic groups in particular asking for this. I think we could improve our information systems. I do not know what it is like in the riding offices of other Members. However, it is often very difficult to keep an effective information system operating when being visited by many constituents. I believe that system could be standardized to a greater extent.
I believe most Members would agree that Members and their staff in those offices should be available to act as ombudspersons. We have a problem-solving role to play, particularly with respect to federal issues. But we are also advocates for citizens and have a responsibility to bring the problems of our constituents to the attention of the bureaucracies. Of course, we must also represent our constituencies in the House.
1 am not sure that all Members of Parliament have set schedules for the public to visit their constituency offices in order to see their Members. I realize that it is very difficult for Members who live on the West Coast to make sure that they can be at the office. One is often called back for votes and other matters. However, if we are going to make reforms in this area, perhaps we could set a standard.
For those of us who come from a distance, we can work much more efficiently by spending one week during a month in our riding. One can be available and accomplish much more, rather than recycling jet lag every two or three days. I suggest most Members would agree with such a procedure.
1 believe there should be a general procedure by which Members have a monthly accountability session for their constituents.
Another question concerns how our constituency offices are used. I believe that, because my constituency office is paid for
Reform of the House of Commons by the taxpayer, it should be available to be used almost as a community resource, provided it is in a non-partisan way. There may be ways in which we can relate to different community organizations. For instance, perhaps some offices could provide help with income tax matters, using volunteers. 1 recall having a UFFI information service from my office. It is a public office and I believe it should be available for community use.
Those are some of the questions that occurred to me. However, 1 am essentially suggesting that at some point this might be another chapter of the reform book. Again, I want to congratulate everyone who has done so much work for us.

One of the reasons 1 have not spoken frequently is that all too often these debates in the House are meaningless because Members are simply repeating what has been said by others. It is part of a game that is played between both sides of the House, and I do not like to participate in that game too often. However, this debate tonight is altogether different.
First, 1 want to congratulate the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Hnatyshyn) for allowing this debate to take place, as well as to congratulate the House Leaders of the opposition Parties for co-operating and allowing this debate to be held.

One is the role of private Members and the other is the role of standing committees. I am sure that when all of us come here in the first year we are rather impressed, but certainly dismayed by the lack of a role for the private Member. Many of our colleagues have spoken about that tonight.
I have been particularly impressed by that problem in the last year when we had a great influx of approximately 140 new private Members. I am deeply concerned about the degree of disillusion that I see among some of the very bright young Members in the House over the lack of opportunity they have to fulfil some of the aspirations they brought with them from their ridings. Perhaps those Members from both sides of the House feel that they do not have the opportunity to express themselves and be heard in an effective way by the powers that be. I have had the privilege of serving on both sides of the House and appreciate the problems faced by Members from both sides.
Let me compliment the Hon. Member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath). He is one of the veterans in the House and, in being chosen as chairman of this special committee, has been able to exercise his experience over the years in helping to

Reform of the House of Commons
formulate some of these new recommendations. He and his committee are to be congratulated.
The Hon. Member for Vancouver East (Ms. Mitchell) suggested that perhaps the public was not too interested in what is being said here tonight. I do not believe that is true. Many of my more concerned constituents express extreme dismay when they learn that I come to the House to vote on an issue without even knowing what the vote is about. One simply comes in and follows the leader. As a private Member, one is not challenged to think about an issue; we can survive very adequately by voting as we are told by our House Leader. One of the points that I believe the Hon. Member for St. John's East and his committee is attempting to make, and which I believe the Government in fairness is trying to recognize, is that we have a right to be adequately heard. I commend the committee on its attempt to allow a so-called free vote in the House, recognizing that there must be votes of confidence on certain issues.
1 also recognize the caveat expressed by the Hon. Member for Carleton-Charlotte (Mr. McCain) that we do not want to have a presidential system here. However, I believe that within the parliamentary system as we know it there is room for more involvement by private Members than we have had heretofor.
I am impressed by the committee's suggestion for the role of private Members in standing committees, including that there be seven Members on the committee, without a parliamentary secretary. I must admit that I have not given much study to that suggestion, but 1 like the idea and hope that the President of the Privy Council and his colleagues will reconsider their move to make it an eight-member committee.
It has occurred to me over the years, as it has to many of my colleagues, that private Members have very little opportunity to effectively influence legislation that goes through the House. Let us assume that the executive branch knew that it would have to gain individual support from Members on all sides of the House when bringing in legislation. If that had happened when the Liberals were in power there would not have been some of the bad legislation we have seen over those years. The same is true now. If we have not already done so, our Government may introduce bad legislation, because most government supporters feel obliged to support a government Bill. I hope there will be more opportunity for private Members to have input before legislation has been drafted by the Government.

Without taking up more time of the House, let me say that I commend the committee, and its Chairman in particular. I hope the Government will see fit, in co-operation with the opposition Parties, to make some appropriate changes to the House which are long overdue.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in the debate tonight. I want to start by complimenting the Hon. Member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) on his excellent work in reform of the House of Commons and on his contributions to this area in the past, as I think all other members of that committee merit praise for trying to make Parliament work better.
It is not often that we have occasion to participate in an excellent debate, as is the case tonight, in a manner which is far less partisan than is sometimes the case. I have been known to have been partisan on rare occasions myself, but I am very pleased to participate in this debate tonight without any partisan overtones. At least, I hope not to inject any of those overtones into my remarks.
One matter I should like to raise with the House concerns possible changes to Private Members' Hour. I had the honour and privilege of being elected at the municipal, provincial and federal levels. When I was in the Ontario legislature, 1 was very fond of the process by which it dealt with Private Members' Business.
In this House, Private Members' Business only lasts one hour, and it is toward the end of the day. In my view the present process here is nothing short of a glorified adjournment debate. When Private Members' Hour comes along everyone leaves. Everyone knows that there will not be a vote at the end. In fact, what we have is an adjournment debate which lasts an hour and 30 minutes instead of a 30 minute adjournment debate. I think that is very unfortunate.
The process in the Ontario Legislative Assembly-and 1 believe it still exists-was better than the one we have here. First, the debate lasted all afternoon, one day a week. There was a very good exchange in which four or five Members from each political Party participated. Also there was no such thing as talking out a Bill. At the end of the day there was a vote. Every Wednesday afternoon at 5.50 o'clock there was a vote. There actually had to be a conscious effort on the part of someone to defeat the Bill, if that was the case. It made for a very interesting afternoon. Often we saw Government Members voting with the Opposition and Opposition Members voting with the Government against one of their own colleagues, and so forth. It was truly a Private Members' Hour in that sense. There was no attempt at trying to be polite and speaking in favour of a colleague's Bill when one was really trying to talk it out, because the whole thing was an embarrassment or something like that. Sometimes this happens in the debates during Private Members' Hour in the House.
December 4, 1985

I note that good improvements are listed in the "McGrath" report, but I do not think that they go far enough. I hope we will take further steps to totally remove the partisan aspect. For instance, in that respect we could have no Whips at voting time. We could probably advocate that the Whips absent themselves from the House during the vote. Perhaps it would be symbolic, but it would be a good way of doing it. In the Ontario House, the Whips voted but they did not actually salute the Speaker prior to the vote in Private Members' Hour. In any case, I believe it would be an improvement over the system we now have.
1 should like to speak briefly about the broadcasting of the House of Commons. The suggestion of televising parliamentary committees is not the way we should be going. I know that many people are in favour of it, but I tend to disagree. If we want to improve the availibility or the opportunity for Canadians to see their Parliament, we should use what we now have. In other words, often 6.20 p.m. or 6.30 p.m. when the House adjourns we could rebroadcast the House of Commons in the evening; we have the channel, and we have the facilities. We have everything. There is no reason that we could not repeat the process. Public opinion polls and surveys indicate that the majority of people watching the proceedings of the House of Commons are senior citizens. Why is that? It is because they are the ones who are at home in the daytime when we are on. Why not replay it at night when most people who work during the daytime can see it?
I should like to address the issue of the Clerk of the House. Of course I support the recommendations of the McGrath committee in that regard. In part, the report reads:
The role of the Clerk of the House of Commons should be one of leadership and inspiration for all employees of the House. For this reason the Clerk of the House must be, and be seen to be, the principal permanent officer of the House, accountable to it, and its bodies, for operations of the House of Commons.
As the McGrath committee indicated, the most senior officer under your jurisdiction, Mr. Speaker, should be the Clerk. There should be only the Clerk with that level of importance relative to the staff of the House of Commons. For one thing, it would enhance the powers of Members of the House-and the McGrath committee agrees with that-in the sense that the principal officer who is concerned with services offered to Members is actually in the House of Commons, where Members can see that principal officer, where Members can easily dialogue with that principal officer, and where Members can easily explain to that principal officer when an ongoing process is not beneficial to Members of Parliament in general, or specifically to an individual Member. There has been considerable discussion back and forth, through previous Speakers and so forth, on this issue. However, I think the McGrath committee goes in the right direction on that recommendation. It is one toward which we should move swiftly.
I should like to speak briefly about Order in Council appointments. Of course we are aware of the recommendations in the McGrath report which basically indicated that some 1,900 appointments should be available for review and that some 64 appointments should be subject to the veto of the House. In other words, the House should have a veto over the
Reform of the House of Commons appointment of officers of the House-the Clerk, the Auditor General and so forth. Because those people are officers of the House, I think that is the right way. I do not think there should be a veto over all political appointments. The mere process of recommending is the right way to go. However, in order for the process to work, the first thing we must do is put it into effect. Of course we have not done that yet, even though there has been a stated intent on the part of the Government in that regard. I think we should be moving in that area.
I should like to deal very quickly with the issue of office space for Members of Parliament. It has been the case in the past with previous Governments, and it is the case now with the present Government, that we see cabinet Ministers hogging space in the Centre Block of the Parliament Buildings. I do not say that in a partisan way, because the situation was the same before. It is not right that a cabinet Minister who uses his or her office here for an hour a day should have eight rooms. Many times there are not even eight people in those eight rooms. At the same time I have, as do other private Members, two rooms in the Centre Block. Many times there are four permanent people there, myself and three staff, and some days there are two temporaries. There are actually six or seven people in those two small rooms in Centre Block. The Board of Health would kick us out if it had any jurisdiction over it. That is not right. We should do something in the very near future to reallocate space so that private Members can have a lot of room.
Looking at previous experience, for example in the Ontario House, cabinet Ministers do not have offices in the building at Queen's Park, but in the surrounding buildings. The Premier and Deputy Premier are the only two members of the executive council who have offices in the Parliament building. The others do not.
I bring those remarks to your attention, Mr. Speaker. I thank the House for listening. Again I would like to compliment all Members for the very good and fruitful debate we have had tonight.

The Hon. Member says "hear, hear". If he would listen, he might learn something. The Parliament in Canada is different from any other Parliament in the British parliamentary system. Our Parliament is a true definition of the word, coming from the French word parler, to speak. If you use the general term "legislature", which is a general term for all Parliaments under the system to which we belong, you would have to say that the British Parliament is a legislature. They legislate. Over the years we have developed a custom of really being a Parliament, to speak.
If you look at the British system and the Canadian system, you find that they have evolved differently. The Australian system and other systems have evolved to meet their own needs. In the British Parliament, there is no seat for you. There are not enough seats for all the Members. Here you take your seat and be part of Parliament and speak. Perhaps there's nothing left of a resemblance between the Canadian Parliament and any of the other so-called Parliaments in the British parliamentary system.
In changing the rules, I am willing to bet that you cannot find one legislature under the British parliamentary system that changed its rules to any degree through a committee of that Parliament. It would be a joke to go to the British Parliament and say that you have a committee of the House to change its rules. The way they change their rule is by having the academics, the outside people who are not a part of the parliamentary system, do that. They deride us as a Parliament in saying that this is a cumbersome system, a system in which nothing can be done. Surely Parliament is first and foremost a legislature. In practically all of the legislatures, a motion comes to a vote at the end of the sitting day.
The systems have evolved and you cannot compare one system to the other. To my knowledge, changes that have been made in other legislatures under the British parliamentary system have evolved in such a way that something else has taken the place of Parliament as we know it today. When looking at changes in our parliamentary system, perhaps we can borrow something from what these other legislatures have done. This brings me to the reason for my standing here today.
Given the fact that the only similarity we have is that the Opposition and the Government are two sword-lengths apart, that you are not allowed to lean on the rail, and you are not allowed to wear a hat in the gallery, perhaps we can borrow something from their committee structure. In the British Parliament, a member of the Government or a member of the Opposition are both equal the way the custom has evolved. The Speaker does not recognize a member of the Official Opposition, then the Opposition, and then get around to a government back-bencher. It goes right and left, right and left.
Something else that is completely different is that a Member has to give notice of a question. That is somewhat distorted because you can give any kind of notice that has
something to do with your question. Government Members, who have no seat stand up as a matter of custom and adamantly criticize their own Government. That is a custom.
My point can perhaps best be described by referring to the chairman of this committee, the Hon. Member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath). Every Member in this Chamber is frustrated. He has a great interest in a particular subject. For example, the Hon. Member for St. John's East has a great interest in search and rescue, as we all know. Everybody has a particular area of great interest which affects the people in their riding and their province. As things now stand, even with the suggested changes, their aspirations will never come to pass unless we have committees which can originate their own terms of reference totally to address immediate and long-term problems.
It does not matter whether the committees are called standing committees or select committees. I believe that could be borrowed from the British parliamentary system. We do not have rules whereby the media cannot tape record the proceedings or that do not allow for television cameras. Committees could be made the forefront of Parliament. 1 do not think Parliament would be robbed of anything other than to decrease the parler part of Parliament. It would decrease the amount of speeches given and the time spent in Parliament. Parliament would automatically adjust its time schedule.
That would require a great sacrifice on the part of the Government. It would require the Government to say to the committees that when something comes up, whether it be search and rescue tonight or tomorrow "buffalogate", a committee can at a moment's notice investigate that matter and have the power to call whomever it wishes before the committee and get the answers to both immediate and long-term problems, such as search and rescue in which the Hon. Member for St. John's East is so greatly interested. It would provide a forum in which the answers would eventually be given. If the Government would not want to make changes, it would certainly be embarrassed into making changes.
That is my contribution tonight. I could go on for hours on this matter. As you know, Mr. Speaker, I am perhaps the only former Clerk of a provincial legislature to sit in the federal House of Commons.

notes into an orderly form so that I could have developed my speech in a logical fashion. However, I am not known to do that. Therefore, I come now to the heart of the whole situation.

I do not usually give him compliments because, quite frankly, I find I usually take a different stance from the Hon. Member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath). However, regarding his leadership of the reform committee that has produced the first, second and third reports which are the reasons why we are here tonight, I would like to give him, as well as the entire committee, my personal compliments.
I do not want to repeat this too many times, but 1 used to sit here listening to the then right hon. gentleman for Prince Albert who had been here longer than I. He used to talk about Parliament and I am going to talk about Parliament. One of the few reasons I want to stay here is to make sure that this institution is fundamentally reformed to reflect the body of opinion of Members of Parliament and is not just rubber stamping things that come from on high. That is the carrot in the sunrise that will encourage me to run again.
The Hon. Member for Gander-Twillingate, whom 1 respect, has had an interesting political history. He is one of the few and at the moment the only former Clerk of a legislative assembly to be a Member of the House. He then warped the political label, but I do not care about labels.
Since we come to the House of Commons to vote on Bills that affect Canadians at large, we have to move to a mutation between a congressional and a parliamentary system. Unless Members of Parliament can rise in the House or contribute in committee on issues that affect their constituents or their own opinions without simply rubber stamping Bills, then this place is a charade.
I compliment the Hon. Member for Humber-Port-au-Port-St. Barbe (Mr. Tobin) who talked a little about the words of a former Prime Minister who said that we are nobodies when we are 50 feet away from the House and somebodies when we are here. The 140-odd brand new Members of the House came here with such excitement, enthusiasm and idealism. Over a period of perhaps six months or a year, they found out that they are fighting the same parliamentary procedure that was the procedure at the time of Sir John A. Macdonald. Of course he was our first Prime Minister in 1867.
You know, Mr. Speaker, because you are relatively new to the chair and you are certainly relatively new to Parliament, as a defanged veteran, that you went through the depression and frustration of these 140 brand new Members who are representing all parts of the country. They came here thinking that they would change things and found out that they were in the strait-jacket of Sir John A. Macdonald.
The one thing 1 love about the McGrath report is its potential for the independence of Members. This independence is not to defeat Governments. I agree with my hon. friend
Reform of the House of Commons
for-I know him better as George but 1 have to call him the Hon. Member for Gander-Twillingate. When I think of Twil-lingate, I think of Pickersgill. He was one of the Hon. Member's predecessors. There have been too many Members. 1 am an old Member as this caucus of mine thinks. Frankly, though, in terms of parliamentary reform I am one of the youngest Members it will ever see.
What these new Members do not understand is what reform really is. Unless we can get in the Chamber and committees the right of Members to represent their constituents, regions and own consciences independently, then 1 would agree with the former Prime Minister who said that we are nobodies, but 1 would say that we are nobodies both inside or outside the House. We can change that around, and we have to change it around.
The mutation system to which I referred must apply to committees and we are trying to do that on an experimental basis in the Transport Committee in which I am privileged to be a participant. We are getting some expert information on issues of the day and we have to do that in a more organized way. Members of the House must come here to speak on Bills.
The matter is not too complicated. I would like this Government to continue in office for another 44 years. 1 sat in Opposition for 20 years and I do not want to switch back.
There are easy ways to effect reform. A Bill can be drafted by the bureaucrats and put forward by the Minister which may not find a majority vote in the House. This is not in the McGrath report but it is the easiest thing in the world. Sometimes the easy things are like Newton's Law. When something falls down, it means that gravity pulls it down. If we wanted to assess that like Einstein, we would have had an Einstein theory on why the apple fell to the ground, or why two feathers fell from the Tower of Pisa at the same rate. I do not want to deal with complicated matters like that.
Regarding parliamentary procedure, we must have the licence, liberty and independence of parliamentary debate. It will take time to happen. The fact that a Bill does not command a majority in the House of Commons simply means that it is sent back to the bureaucratic catacombs to be redrafted, after which it then gets the consent of the House. When a Government Bill goes down to defeat, I hope that in my lifetime as a parliamentarian there will be a procedure whereby, without any debate, the Speaker would ask if the Government has lost the confidence of the House. Without any hesitation or even a burp, the votes would return saying that the Bill was defeated but the Government had not lost the confidence of the House. It would be a clear message to send back to the bureaucracy and the ministry that the Bill be redrafted to command the respect and the vote of Members of the House of Commons.

Mr. Speaker, I must say that in looking at the clock I can see that it is nearly 11 o'clock and I know that I am competing with the national news. At this point in time I know what most of the ears of the nation are tuned into. However, it is still important for me to enter this debate.
What the debate and the underlying question with regard to it mean to me has to do with democracy in the sense of the distribution of power between the private and public arena. Most citizens are familiar with the fact that, by and large, civil servants and bureaucrats run the Government. It is civil servants and bureaucrats who largely frustrate the people we represent. Thus, reform of the House of Commons has to do not just with updating some quaint institution which is of interest only to the few of us who happen to be elected here and have the duty to serve here, but it is something which is central to the democratic life of the country.
As a Member of Parliament who has been here for a few years, but not that many, one thing I find shocking about this place is the lack of financial control which the House has over public expenditures. Parliament was bom out of the recognition that the executive, the people who run the country and spend taxpayers' money, had to be accountable. If there is one thing that this place demonstrates it is the lack of accountability with regard to the expenditure of public dollars. Any real reform of Parliament has to increase accountability in terms of financial matters. It is not enough to have the Auditor General issue a report to Parliament once a year which is discussed in Question Period for one, two or three days and is then forgotten. We have to find some means, some mechanism, by which to examine in a thorough way the expenditures which are authorized by the House.
It is not enough to have just one committee, such as the Public Accounts Committee, perform such a function. All Members of Parliament and all committees of Parliament should be involved in a thorough analysis with respect to public spending. In today's political and social climate if we are to find the money which is necessary to meet the many needs of our constituents, then we have to demand a new excellence in public spending. We have to demonstrate to bureaucrats that as parliamentarians we will not put up with the waste of public dollars. We must ensure that public dollars are spent wisely and effectively. Any real parliamentary reform should first address the issue of financial accountability-
I would now like to address another area of parliamentary reform which interests me. It has to do with Order in Council appointments. Given the fact that bureaucrats have such a stranglehold on public power in the country, it seems to me we should find a way to subject senior bureaucrats, Deputy Ministers, presidents of Crown corporations and, since the introduction of the Charter of Rights I would say Supreme Court Justices, to some sort of public review as a part of the nomination process before they are finally put into their ultimate positions. These are people who carry real power in our society. They are the ones who make the real decisions. Their views and values should be examined in a public forum before they are given our blessing and those high positions. 1 would like to see us find a way for Order in Council appointments to be reviewed before the appointments are made. There is another function of the House to which we should pay more attention. That is the matter of petitions. With respect to the debate concerning family allowances and the debate on pensions, petitions played a significant role in the House. Petitions offer an opportunity for public input into the policy-making process. If petitions could come to this place asking specific questions of the executive, which Government Departments would have to answer in writing to the petitioners, then perhaps we could find a way for the public to have a more significant input into this place and into public policy.
The question of legislation in terms of Parliamentary reform has received a fair amount of comment. Primarily, it has been in terms of the freedom of the private Member to vote this way
December 4, 1985

or that following his or her own conscience. 1 believe there is another aspect of legislation which has to do not only with our individual values but our collective values. As members of different political Parties there should be a way by which we could allow a real and significant impact on the legislation which comes before the House and the way in which it is drafted. Through our collective values, having been elected to this place, we should find a way by which we could have a greater impact upon the type of legislation which finally passes through the House.
1 know that there is a negotiation process in this respect which goes on among House Leaders. Surely that process could be made more meaningful and could be handled in a way by which legislation would actually be amended, changed and improved upon, which could become a part of our policymaking and political process.
In conclusion, it seems to me that the question of parliamentary reform, whether it concerns financial matters, appointments of senior bureaucrats, public input or the type of legislation which is proposed by the House, is about democracy. It is about the private and public distribution of power. As an elected Member of Parliament, my commitment is to public power rather than private power. If we are going to have significant reform in this place, we have to bring decisions made by Government into a public forum. That really means bringing a lot of the decisions which are made by permanent members of the Civil Service into some forum for review by elected officials. The most important decisions which must be brought in for review are the financial decisions.
As 1 have said, 1 welcome the opportunity to say a few words in this debate about parliamentary reform. I must say that if parliamentary reform is to be significant, then it has to impact, first, on how public dollars are spent. Unless we can raise the level at which we examine public dollars, and unless we can reach a new attitude with regard to the expenditure of public dollars, we will not have the resources to meet the needs of our citizens.
