speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened at the opening of this debate to the very learned and carefully crafted remarks of the Hon. Member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath). I feel a little humble with my few notes here in winding up the debate. I know that the Hon. Member for St. John's East was, and has been, totally wrapped up in the issue of reform of the House for a number of years. He sat as a Member from the Conservative caucus on the Lefebvre Committee, along with some other Hon. Members, and he contributed then, as he has contributed tremendously to this particular report.
History has shown us the evolution of the House of Commons. Some of us who have been in Parliament a little longer than others have watched it grow and change. Yet it is fair to say that many of the rules which were put in place by Sir John A. Macdonald are still with us. It is interesting to me that some of the changes which we recommended in our speeches
Reform of the House of Commons this evening were some of the things I would have liked to have seen discussed at a little more length.
In looking at the index of our last report, I see such things as the disciplinary powers of the Chair and I think we could spend a great deal of time on that, given some of the unruliness in the House over these past few months. I look at things such as the reorganization of Private Members' Business. I have heard other Hon. Members comment on that at length and I do not intend to go into it.
A good deal of time was spent on the prayer in committee, as well as a good deal of time spent on many other items. I think there is a need for change there. Perhaps reports from official parliamentary delegations would do away with articles like the one in the weekend Citizen about the travels of Members of Parliament around the world. Perhaps if we had those reports in place at least some of the press who now know, but who like to print differently, would understand as well as know why those trips take place.
I could speak about all of the various things which took place in committee but I want to take a moment to talk about the committee system and tell you, Mr. Speaker, that I am concerned that right now there is a great deal of criticism of the new legislative committee system. I believe we all have to be very careful and give that idea a good try. 1 know that as of today there is at least one Bill which is now going to be referred to a Standing Committee instead of a legislative committee. That concerns me. We have only had the legislative committee in place for a very short time and already we are short-circuiting it. I am concerned because the Hon. Member for St. John's East made the point that those of us who sat on the committee had an aggregate of about 100 years of parliamentary experience. I would hate to think that that much experience, having put some of these ideas in place, would be erased much too soon.
I would like to say again in my very brief remarks that when the chairman of the task force, the Hon. Member for St. John's East, said that there were no heated partisan exchanges in the committee, he was absolutely right. However, there were heated exchanges. They were not partisan but there were a number of heated exchanges. I am going to take about a minute and put on record, as I did on the 26th of this month in a Private Members' Bill, brief notice that I have a major disagreement with the report when it deals with the administration of the House of Commons. I have, perhaps, spent more time dealing with the administration of the House of Commons than most of my colleagues and I am sure that they get tired and fed up to the teeth hearing me talk about it. But, having been that close to it, I think I can say with some authority that the system we now have in place, the system which has been in place in other major western Parliaments for many years, is a system to which we must adhere if we are to retain the supremacy of Parliament and if we are to retain for Members of Parliament those services which they need and desire. I suggest that to go back to the old ways would get us into a great deal of trouble.

December 4, 1985
Reform of the House of Commons
I could go on at great length about the many services which we have received as a result of the administration of the House of Commons and which have been in place effectively for five or six years. I would like to take a moment and compliment you, Mr. Speaker, for having had the courage to broadcast our Question Period to 22 million Americans last week. It seems to me that to have taken that step required a great deal of courage. To have the temerity to put our happenings over American television must have taken a great deal of thought. I could go on about that but, if I did, I am sure that some of my colleagues would want to hang me with the telephone wires which have been causing them all so much trouble this last little while, and I know they would not really want to do that.
1 would like to say one other thing. At the table this evening were two of the staff who served us very well, and added to the 100 years of service which members of the committee had. The staff had a huge number of years. They served us with patience and willingness to put up with us and a willingness, where necessary, to argue for things they saw that we might not have seen. 1 want to give them a pat on the back as well.
I am proud to have participated in this particular task force. Hon. Members of the House must look at what we have put before them and understand that, whether they like it or not, we put it before them with the highest expectations, after giving it the most serious consideration, discussion, thought and argument. Nothing was put in that report lightly or frivolously, and as I said before there are parts of the report with which I disagreed. Nothing was put in that report without all of us putting a great deal of thought and effort into it. I would ask the House to give it a good try. Perhaps in a year or two years from now it may be necessary to appoint another similar task force to clean up some of the things we missed. The Hon. Member for St. John's East made the point to the Government House Leader this evening that in retrospect he saw a couple of items he would have liked to have changed, and there will be others. We did try, and tried hard, and 1 ask the House to give it every opportunity to work. If, down the road, the House thinks there needs to be a change, at least give us credit for doing what we could.

subtopic: REFORM OF THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it was really a pleasure for me to be able to participate in this debate at this hour. It is somewhat late, but Members are still here and I think they might listen to a new Member who has comments to make on his experience in this House of Commons.
As I came here I had some expectations that we were going to produce something positive for our country. We have been doing pretty well in certain areas, but in others we can formulate criticism. That criticism is that as a Member of Parliament one has very little input into legislation. As the Hon. Member for Annapolis Valley-Hants (Mr. Nowlan) said, we are just rubber-stamping most of the legislation that is brought in through the Departments. The legislation is drafted by bureaucrats, and brought to a Minister, whether it is good or bad. If the Minister is weak he accepts that legislation and
brings it to the House. Then we have to vote on it, whether we like it or not. I think this is the problem. This is the fundamental problem that we have to address.
Among the different systems in the world there is a system that exists in the United States where they have a separation of the executive branch and the legislative branch. If a Democratic Congressman is elected he can still vote with the Republicans, and if their President is a Republican he can still vote for that President on certain legislation. It does not mean that he is against his own Party. He votes for what he believes his constituents want. This is a fundamental point.
Our Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) said the other day in the House, looking at the Opposition: "You are just trained seals". But I was sitting on the opposite side and I looked at the members of the Government and they were all applauding. The Member beside me said: "Look at those trained seals." Those are maybe not nice words but this reflects reality. [Translation]
Mr. Speaker, perhaps 1 should continue in French. In my opinion, there has been very little debate this evening in the other official language of the country. We have quite a few new Members from Quebec. Those Members can contribute a lot to the democratic system of our great country. The only thing is they have to feel they are part of this great assembly which is the Parliament of Canada.
There was an election in Quebec two days ago. Unfortunately, I must say that the Conservative Party was not strongly represented in that election. It is really too bad, because democracy means more that the immediate vote or the immediate result. A great Party like the Progressive Conservative Party of Canada should have taken part in that debate in the Province of Quebec. It left the road clear for the Quebec Liberal Party and the Parti quebecois. That is how we as a national Party came to be left out of that great debate in the Province of Quebec. This is to indicate that, as parliamentarians, we do not act freely. It is because the national Party had decided it would not be advisable to get involved in a provincial election that the federal Conservative Party refrained from supporting a provincial Party, the Conservative Party, and this is how it is not now represented in a province which will strongly influence the future of Canada.
This, Mr. Speaker, is perhaps . . . You will be wondering why I am talking about this, but 1 am doing it because a debate must be open, in Parliament we must be able to express ideas, try to sell them, debate them. Through the process of debate we reach conclusions which are good for the country. [English]
Mr. Speaker, I would like to conclude by saying that we have made progress in this Parliament. We have brought in some reforms, but those reforms do not go far enough. 1 would like to see that we are able to vote against the Government and that the Government is not defeated because of that. If we move in that direction we are going to help democracy and help our nation.
December 4, 1985

I think it is fair to say that in the last election campaign all three Parties promised parliamentary reform.
